☸️ Kubernetes CKA — Certified Kubernetes Administrator

The Complete, Self-Contained Mastery Guide

From total beginner to CKA-certified administrator — and beyond. Every concept is built on the easypj Django project (jobpost app, PostgreSQL), aligned to the official 2025 CKA syllabus and packed with diagrams, labs, and real-world Day-2 operations.

🟢 Beginner-Friendly ☸️ Kubernetes v1.31+ 🐍 Django · easypj / jobpost 📚 14 Parts · 45 Chapters 🎯 2025 Syllabus · 100% Coverage 📋 12 Appendices

👋 Welcome. This is a complete, self-contained path from "what is a container?" to CKA-certified administrator — and the real-world operations beyond the exam. You never need another doc, blog, book, or video.

Everything is taught on one real app, easypj (a Django jobpost project on PostgreSQL): you'll containerize it, deploy it, scale it, secure it, break it, fix it, and ship it. Aligned 100% to the official 2025 CKA syllabus. Use the ☰ sidebar to jump anywhere.

🟢 Part 1 · Foundations

Think Like Kubernetes

Chapters 1–4 · Beginner · "What is all this, and why?"

Before you can administer a cluster, you have to be able to see it in your head. Part 1 builds that picture from nothing: why Kubernetes exists, what a container actually is, the machines and brains that make up a cluster, and the handful of objects you'll touch every single day. Every abstraction is anchored on easypj so it has a face.

🎯 What you'll be able to do by the end: explain the control-plane / worker split, draw how kubectl apply turns YAML into a running easypj pod, and identify what every object in a manifest does — all without having installed a thing yet.
How the chapters fit — the Part 1 mental model
   Ch 1 — WHY            Ch 2 — HOW                 Ch 3 — WHERE
   the problem    ─────▶ the unit K8s runs   ─────▶ the machines & brains
   (orchestration)       (containers/images)        (control plane + nodes)
        │                                                  │
        └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                                   ▼
                       Ch 4 — WHAT  (the objects you declare)
              📦 Pod · 🎛️ ReplicaSet · 🚀 Deployment · 🌐 Service · 🏷️ Namespace
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   the through-line: take easypj from "an app that runs on my laptop"
                     to "an app described as desired state a cluster keeps alive."

Chapter 1 · What Is Kubernetes & Why Administrators Need It

easypj runs fine on your laptop with python manage.py runserver. The moment real users arrive, it must survive a 3 AM crash, a traffic spike, a bad deploy, and a dead server — automatically, without you waking up. That automation is Kubernetes, and building & operating the platform that provides it is the CKA's job. This chapter installs the mental model the rest of the guide is built on.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📖 Concepts & Foundation 🐍 easypj / jobpost

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Define container orchestration in one sentence
  • ✅ Give the one-line definition of Kubernetes + the desired vs actual state model
  • ✅ Distinguish CKA (administrator) from CKAD (developer) work
  • ✅ Name & place the 5 core concepts — cluster, control plane, nodes, pod, desired state
  • ✅ Identify the major ecosystem tools (CNCF, runtimes, CNI, Helm, GitOps)
  • ✅ Describe what a Kubernetes administrator actually does day to day
🎓 CKA Relevance
Cluster Architecture 25% Foundation ALL DOMAINS
🎯 Why "Why" Matters on the CKA

The CKA is a performance-based exam — 2 hours, 15–20 hands-on tasks in a live terminal, 66% to pass. Chapter 1 isn't a graded task by itself, but every Architecture (25%) and Troubleshooting (30%) question assumes this mental model. Get it wrong and nothing else lands. Internalize three ideas now:

  • Desired vs Actual State — controllers constantly reconcile the two. This is why the control plane and etcd exist.
  • Self-Healing — a node dies, K8s reschedules its pods. The exam tests your ability to manage this.
  • The administrator owns everything below the app — install, certs, etcd, upgrades, nodes, networking, storage.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 1 Learning Arc

This chapter isn't a random list of topics — it follows a deliberate arc that takes you from "why does this even exist?" to a complete mental model. We start with the pain (so the solution makes sense), name the solution, clarify your role in it, build the mental model, show what plugs in, and finish by grounding it in real-world practice. Each stop answers one question and feeds the next:

   ✅ READY — you now hold the mental model the entire rest of the guide builds on.

If you ever feel lost later, come back to this map — every advanced topic (etcd, RBAC, networking, troubleshooting) is just a deeper look at one of these six ideas. Here's the same arc as a quick-reference table:

SectionAnswers the question…One-line takeaway

1.1 The Problem Before Kubernetes

You've built easypj — a Django jobpost app where employers list jobs filtered by Skills, Location, and Author, backed by PostgreSQL. It works perfectly on your laptop. But how do you run it in production so thousands of users can reach /jobs/ reliably, 24/7, while you sleep?

📖 Key Term — Container Orchestration

Container orchestration is the automated management of containerized applications across many machines — placement, scaling, networking, healing, and rollout — done by software, not humans. Kubernetes is the industry-standard orchestrator, and as a CKA administrator you build and maintain the orchestration platform itself.

The Evolution of Deployment

Deployment has moved through four eras. Each fixed the previous one's pain — and introduced new challenges:

🖥️
2000s
Bare Metal

One app per physical server. No isolation, massive waste. easypj would need its own dedicated box.

❌ Wasteful & rigid
💻
2010s
Virtual Machines

Many VMs per server. Better isolation, but each runs a full guest OS — heavy and slow to provision.

⚠️ Heavy overhead
📦
2015+
Containers

Lightweight, fast, shared kernel. But managing hundreds by hand across servers is a nightmare.

🟡 Almost there…
☸️
2018+
Kubernetes

Orchestrated containers: auto-heal, auto-scale, zero-downtime deploys. The admin builds & maintains this platform.

✅ Production-ready
Without Kubernetes vs With Kubernetes — the easypj story
  ❌ WITHOUT KUBERNETES — one box, all your eggs in it
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 🖥️  ONE server   (you hand-installed the whole stack)                      │
  │     🐍 easypj-web :8000      🐘 postgres :5432      🌐 nginx :80            │
  │                                                                          │
  │   💀 the process crashes   →  the WHOLE site is down until you log in      │
  │   📈 traffic doubles       →  buy & configure another server, by hand      │
  │   🚀 ship a new version    →  scp files, restart, pray; no clean rollback  │
  │   🌙 3 AM page             →  YOU wake up and fix it                        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                          ────▼────   the SAME app, orchestrated:
  ✅ WITH KUBERNETES — a self-healing, self-scaling fleet
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              🌐 users ──▶ Service / Ingress   (one stable address)         │
  │                                │ load-balances across replicas           │
  │              ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐                       │
  │              ▼                 ▼                 ▼                        │
  │         📦 easypj-web      📦 easypj-web      📦 easypj-web    :8000         │
  │         └── Node 1 ──┘     └── Node 1 ──┘     └── Node 2 ──┘                │
  │         🐘 postgres :5432   ── mounts ──▶  💾 PVC   (data survives)          │
  │                                                                          │
  │   🔄 a pod crashes  →  recreated in seconds      📈 load up  →  autoscaled  │
  │   🚀 new version    →  rolling update, 0 downtime    😴 3 AM  →  you sleep   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why Containers Alone Aren't Enough

Docker gives you a container. Kubernetes gives you an army of containers that manage themselves. Compare the two on-call realities:

😰 Running easypj WITHOUT Kubernetes
  • 🔴 SSH in at 3 AM when the process crashes
  • 🔴 Restart Django by hand every time it dies
  • 🔴 No load balancing — one box serves all /jobs/ traffic
  • 🔴 Deploy = SCP files + pray nothing breaks
  • 🔴 Scale = buy a server, install everything from scratch
  • 🔴 Rollback = restore from backup (if you made one)
🎉 Running easypj WITH Kubernetes
  • ✅ Pod crashes → restarted in seconds; you stay asleep
  • ✅ Traffic spikes → HPA adds pods automatically
  • ✅ New version → rolling update, zero downtime
  • ✅ Bad deploy → kubectl rollout undo, instant
  • ✅ Node fails → pods migrate to healthy nodes
  • ✅ Config change → update a ConfigMap, pods pick it up

Make It Concrete — Anatomy of a 3 AM Outage

Abstract benefits are easy to nod along to. Here's the same incident — easypj's process dies at 3:00 AM — played out second-by-second in both worlds. This is why teams adopt Kubernetes:

Same crash, two timelines
  ❌ WITHOUT KUBERNETES                        ✅ WITH KUBERNETES
  ───────────────────────────────────────     ───────────────────────────────────────
  03:00  easypj process crashes 💥             03:00  easypj pod crashes 💥
  03:00  users get 502s, /jobs/ is DOWN        03:00  kubelet's liveness probe fails
  03:12  monitoring finally pages you 📟        03:01  K8s restarts the container (10s) 🔄
  03:18  you wake up, find your laptop 😴       03:01  readiness probe passes → back in
  03:25  VPN in, SSH to the box                       the Service's endpoints
  03:32  read logs, guess the cause             03:01  users never noticed ✅
  03:40  restart by hand, watch it              03:00  YOU ARE ASLEEP 😴 the whole time
  03:45  service restored — 45 MIN DOWN ⛔
  next day: write the post-mortem 📝            next day: nothing to write 🎉

  Downtime:  ~45 minutes, 1 very tired human    Downtime:  ~10 seconds, 0 humans
📖 What just happened (preview of mechanisms)

In the "with" column, three Kubernetes features cooperated automatically: a liveness probe detected the dead container, a controller restarted it to honor "I want 1 running," and a readiness probe + Service kept traffic away until it was healthy again. You'll build all three on easypj in Part 4 — for now, just notice that detection, recovery, and traffic-routing all happened with no human in the loop.

🧠 Analogy

A lone server is a solo musician — if they stop, the music stops. Kubernetes is the conductor of an orchestra: it decides who plays what and instantly covers anyone who drops out, so the performance never stops.

What an Orchestrator Actually Does — the 6 Hard Problems

"Orchestration" is an abstract word. Concretely, Kubernetes automates six jobs you would otherwise do by hand. Every feature in this entire guide is one of these six in disguise — so it's worth memorizing the list:

#ProblemBy hand (without K8s)Kubernetes does it via…
1Scheduling — where does each container run?You pick a server and SSH inkube-scheduler places pods by resources/affinity
2Self-healing — what if it dies?You get paged, restart it manuallyControllers recreate pods; probes restart sick ones
3Scaling — handle more/less loadBuy + configure servers; edit configskubectl scale / HPA / Cluster Autoscaler
4Service discovery + load balancingHard-code IPs; configure nginx upstreamsServices + CoreDNS give a stable name & VIP
5Rollouts & rollbacksCopy files, restart, hope; restore backupsDeployments: rolling update + rollout undo
6Config & secret managementEdit files on each box; secrets in plaintextConfigMaps & Secrets injected at runtime

"Why Can't I Just Use Docker + a Restart Script?"

This is the beginner question — and answering it precisely is what makes the rest of the guide click. A bash script wrapping docker run in a while true; do … done loop really can keep a container alive… on one machine. The catch is that every serious production need is a distributed-systems problem, and a single-machine script is structurally blind to the rest of the fleet:

What you actually needWhy a single-box script structurally can't do it
Place each container on the machine with free CPU/RAMThe script only sees its own box — it has no view of the whole fleet's spare capacity
Keep running when a machine diesIf the box dies, the script dies with it — nothing is left to react or move the work
One stable address for N moving replicasReplicas come and go with changing IPs; a script can't track them or load-balance across them
Zero-downtime version upgradesNeeds coordinated, health-gated replacement across replicas — not a blind local restart
Identical config & secrets everywhereA script edits one box at a time; configuration drift creeps in across the fleet

Kubernetes is the program that holds the whole-cluster view and solves all of these continuously. That's the real leap: from "keep this process up on this box" to "keep this service healthy across the entire fleet." Containers gave us a portable unit; Kubernetes gives us a brain that places, heals, connects, and upgrades thousands of those units without a human deciding where or when.

The blind spot — a script sees one box; Kubernetes sees the cluster
   🔧 DOCKER + RESTART SCRIPT                ☸️  KUBERNETES (the orchestrator)
   ┌──────────────────────────┐             ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 🖥️ node-1  (all it sees)  │             │  sees ALL nodes + their free capacity   │
   │   while true:             │             │  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐       │
   │     docker run easypj     │             │  │ node-1 │ │ node-2 │ │ node-3 │       │
   │   ↳ restarts here ONLY    │             │  │ 60% used│ │ 20% used│ │ 90% used│      │
   │   ✗ node dies? script too │             │  └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘       │
   │   ✗ no idea node-2 exists │             │   ↳ "place the new easypj pod on node-2 │
   │   ✗ can't load-balance    │             │      (most free), and if node-1 dies,   │
   │   ✗ can't roll out safely │             │      reschedule its pods elsewhere"      │
   └──────────────────────────┘             └───────────────────────────────────────┘
        one machine's view                          the whole-cluster view
🐮 Mental Model: Pets vs Cattle

The single most important shift Kubernetes asks of you:

🐶
Pets (the old way)

Servers have names, are hand-fed, and you nurse them back to health when sick. One dies → crisis. "server-prod-01 is acting up again."

🐄
Cattle (the K8s way)

Pods are numbered, identical, and disposable. One dies → it's replaced automatically and you never notice. You manage the herd, not the individual.

This is why pods are ephemeral (they come and go), why you never SSH into one to "fix" it, and why state lives outside the pod (in a database or a PersistentVolume). Internalize this now — it explains 80% of Kubernetes design decisions.

💡 CKA Admin Perspective

Your job isn't just deploying apps — it's building and maintaining the platform that makes all of the "with Kubernetes" column possible: installing the cluster, managing certificates, upgrading versions, backing up etcd, and troubleshooting at the infrastructure level.

1.2 What Is Kubernetes? (The Simple Answer)

📖 Official Definition

"An open-source system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications."

In plain English: Kubernetes is an operating system for your containers. You tell it what you want — "3 copies of easypj:v2, always running" — and it figures out how to make that true across your cluster, and keeps it true.

🚢 Analogy: the Shipping Port (why the logo is a ship's wheel)

The name comes from the Greek κυβερνήτης — "helmsman," the person who steers a ship. The ☸️ logo is a ship's wheel. The analogy runs deep:

Shipping port 🚢Kubernetes ☸️
A standard shipping container — any cargo, any ship, any craneA container image — runs the same anywhere
The ship that carries many containersA node running many pods
The harbor master deciding which ship docks whereThe scheduler deciding which node runs each pod
The manifest — the document listing what's aboardYour YAML manifest — what should be running
The helmsman steering it all to the goalKubernetes steering actual state toward desired

You don't tell the helmsman every rudder movement — you give the destination and trust the steering. That's declarative control in one image.

The Heart of It: Declarative Control

You describe the end state you want; Kubernetes continuously makes reality match it — restarting, rescheduling, and scaling on its own. You never say "start a container on node 2."

Declarative — you DECLARE, Kubernetes DELIVERS
  📝 YOU WRITE (deploy.yaml)                ⚙️ KUBERNETES CONTINUOUSLY GUARANTEES
  ┌───────────────────────────┐            ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ apiVersion: apps/v1       │            │ ✅ exactly 3 easypj pods are RUNNING     │
  │ kind: Deployment          │   apply    │ ✅ every pod runs image easypj:v2        │
  │ spec:                     │  ───────▶  │ ✅ each pod capped at 256Mi memory       │
  │   replicas: 3             │            │ ✅ a pod crashes  → restarted in seconds │
  │   image: easypj:v2        │            │ ✅ a node dies    → pods rescheduled     │
  │   resources: 256Mi        │            │ ✅ new version    → rolled out, 0 downtime│
  └───────────────────────────┘            └───────────────────────────────────────┘
        "DESIRED state"                              "ACTUAL state"
        (you declare it; stored in etcd)             (what's really running on nodes)
              │                                              ▲
              │                  🔄 THE RECONCILE LOOP        │
              └──▶ observe ACTUAL ──▶ compare to DESIRED ──▶ act to close the gap ──┘
                   (runs forever — this is essentially the ONLY thing Kubernetes does)

  ┌─ what "act to close the gap" actually means ─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   actual 2  < desired 3   →  create 1 pod         pod is unhealthy   →  restart it  │
  │   actual 4  > desired 3   →  delete 1 pod         image v1 ≠ v2      →  roll out v2  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  💡 You never list the STEPS — only the DESTINATION. The loop figures out the rest.

Why "Declarative + Reconciliation" Is Such a Big Deal

It's easy to read "you declare desired state" and shrug. But this single design choice is why Kubernetes won — it hands you three superpowers for free, none of which a step-by-step (imperative) system can offer:

♻️
1 · Idempotency

Apply the same manifest once or a hundred times — same result. If reality already matches, the loop finds no gap and does nothing. No "already exists" errors, no half-applied state.

🔄
2 · Self-healing

Because the loop never stops checking, a crash or a dead node is just a new gap to close. Recovery isn't a special code path — it's the same reconciliation running again.

📜
3 · Git as source of truth

Desired state is a file, so it can live in Git — reviewed, versioned, diffed, rolled back. That's the entire basis of GitOps (Chapter 39).

Contrast that with an imperative script ("create this, then start that, then…"). If it fails halfway, you're left in an unknown in-between state, and re-running it may double-create or error out. The declarative model sidesteps all of that: you never describe the steps, only the destination — so there's no fragile sequence to get wrong, and the cluster is free to reach the goal whatever way is currently safe. Hold onto this; literally every feature ahead (Deployments, HPA, rollouts, operators) is just a controller closing a gap.

Declarative vs Imperative — See the Difference

This distinction is the heart of working with Kubernetes (and a recurring exam theme). Imperative = you give step-by-step commands ("do this, now"). Declarative = you describe the end state in a file and let K8s reconcile it. Same result, very different philosophy:

imperative — fast, one-off 
# Tell K8s exactly what to do, step by step
kubectl create deployment easypj \
  --image=easypj:v2 --replicas=3
kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5
kubectl set image deployment/easypj \
  easypj=easypj:v3
# Great for speed on the exam,
# but nothing records your intent.
declarative — the K8s way 
# Describe the end state in a file…
# deploy.yaml:  replicas: 5, image: easypj:v3
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
# Run it again? No harm — already matches.
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml   # idempotent
# The file is the source of truth → Git,
# code review, and GitOps all work.
💡 Best of both on the exam

Generate YAML imperatively, then apply it declaratively: kubectl create deployment easypj --image=easypj:v2 --dry-run=client -o yaml > d.yaml, tweak, then kubectl apply -f d.yaml. You get imperative speed and a declarative artifact.

What Kubernetes Is NOT

Understanding the boundaries is as important as understanding the features — it stops you from expecting things K8s doesn't do:

🏗️
Not a build tool

It does not build container images. You build with Docker/BuildKit/Kaniko in CI; K8s only runs the resulting images.

🔁
Not a CI/CD system

It doesn't run your test pipeline. Tools like GitHub Actions, Jenkins, or Argo/Flux sit around K8s to deliver into it.

☁️
Not a PaaS

Unlike Heroku, it won't "just run my code." It orchestrates containers — you still package the app and declare how it runs.

🗄️
Not a database (and won't manage your data)

etcd stores cluster state, not your app data. Persisting easypj's PostgreSQL data is your job (PersistentVolumes, backups).

💡 Remember the equation

Desired State → [control loops] → Actual State. Every Kubernetes feature you'll learn — Deployments, self-healing, autoscaling, rollouts — is just a controller closing the gap between what you declared and what's actually running.

1.3 The CKA Perspective: Administrator vs Developer

There are two Kubernetes certifications from the Linux Foundation, and they test fundamentally different skills. Knowing the boundary tells you exactly what to study.

👩‍💻

🔧

"I build, operate & troubleshoot the cluster itself."

  • Manage certificates, PKI & RBAC

  • Configure networking (CNI, CoreDNS)

CKA Exam Domain Weights

The CKA tests five domains. Know exactly where each topic fits — and that troubleshooting is the single biggest slice:

Cluster Architecture, Installation & Configuration 25%
Workloads & Scheduling 15%
Services & Networking 20%
Storage 10%
Troubleshooting 30%
⚠️ Troubleshooting is 30% of the CKA

Unlike the CKAD (which is about building apps), the CKA dedicates 30% to fixing broken clusters — failed nodes, crashed control-plane components, networking and DNS issues — under time pressure. Part 9 of this guide is built entirely around a repeatable diagnostic method for exactly this.

The Five Domains, Explained — What Each One Actually Tests

The percentages above are just bars until you know what hides behind each. Here's the plain-English meaning of every domain, the kind of task you'll be handed, and where easypj meets it in this guide — so the exam blueprint becomes a concrete study plan instead of five numbers:

📋 The CKA 2025 blueprint, decoded

🏗️ Cluster Architecture 25%
Build & configure the cluster itself: install with kubeadm, manage RBAC, set up Helm/Kustomize, understand the control plane. Typical task: "create a ServiceAccount + Role + RoleBinding so easypj can read its ConfigMap." → Parts 1, 3, 7, 11.
⚙️ Workloads & Scheduling 15%
Run apps correctly: Deployments, rolling updates/rollbacks, scaling, scheduling (affinity, taints), resource limits, config/secrets. Typical task: "roll easypj to v2 with zero downtime, then roll it back." → Part 4.
🌐 Services & Networking 20%
Connect & expose: Services, DNS/CoreDNS, Ingress, the Gateway API, NetworkPolicies. Typical task: "expose easypj on a NodePort and restrict who may reach the DB." → Part 5.
💾 Storage 10%
Persist data: PersistentVolumes, PVCs, StorageClasses, dynamic provisioning. Typical task: "give easypj's PostgreSQL a 5Gi PVC that survives a pod restart." → Part 6.
🩺 Troubleshooting 30%
Diagnose & fix broken things: NotReady nodes, crashed control-plane pods, failing Services/DNS, stuck workloads. Typical task: "easypj pods are Pending / the node is NotReady — find and fix it." → Part 9 (the biggest, most point-dense domain).
🎯 How to read these weights as a strategy

Troubleshooting (30%) + Architecture (25%) = over half the exam, and both reward method over memorization. Storage is only 10% but its tasks are quick, high-certainty points — never skip them. The smart play: bank the fast Storage/Workloads tasks first, then spend your remaining time on the heavier Troubleshooting and Architecture problems.

The Kubernetes Release Cycle — What an Admin Must Track

Kubernetes ships three minor versions a year (~every 4 months: v1.31, v1.32, v1.33…). As the admin, keeping the cluster inside the supported window — and upgrading it safely — is your recurring job, and a guaranteed exam task. Each release has a life:

🆕
Month 0
New Release

e.g. v1.33 ships — new features, deprecations, and bug fixes land.

✅ Latest
🛡️
~0–14 months
Supported

Gets patch releases (security & bug fixes). The CKA tests within this window.

✅ Patched
⚠️
14+ months
End of Life

No more patches. Running EOL = a growing security risk → you must upgrade.

❌ Unsupported
⚠️ The Golden Upgrade Rule: one minor version at a time

Kubernetes only supports upgrading one minor version at a step — 1.31 → 1.32 → 1.33. You cannot skip (no 1.31 → 1.33 jump). There's also a version-skew rule: the kubelet may lag the API server by up to 3 minors but never run ahead of it. The CKA puts you in front of a real cluster and asks you to upgrade it with kubeadm upgrade (control plane first, then workers) — you'll do exactly this in Chapter 28.

What Exam Day Actually Looks Like

Knowing the format removes half the stress. The CKA is taken remotely, in your browser, proctored live through the PSI platform — here's the flow end-to-end:

1
Check-in

Show photo ID, do a 360° room scan via webcam. Desk must be clear; you're watched the whole time.

2
The terminal

A real Linux terminal in the browser, with multiple clusters. You SSH/context-switch between them per task.

3
15–20 tasks

Each is weighted and independent. A score bar shows weights — do the cheap, high-value ones first.

4
Docs allowed

One extra tab to kubernetes.io/docs (+ blog, GitHub). Nothing else. Practice copy-paste from the docs.

5
Flag & move on

Stuck > a few minutes? Flag it, move on, return later. Never leave a task blank — partial credit is real.

6
Results & retake

Score by email in ~24 h. 66% to pass. One free retake included; the cert is valid 3 years.

🎯 The #1 exam-day habit: set context first, every task

Each task may use a different cluster/namespace. The most common way to lose points is doing correct work in the wrong place. Start every single task with the context switch the question gives you:

muscle memory for the exam
kubectl config use-context <cluster-from-the-question>
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns>   # then work

Free, realistic practice: the killer.sh CKA simulator (2 sessions included with your exam registration) mirrors the real environment closely — Chapter 45 builds a full timed simulator on easypj.

The Three Kubernetes Certifications

The Linux Foundation offers three hands-on Kubernetes certs. They build on each other — and the CKA (this guide) is the foundation the others assume:

👩‍💻
CKAD — Developer

Focus: deploying & configuring apps.
Owns: Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, probes, multi-container patterns.

2 h · 66% to pass

🔧
CKA — Administrator ← this guide

Focus: building & operating the cluster.
Owns: install, etcd, certs, upgrades, nodes, RBAC, networking, storage, troubleshooting.

2 h · 66% to pass

🛡️
CKS — Security Specialist

Focus: hardening & securing clusters.
Owns: Pod Security, supply-chain, runtime security, network policy, audit. Requires a valid CKA first.

2 h · 67% to pass

📖 Which order?

CKA is the natural starting point: it's the platform layer the other two stand on. CKAD overlaps with CKA on workloads; CKS literally requires you to already hold the CKA. Master this guide and you're well-positioned for all three.

🧠 Analogy

CKAD furnishes the rooms; CKA builds & maintains the house — foundations, plumbing, and wiring included; CKS installs the locks, alarms, and security cameras. This guide is the house.

1.4 Kubernetes Core Concepts — The Big Picture

Everything in Kubernetes is built from five ideas. Lock these in now — they're the mental model you'll use for the entire CKA journey.

🗂️
1 · Cluster

A set of machines (nodes) Kubernetes manages as a single unit.

🧠
2 · Control Plane

The "brain" — makes all scheduling & orchestration decisions.

💪
3 · Worker Nodes

The "muscle" — actually run your containerized apps.

📦
4 · Pod

Smallest deployable unit — 1+ containers sharing IP & storage.

🎯
5 · Desired State

You declare what you want; K8s continuously keeps it that way.

The Words You'll Keep Hearing — a Beginner's Glossary

Before the diagrams, here's a plain-English decoder for the terms that appear on every page from here on. Bookmark this — you won't feel lost again:

📖 Core vocabulary

🐋 container
A packaged, isolated process — your app + its dependencies. The thing that actually runs easypj.
🖼️ image
The read-only template a container is started from, e.g. easypj:v2. Built once, run anywhere.
📦 pod
The smallest thing K8s schedules — one (or a few) containers that share an IP & storage.
💪 node
A machine (VM or physical) that runs pods. The cluster is a set of nodes.
🗂️ cluster
All your nodes + the control plane, managed as one system.
🏷️ namespace
A virtual folder that partitions a cluster (e.g. easypj, kube-system) for isolation & quotas.
📄 manifest
A YAML file describing a desired object (a Deployment, Service…). The "what you want."
🧩 object / resource
Any thing K8s tracks in etcd — Pod, Service, ConfigMap, Node. Everything is an object.
🔄 controller
A loop that watches objects and drives actual → desired (e.g. the Deployment controller).
⌨️ kubectl
The command-line tool you use to talk to the API server ("koob-cuddle" / "koob-control").

How the Objects Nest — the Workload Hierarchy

Beginners often blur Pod, ReplicaSet, and Deployment. They're layers, each wrapping the one below and adding a capability. You almost always create the outermost one and let it manage the rest:

Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod → Container (inside a Namespace)
  🏷️ Namespace: easypj   (a virtual folder that isolates these objects)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 🚀 Deployment  "easypj-web"                       ← you create THIS     │
  │    adds ▶ rolling updates · rollback · revision history                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 🎛️ ReplicaSet  "easypj-web-6d8f9"   (one per pod-template version) │ │
  │  │    adds ▶ "keep exactly N pods alive"  → self-healing              │ │
  │  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐   N = 3      │ │
  │  │  │ 📦 Pod         │  │ 📦 Pod         │  │ 📦 Pod         │            │ │
  │  │  │  …-6d8f9-x7k2 │  │  …-6d8f9-m9p4 │  │  …-6d8f9-q2j7 │            │ │
  │  │  │ ┌──────────┐ │  │ ┌──────────┐ │  │ ┌──────────┐ │            │ │
  │  │  │ │🐋 web :8000│ │  │ │🐋 web :8000│ │  │ │🐋 web :8000│ │ ← container│ │
  │  │  │ └──────────┘ │  │ └──────────┘ │  │ └──────────┘ │            │ │
  │  │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘            │ │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │  🕓 old ReplicaSet "easypj-web-5a1c" → scaled to 0, kept for rollback   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   naming chain ▶  Deployment ──(+ pod-template-hash)──▶ ReplicaSet ──(+ random)──▶ Pod
   rule of thumb ▶  you create the Deployment; it makes the ReplicaSet; the RS makes the
                    Pods; each Pod runs your container(s). You almost never make a bare Pod.
💡 Why not just create Pods directly?

A bare Pod is a pet — if it dies, it's gone for good (nothing recreates it). Wrap it in a ReplicaSet and you get self-healing; wrap that in a Deployment and you also get rolling updates & rollback. That's why in real life you create Deployments, almost never naked Pods.

📖 Preview — the components (full deep-dive in Chapter 3)

You'll meet each component properly in Chapter 3: Kubernetes Architecture. For now, just learn the one-liners — they make every later chapter click.

🧠 Control Plane Components — the admin must know these (Architecture = 25%)

📡 kube-apiserver
The front door — ALL communication goes through it (kubectl, node heartbeats, controllers). It's the only component that talks to etcd. If it's down, the cluster is blind.
🗄️ etcd
The cluster's memory — a distributed key-value store holding ALL cluster state. CKA tests backup & restore. Lose etcd with no backup = lose the whole cluster.
📋 kube-scheduler
The matchmaker — watches for unscheduled Pods and picks the best node by resources, affinity, and taints/tolerations.
🔄 kube-controller-manager
The watchdog — runs control loops that compare desired vs actual and act ("only 2 of 3 replicas → create 1 more").
☁️ cloud-controller-manager
Cloud glue (optional) — integrates with AWS/Azure/GCP for load balancers, disks, and node lifecycle. Absent on bare-metal.

What Happens When Each Component Goes Down?

Memorizing what each component does is half the battle; the deeper understanding — and what the 30% troubleshooting domain really tests — is knowing what breaks when each one fails. This table is worth more than any definition, because it turns "the scheduler schedules pods" into "if pods are stuck Pending, look at the scheduler":

If this is down…What you observeWhy
kube-apiserverkubectl fails; nothing can be changed. Running pods keep running.It's the only door to the cluster — no reads/writes, no scheduling, no controller actions. The cluster "freezes" but doesn't crash.
etcdAPI server can't serve → whole control plane unusable. Lost with no backup = cluster gone.It holds all state. No etcd, no source of truth to read or write.
kube-schedulerNew pods stay Pending forever. Existing pods are unaffected.Nothing is left to assign pods to nodes — they sit unscheduled.
kube-controller-managerNo self-healing: a crashed pod isn't replaced, scaling/rollouts stall, dead nodes aren't acted on.The reconciliation loops live here — without them, desired ≠ actual is never corrected.
kubelet (on a node)That node goes NotReady; after a grace period its pods are rescheduled elsewhere.No agent to run/report pods on that node, so the control plane writes it off.
💡 The one insight that makes troubleshooting click

The control plane is the brain; running pods are the body. Knock out the brain (API server / etcd) and the body keeps moving on reflex — your apps stay up, you just can't change anything. This is why an etcd or apiserver outage is silent to users but paralyzing to admins, and why "my app still works but kubectl is dead" points straight at the control plane, not the workload. Match the symptom to the component and you've solved most of the exam's troubleshooting tasks before typing a command.

💪 Worker Node Components

🤖 kubelet
The node agent — takes pod specs from the API server, makes the containers run & stay healthy, and reports node status back.
🔀 kube-proxy
The network plumber — programs the node's dataplane rules so Services route to the right pods.
🐋 container runtime
The engine that actually runs containers — containerd (default) or CRI-O via the CRI. Docker-shim was removed in v1.24.

Desired vs Actual State — the Declarative Magic

The Reconciliation Loop
                 ┌────────────────── 🔄 ONE CONTROLLER, RUNNING FOREVER ──────────────────┐
                 │                                                                        │
     ┌───────────▼───────────┐      ┌───────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────┐
     │ 1. 👁️ OBSERVE           │ ───▶ │ 2. 🧮 DIFF          │ ───▶ │ 3. 🛠️ ACT                 │
     │ read ACTUAL (cluster)   │      │ does ACTUAL match  │      │ create / delete / update │
     │ + DESIRED (from etcd)   │      │ DESIRED? a gap?    │      │ objects to close the gap │
     └─────────────────────────┘      └───────────────────┘      └────────────┬────────────┘
                 ▲                                                             │
                 └──────────────────────────── repeat ◀─────────────────────────┘

  easypj tick-by-tick — the Deployment controller, desired replicas = 3:
    t0   observe 0 pods    · diff: need 3    · act: create 3            → 3 running
    t1   observe 3 pods    · diff: none       · act: nothing  (idempotent — no churn)
    t2   a pod crashes 💥   · observe 2 pods  · diff: need 1   · act: create 1  → 3 running
    t3   you set image v2  · diff: v1 ≠ v2    · act: replace pods one-by-one  → all v2

  💡 Recovery is NOT a special code path — it's the SAME loop noticing a NEW gap.

How a Pod Gets Created — the Full Journey

Here's the single most clarifying flow in all of Kubernetes: what actually happens between you typing kubectl apply and easypj serving traffic. Watch how every component plays its part. (Chapter 3 dissects each step; this is the map.)

kubectl apply → a running easypj pod
  👩‍💻 kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
        │  (1) HTTPS request
        ▼
  📡 kube-apiserver ──(2) authn → authz → admission → validate──┐
        │                                                       │
        │  (3) write DESIRED object                             │
        ▼                                                       │
  🗄️ etcd  "Deployment easypj wants 3 pods"  ◀─────────────────┘
        │
        │  (4) controller-manager sees Deployment → makes ReplicaSet → 3 Pod objects
        │      (Pods exist but have NO node yet → "Pending")
        ▼
  📋 kube-scheduler  (5) "which node fits?"  → binds Pod → Node 2 (writes to API→etcd)
        │
        ▼
  🤖 kubelet on Node 2  (6) "a pod was assigned to me!"
        │   ├─ 🐋 tells containerd to PULL easypj:v2 and START the container
        │   └─ 🌐 CNI plugin gives the pod its IP
        ▼
  📦 easypj pod RUNNING :8000   (7) kubelet reports status ──▶ API server ──▶ etcd
        │
        ▼
  🔄 controllers keep watching forever: actual=3 = desired=3  ✅  (reconciled)
1
Submit

kubectl sends your YAML to the API server over TLS.

2
Admit

API server authenticates, authorizes (RBAC), runs admission, validates.

3
Persist

Desired state is written to etcd — the single source of truth.

4
Expand

Controllers turn the Deployment into a ReplicaSet into Pod objects (Pending).

5
Schedule

The scheduler picks the best node and binds each pod to it.

6
Run

That node's kubelet pulls the image, starts the container, CNI assigns an IP.

7
Report

kubelet reports status up; controllers reconcile forever.

⚠️ Why this matters for troubleshooting

Every "my pod won't run" problem lives at one of these steps. Pending = stuck at step 5 (scheduler can't place it). ImagePullBackOff = step 6 (kubelet can't pull). CrashLoopBackOff = step 6 (container starts then dies). Knowing the journey tells you exactly where to look — the core skill behind the 30% troubleshooting domain.

💡 Why declarative matters for the CKA

The exam rewards working declaratively: declare desired state, kubectl apply -f, and trust the controllers. It's also the key to troubleshooting — when something breaks, you compare desired state (in etcd) against actual state (on the nodes) and find the gap.

1.5 The Kubernetes Ecosystem

Kubernetes is a core that everything plugs into. It sits at the center of a large ecosystem of runtimes, plugins, and platforms — all governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). As an admin you'll touch many of these daily.

The ecosystem orbit — a core everything plugs into
                  📦 PACKAGING                          🔄 GitOps / DELIVERY
               Helm · Kustomize                          Argo CD · Flux
                        ╲                                    ╱
                         ╲                                  ╱
   🐋 RUNTIME (CRI)    ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐    🌐 NETWORK (CNI)
   containerd · CRI-O ─┤                                        ├─ Calico · Cilium · Flannel
                       │        ☸️   KUBERNETES  CORE             │
   💾 STORAGE (CSI)    │   the orchestration engine:            │    📊 OBSERVABILITY
   EBS · PD · Ceph ───┤   schedule · heal · scale · reconcile   ├─ Prometheus · Grafana
   NFS                 │        (drives desired → actual)        │    Loki · OpenTelemetry
                       └────────────────────────────────────────┘
                         ╱                                  ╲
                        ╱                                    ╲
                  🕸️ SERVICE MESH                       🛡️ SECURITY / POLICY
               Istio · Linkerd                          Kyverno · OPA Gatekeeper

   ☁️  Everything around the core is governed by the CNCF (Cloud Native Computing Foundation).
   💡 CRI · CNI · CSI are the three "sockets" Kubernetes DEFINES — vendors just supply the plugs.

Key Ecosystem Categories for the CKA

🐋
Container Runtimes (CRI)

containerd (default since v1.24), CRI-O. K8s talks to them via the Container Runtime Interface; the Docker shim was removed.

🌐
CNI Plugins (networking)

Calico & Cilium (with NetworkPolicy), Flannel (simple overlay), Weave. You install a CNI during cluster setup — no CNI = NotReady nodes.

📦
Packaging

Helm (templated charts — the "apt for K8s") and Kustomize (template-free overlays). Both are 2025 CKA topics.

🔄
GitOps

ArgoCD, FluxCD — Git is the source of truth; a controller syncs the cluster to match and self-heals drift.

🕸️
Service Mesh

Istio, Linkerd — observability, traffic management, and mTLS between services without touching app code.

📊
Observability

Prometheus (metrics), Grafana (dashboards), Loki (logs), Jaeger / OpenTelemetry (traces). The CKA expects kubectl top + metrics-server.

📖 CNCF — who governs Kubernetes?

The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (part of the Linux Foundation) stewards Kubernetes and 170+ related projects through three maturity levels — Sandbox → Incubating → Graduated. Kubernetes was the first to graduate (2018). The CNCF also runs the CKA & CKAD certifications.

🎓 Graduated Production-proven, widely adopted
KubernetesPrometheuscontainerdCoreDNSetcdHelm
🧪 Incubating Growing adoption, maturing features
ArgoCiliumKnativeKyvernoBackstage
🌱 Sandbox Early-stage, experimental
HeadlampOpenCostInspektor Gadget

What "Cloud Native" Actually Means

"Cloud native" is the phrase behind the CNCF's name and gets thrown around constantly — but it's rarely defined. It's not "runs in the cloud." It's a way of building software so it can be operated by software (like Kubernetes). Five properties define it, and easypj will gain each one as we go:

📦
Containerized

Each piece is packaged with its dependencies into an image — portable and isolated. (easypj → a container in Ch 2.)

🧩
Loosely coupled

Independent services talk over the network (web ↔ DB), so each can scale, fail, and deploy on its own.

🤖
Dynamically orchestrated

A platform schedules, scales, and heals it automatically — no human placing processes on machines.

📝
Declarative

Desired state lives in version-controlled manifests, not in someone's head or a runbook.

🛡️
Resilient & observable

It expects failure and recovers; it exposes metrics, logs, and traces so you can see what it's doing.

📖 Why the term matters to you

Every tool in the orbit above exists to deliver one of these five properties. So "cloud native" isn't marketing — it's the checklist the whole ecosystem is built around. When you finish this guide, easypj will satisfy all five, and you'll be the administrator who keeps the platform that makes that possible running.

The Three "Sockets" — How Kubernetes Stays Pluggable (CRI · CNI · CSI)

Why does such a huge ecosystem exist? Because Kubernetes itself doesn't run containers, wire up networks, or attach disks. Instead it defines three standard interfaces — think of them as universal sockets — and lets vendors plug in. This is the reason Kubernetes runs identically on your laptop, on bare metal, and on every cloud.

Kubernetes defines the socket; you choose the plug
                       ☸️  KUBERNETES  (defines 3 standard interfaces)
                                       │
        ┌──────────────────────┬───────┴───────────────┬──────────────────────┐
        ▼                      ▼                        ▼
   🔌 CRI                  🔌 CNI                    🔌 CSI
   Container Runtime IF    Container Network IF      Container Storage IF
   kubelet asks:           K8s asks:                 K8s asks:
   "run / stop this        "give this pod            "attach this disk
    container"              an IP & connect it"        to the pod"
        │                      │                         │
   any plug speaking ▼     any plug speaking ▼       any plug speaking ▼
   🐋 containerd · CRI-O   🌐 Calico · Cilium ·       💾 AWS EBS · GCP PD ·
                             Flannel                    Ceph · NFS
        │                      │                         │
        ▼                      ▼                         ▼
   starts the easypj       easypj pod 10.244.1.5     postgres data lives on a
   container on the node   reaches any pod, no NAT   real disk, survives restarts

   💡 Swap any plug (e.g. containerd → CRI-O) and Kubernetes ITSELF doesn't change.
      THAT is why one set of easypj manifests runs on a laptop, bare metal & every cloud.
🐋
CRI — Runtime

How the kubelet asks something to run a container. Default: containerd. (You'll configure this in Chapter 9 when installing the cluster.)

🌐
CNI — Network

How pods get an IP and reach each other. You install a CNI (Calico/Cilium) right after kubeadm init — without one, nodes stay NotReady (Chapter 17).

💾
CSI — Storage

How a real disk gets attached to a pod for durable data — exactly how easypj's PostgreSQL keeps its files (Chapter 22).

📖 The big idea

Kubernetes is a platform for building platforms: it owns the orchestration logic and delegates the "hardware-touching" parts to pluggable drivers. Whenever you see "install a CNI" or "pick a StorageClass," you're choosing a plug for one of these sockets. Keep this model in your head — it makes Parts 5 (networking) and 6 (storage) click instantly.

1.6 How Companies Use Kubernetes (a day in an admin's life)

Kubernetes isn't just for tech giants. Companies of every size run it — scale changes the job, not the fundamentals.

Company SizeK8s SetupAdmin TasksTeam
🏠 Startup (5–20)
e.g. easypj		 1 cluster, few nodes. Minikube → managed cloud (EKS/AKS/GKE). Deploy, monitor, basic troubleshooting, simple CI/CD. 1 admin does it all
🏢 Mid-size (50–200) 2–5 clusters. Separate dev / staging / prod; multi-team RBAC. CI/CD, RBAC, upgrades, monitoring, cost control, policies. 2–4 admins

A Day in the Life of a CKA Administrator

1
Morning Check

Review dashboards; check node health, pod restarts, and overnight alerts.

2
Troubleshoot

Investigate failed pods/nodes: describe, logs, journalctl -u kubelet.

3
Ship Changes

Apply upgrades/RBAC/config via GitOps or PRs — staging first, then prod.

4
Secure & Audit

Review audit logs, rotate certificates that are due, verify NetworkPolicies, and check RBAC for over-permissioned accounts.

5
Maintain

6
Capacity Plan

Watch resource trends; add nodes or right-size requests/limits.
