3.1 Cluster Architecture Overview

A Kubernetes cluster is two layers: a control plane (the brain — makes every decision) and one or more worker nodes (the muscle — actually run the workloads). As a CKA admin you install, configure, and repair both. Everything else in this chapter is a zoom-in on one of these two halves.

The complete cluster — brain + muscle
   ┌──────────────────────────────────── ☸️ CLUSTER ───────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  🧠 CONTROL PLANE  (decides)                                                            │
   │   ┌──────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────────┐    │
   │   │ 📡 apiserver  │ │ 🗄️ etcd     │ │ 📋 scheduler    │ │ 🔄 controller-manager       │    │
   │   │ the ONLY door │ │ ALL state  │ │ places pods    │ │ reconcile loops             │    │
   │   │ :6443         │ │ :2379/2380 │ │ filter→score→  │ │ (node · ReplicaSet ·        │    │
   │   │ authN/Z/admit │ │ (Raft)     │ │ bind           │ │  endpoint · serviceaccount) │    │
   │   └──────┬───────┘ └────────────┘ └────────────────┘ └────────────────────────────┘    │
   │          │   ⚠️ ONLY the apiserver talks to etcd; every component & kubectl goes        │
   │          │      THROUGH the apiserver (the single choke point).                          │
   │  ────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
   │  💪 WORKER NODES  (run)                                                                  │
   │   ┌──────▼──────────────────┐                  ┌─────────────────────────┐              │
   │   │ Node 1                   │                  │ Node 2                   │             │
   │   │ 🤖 kubelet  🌐 kube-proxy │                  │ 🤖 kubelet  🌐 kube-proxy │             │
   │   │ 🐋 containerd            │                  │ 🐋 containerd            │             │
   │   │ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐   │                  │ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐   │             │
   │   │ │📦 easypj│ │📦 easypj│   │                  │ │📦 easypj│ │🐘 postgres│ │             │
   │   │ │  web    │ │  web    │   │                  │ │  web    │ │  :5432   │ │             │
   │   │ └────────┘ └────────┘   │                  │ └────────┘ └────────┘   │             │
   │   └─────────────────────────┘                  └─────────────────────────┘              │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧠 Control Plane Makes every orchestration decision
kube-apiserveretcdkube-schedulercontroller-manager
💪 Worker Nodes Run the actual workloads
kubeletkube-proxycontainerd/CRI-OPods
🌐 Networking Layer Connects everything together
CNI pluginCoreDNSService networkPod network
📖 The mental shortcut

For the rest of your CKA life, sort every problem into one bucket: is it a decision problem (control plane — won't schedule, won't reconcile, can't reach the API) or a run problem (a node — container won't start, NotReady, networking)? That single split routes you to the right component before you type a command.

3.2 Control-Plane Components — Deep Dive

These are the components you maintain, troubleshoot, and restore. For each, learn three things: its job, its config location, and — most exam-relevant — what breaks when it's gone.

🍽️ In plain English — the cluster as a restaurant

If the components feel abstract, map them to a busy restaurant — it makes every role (and every failure) intuitive:

RestaurantKubernetesSo if it's gone…
🛎️ the front desk — every order/request goes through it📡 kube-apiservernobody can place or change orders (no kubectl)
📖 the order ledger — the single written record of every order🗄️ etcdlose the ledger = lose the whole restaurant's state
🪑 the host who seats each party at the best table📋 schedulernew parties wait at the door (pods Pending)
🧑‍💼 the floor manager watching everything & fixing gaps🔄 controller-managerno one refills empty tables (no self-healing)
👨‍🍳 the line cook at each station who actually makes the food🤖 kubelet (on each node)that station stops cooking (node NotReady)
🏃 the runner delivering plates to the right table🌐 kube-proxyfood's made but never reaches diners (Services break)

Notice the front desk (apiserver) is the only one who reads/writes the ledger (etcd) — exactly like the real cluster. Keep this picture; the rest of §3.2 just adds detail to each role.

a) 📡 kube-apiserver — the front door

📡 kube-apiserver

🎯 Role
The only entry point. Every kubectl call, every kubelet, every controller talks to it — and it's the only component that reads/writes etcd.
🔐 Pipeline
Each request: authentication (certs/tokens) → authorization (RBAC) → admission (validate/mutate) → persist to etcd.
📂 Config
Static-pod manifest: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
🔌 Port
6443 (secure HTTPS)
💀 If it fails
No kubectl, no new pods, nodes can't report status. Existing pods keep running — the kubelet is independent.

b) 🗄️ etcd — the cluster database

🗄️ etcd — the brain's memory

🎯 Role
A distributed key-value store holding ALL cluster state under /registry/… — pods, services, secrets, RBAC, everything.
🔄 Consensus
Uses Raft — a quorum (majority) must agree on every write. That's why HA clusters run 3 or 5 etcd members.
🔌 Ports
2379 (client) · 2380 (peer)
📝 CKA
Backup & restore is directly tested — know etcdctl snapshot save / restore cold.
🚨 etcd lost = cluster lost

Lose etcd without a backup and your entire cluster — every pod, service, secret, and RBAC rule — is gone. This is precisely why "back up etcd" is the #1 admin task and a guaranteed exam item (Ch 29).

terminal — etcd backup (CKA skill)
# snapshot (cert paths come from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# verify it's readable
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /opt/etcd-backup.db --write-table

c) 📋 kube-scheduler — the matchmaker

📋 kube-scheduler

🎯 Role
Watches for Pods with no node assigned, evaluates every node, and binds the pod to the best fit.
🔍 Process
Filter (which nodes can run it?) → Score (which is best?) → Bind (assign the winner).
📊 Considers
CPU/mem requests, nodeSelector, affinity/anti-affinity, taints/tolerations, PV topology, spread constraints.
💀 If it fails
New pods stay Pending (existing pods unaffected). Spot it: kubectl get pods -A | grep Pending.
1
Watch

See a Pod with empty nodeName

2
Filter

Drop nodes that can't fit (resources, taints, affinity)

3
Score

Rank the survivors (spread, balance, preferences)

4
Bind

Assign the top node → write to etcd → kubelet takes over

d) 🔄 kube-controller-manager — the watchdog

🔄 kube-controller-manager (many controllers, one process)

🖥️ Node ctrl
Watches node heartbeats; marks a node NotReady after ~40s of silence, evicts its pods after ~5 min.
📦 ReplicaSet ctrl
Keeps the pod count right — spec says 3, only 2 running → creates 1 more.
🔗 Endpoint ctrl
Wires Services to Pods by maintaining the EndpointSlice (the list of ready pod IPs).
👤 ServiceAccount ctrl
Creates the default ServiceAccount for each new namespace.
💀 If it fails
No self-healing: crashed pods aren't replaced, scaling/endpoints stall, dead nodes aren't acted on.
A controller loop — the heart of Kubernetes
   ┌─────────── CONTROLLER LOOP (runs forever) ───────────┐
   │  👁️ OBSERVE  ──▶  🧮 COMPARE  ──▶  🛠️ ACT  ──┐         │
   │  actual state    desired vs       reconcile          │
   │  "2 pods"        actual "want 3"  "create 1 pod"      │
   │      ▲                                    │           │
   │      └────────────────────────────────────┘           │
   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   easypj ReplicaSet: spec replicas=3, see 2 → create 1 → repeat

e) ☁️ cloud-controller-manager — the cloud glue (optional)

📖 Only on cloud clusters

The cloud-controller-manager integrates a cloud provider: provisioning LoadBalancers, managing routes, and handling node lifecycle (detecting deleted VMs). Bare-metal/kubeadm clusters don't run it. It exists so the core controllers stay cloud-agnostic — another example of Kubernetes keeping vendor specifics behind a plug.

3.3 Worker-Node Components — Deep Dive

Every node — worker and control-plane — runs three things that actually make containers happen: the kubelet (agent), kube-proxy (service routing), and a container runtime. These are where "run" problems live.

a) 🤖 kubelet — the node agent

🤖 kubelet

🎯 Role
Receives PodSpecs from the API server, drives the runtime to start/stop containers, runs probes, and reports status back.
⚡ Key fact
The kubelet is NOT a pod — it's a systemd service on the node. Check it with systemctl status kubelet.
📂 Config
/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
🔌 Port
10250 (HTTPS API)
🔍 Troubleshoot
journalctl -u kubelet -f — most common causes: expired cert, runtime down, swap on, or cgroup-driver mismatch.

b) 🌐 kube-proxy — the network plumber

🌐 kube-proxy

🎯 Role
Programs each node's dataplane so a Service VIP load-balances to the right backing Pod IPs.
⚙️ Modes
iptables (default), IPVS (faster at 1000+ services), nftables (newer).
📦 Runs as
A DaemonSet (one pod per node) in kube-system — unlike the kubelet, it is a pod.
💡 Remember
kube-proxy handles Service networking; the CNI handles pod-to-pod networking. Pods ping by IP but Services fail → suspect kube-proxy.

c) 🐋 container runtime

🐋
containerd

The default for kubeadm, EKS, AKS, GKE. CNCF-graduated. Drives the actual container lifecycle via the CRI.

🔴
CRI-O

Kubernetes-native, minimal. Used by OpenShift; versioned in lockstep with K8s.

⚠️ CKA triage: node shows NotReady? Check in this order
  • systemctl status kubelet — is the agent running?
  • journalctl -u kubelet — what's the error? (cert / swap / CNI / cgroup)
  • systemctl status containerd — is the runtime up?
  • crictl ps — can the runtime even list containers?

Everything the kubelet Actually Does

"The kubelet runs containers" undersells it — it's the busiest agent in the cluster and the prime suspect in most node problems. Knowing its full job list tells you exactly what can break:

🤖 the kubelet's responsibilities

📝 Register
Registers the node with the apiserver on startup (creates the Node object, advertises capacity/labels).
💓 Heartbeat
Renews a node Lease (in kube-node-lease) every few seconds so the control plane knows it's alive — stop renewing → NotReady.
👁️ Watch
Watches the apiserver for Pods bound to its node (and the static-pod dir on disk).
🐋 Run
Drives the CRI to pull images and start/stop containers; sets up the pod sandbox.
💾 Mount
Attaches/mounts volumes via the CSI before starting containers (emptyDir, PVC, configMap/secret).
🩺 Probe
Runs liveness/readiness/startup probes → restarts dead containers, gates traffic on readiness.
📊 Report
Reports pod & node status back to the apiserver; exposes stats (cAdvisor) for kubectl top.
🧹 Evict
Under node pressure (disk/memory) it evicts pods and applies the matching taint (e.g. DiskPressure).
📖 Why this matters: the kubelet is "trusted" but standalone

Because the kubelet reads its work from the apiserver but acts independently, two important things follow: (1) if the apiserver dies, running pods keep running — the kubelet doesn't need it to keep containers alive; and (2) the kubelet can run static pods with no control plane at all, which is exactly how kubeadm bootstraps the cluster (§3.6). It's the one component that bridges "declared in the API" and "actually running on Linux."

3.4 How a Pod Is Born — The Full Journey

This is the single most important sequence in Kubernetes — every troubleshooting task assumes it. Watch what happens after kubectl apply -f easypj-deploy.yaml, and notice that no single component runs the show: each one reconciles its own slice and the pod emerges.

1
kubectl → apiserver

HTTPS request to :6443 with a client cert.

2
authN → authZ → admit

Who are you? (cert) · Allowed? (RBAC) · Valid? (admission).

3
apiserver → etcd

The Deployment object is persisted — desired state recorded.

4
controllers

Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod objects (still nodeless).

5
scheduler

Sees a nodeless Pod → filter → score → binds to a node.

6
kubelet

On that node: pulls easypj:v2, starts the container, CNI gives it an IP.

7
kube-proxy

Programs Service routing to the new Pod IP.

8
Running ✅

kubelet reports status → apiserver → etcd; the loops keep watching.

kubectl apply -f easypj-deploy.yaml → a Running pod
   👩‍💻 kubectl apply
        │ ① HTTPS :6443 + client cert
        ▼
   📡 apiserver ──② authN → authZ(RBAC) → admission──┐
        │ ③ persist Deployment                       │
        ▼                                            │
   🗄️ etcd  (desired state)  ◀───────────────────────┘
        │ ④ controller-manager: Deployment → ReplicaSet → 3 Pod objects (Pending)
        ▼
   📋 scheduler ── ⑤ filter → score → BIND each Pod → a node
        ▼
   🤖 kubelet (on the node) ── ⑥ 🐋 pull easypj:v2 · start container · 🌐 CNI assigns IP
        ▼
   🌐 kube-proxy ── ⑦ program Service routing to the new Pod IP
        ▼
   📦 easypj Running :8000 ── ⑧ status ─▶ apiserver ─▶ etcd     (loops keep reconciling)
💡 The troubleshooting map — match the symptom to the broken step
  • Connection refused / kubectl hangs → step 1–3 (apiserver/etcd down)
  • Forbidden / Unauthorized → step 2 (RBAC or certs)
  • Pod stuck Pending → step 5 (scheduler can't place it)
  • ImagePullBackOff → step 6 (kubelet can't pull the image)
  • CrashLoopBackOff → step 6 (container starts, then dies)
  • Service unreachable → step 7 (kube-proxy / endpoints)
🍽️ In plain English — the same journey, as a restaurant order

Tie it back to §3.2's restaurant: "You hand your order to the front desk (apiserver), which checks you're allowed and writes it in the ledger (etcd). The floor manager (controllers) turns 'a table of 3' into three seat requests; the host (scheduler) seats each at a table (node); the line cook there (kubelet) actually makes the dish (starts the container); and the runner (kube-proxy) makes sure diners can find it (Service routing)."

Same eight steps, zero jargon — and the failure map still works: nobody seated = the host (scheduler) is out; food never delivered = the runner (kube-proxy) is out.

3.5 Cluster Networking Overview

Kubernetes networking has one founding rule: every Pod gets its own unique IP, and all Pods can reach all Pods without NAT — one flat network. A CNI plugin makes that real. Keep the layers straight and networking stops being scary (full depth in Part 5).

The four network layers — from the wire up to the user
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 🌍 EXTERNAL traffic (users, internet)                          │
   │    enters via: NodePort · LoadBalancer · Ingress · Gateway     │
   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 🔗 SERVICE network  (stable virtual IPs, e.g. 10.96.0.0/12)    │
   │    kube-proxy DNATs a Service VIP → a ready Pod IP             │
   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 📦 POD network  (real pod IPs, e.g. 10.244.0.0/16)            │
   │    assigned by the CNI · flat · every pod reaches every pod     │
   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 🖧 NODE network  (the machines/VMs, e.g. 192.168.1.0/24)       │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   easypj-web pod 10.244.1.5  ──reaches──▶  easypj-db 10.244.2.4 (no NAT)
   a client hits the Service VIP → kube-proxy picks a ready easypj-web pod

CNI Plugins — Your Choice as Admin

🐯
Calico

Most popular. Full NetworkPolicy, BGP routing. Common in CKA environments.

🐝
Cilium

eBPF-based, deep observability (Hubble), high performance. NetworkPolicy +.

🟦
Flannel

Simple VXLAN overlay, easy setup — but no NetworkPolicy.

🕸️
Weave

Encrypted mesh, auto-discovery, NetworkPolicy support.

📖 CKA task: install a CNI right after kubeadm init

A fresh cluster's pods (including CoreDNS) sit Pending and nodes stay NotReady until a CNI is installed — e.g. kubectl apply -f calico.yaml. "No CNI" is a classic NotReady cause: the fix is install a CNI, not restart the kubelet.

Why it's all pluggable — the three "sockets" (CRI · CNI · CSI)
   🤖 kubelet   ──CRI──▶  🐋 containerd / CRI-O          RUN containers
   pod network ──CNI──▶  🌐 Calico / Cilium / Flannel   WIRE pods (give IPs)
   volumes     ──CSI──▶  🧱 EBS / PD / Ceph / NFS driver ATTACH storage
   📖 CRI = runtime · CNI = network · CSI = storage — swap the plug, K8s is unchanged.

The Rules of the Kubernetes Network Model

Every CNI must honour the same contract — four rules that make the "flat network" promise concrete. Memorize these; they're the foundation of all Part 5 troubleshooting:

#RuleWhy it matters
1Every Pod gets its own unique IPNo port-mapping juggling — each pod is a "real host" on the network
2All Pods reach all Pods without NATThe destination sees the real source pod IP (flat L3 network)
3Nodes reach all Pods without NATThe kubelet & health checks talk to pods directly
4A Pod sees its own IP as others see itNo surprising address translation inside the pod
📖 CoreDNS — names instead of IPs

Pods come and go with changing IPs, so apps address each other by name. CoreDNS (a Deployment in kube-system, fronted by the kube-dns Service, usually 10.96.0.10) resolves Service names to ClusterIPs — e.g. easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local. Every pod's /etc/resolv.conf points at it. If name resolution breaks cluster-wide, suspect CoreDNS first (full chapter: Ch 19).

⚠️ kube-proxy vs CNI — keep them separate when debugging

The CNI implements rules 1–4 (pod-to-pod). kube-proxy implements the Service abstraction on top (VIP → pod). So: pods can ping each other by IP but a Service is unreachable → kube-proxy/endpoints problem; pods can't reach each other by IP at all → CNI problem. That one split routes most networking tickets.

3.6 Static Pods — an Admin-Only Concept

Static pods are managed directly by the kubelet on one node — not by the scheduler or API server. They're how kubeadm runs the control plane itself, and they're tested directly on the CKA.

📦
Regular pods

Created via the API server (kubectl) → stored in etcd → scheduled by the scheduler → managed by controllers.

📌
Static pods

Created by the kubelet from YAML in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. The kubelet watches that dir and owns the lifecycle. Drop a file → pod appears; remove it → pod gone.

💡 The control plane IS static pods

On a kubeadm cluster, the apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager, and etcd all run as static pods — which is why you configure them by editing YAML in the manifests dir (the kubelet reloads automatically):

terminal — the control-plane static pods
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml

kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep controlplane
# etcd-controlplane                       1/1  Running   ← note the -<nodename> suffix
# kube-apiserver-controlplane             1/1  Running
# kube-controller-manager-controlplane    1/1  Running
# kube-scheduler-controlplane             1/1  Running

Creating a Custom Static Pod

/etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-easypj.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: static-easypj
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  containers:
  - name: easypj
    image: easypj:v1
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
⚠️ Static-pod facts the exam loves
  • You cannot kubectl delete a static pod — the kubelet instantly recreates it. Remove the manifest file instead.
  • The kubelet creates a read-only "mirror pod" in the API so you can see it; that's why the name carries a -<nodename> suffix.
  • The watched directory is set by staticPodPath in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml.
  • Static pods (kubelet-managed) ≠ DaemonSets (API-managed) — both put one pod per node, but only DaemonSets are API objects.

etcd Restore — the Companion Procedure

You saw backup in §3.2; restore is the other half (and a classic exam task). Always restore to a new data dir, then repoint the etcd static pod at it:

terminal — etcd restore
# 1) restore the snapshot into a NEW directory
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored

# 2) edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml → point the data hostPath
#    volume from /var/lib/etcd  →  /var/lib/etcd-restored

# 3) the kubelet sees the manifest change & recreates etcd automatically
# 4) verify
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
kubectl get nodes
🚨 Restore gotcha

--data-dir must be a new path (e.g. /var/lib/etcd-restored), then repoint the manifest. Restoring over the live dir while etcd runs can corrupt it. Full DR drill in Chapter 29.

Component Quick Reference — Ports · Config · Logs

ComponentPortConfig / manifestLogs
kube-apiserver6443/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yamlkubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-*
etcd2379/2380/etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yamlkubectl logs -n kube-system etcd-*
kube-scheduler10259…/kube-scheduler.yamlkubectl logs -n kube-system kube-scheduler-*
controller-manager10257…/kube-controller-manager.yamlkubectl logs -n kube-system kube-controller-manager-*
kubelet10250/var/lib/kubelet/config.yamljournalctl -u kubelet -f
kube-proxy10256ConfigMap kube-proxykubectl logs -n kube-system kube-proxy-*
containerd—/etc/containerd/config.tomljournalctl -u containerd
CoreDNS53ConfigMap corednskubectl logs -n kube-system coredns-*
💡 Key file paths to memorize
  • /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — static-pod manifests (control plane)
  • /etc/kubernetes/pki/ — all cluster certs (CA, server, client)
  • /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf — the admin kubeconfig
  • /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml — kubelet config (incl. staticPodPath)
  • /var/lib/etcd/ — etcd data directory
  • /etc/cni/net.d/ & /opt/cni/bin/ — CNI config & binaries

3.7 Node Health & Control-Plane ↔ Node Communication

§3.3 named the node's components; this is how the control plane knows a node is alive, how much it can schedule onto it, and how the two halves talk securely. It's the backbone of "node NotReady" troubleshooting (30% domain).

① Node status conditions — the health report

Each Node object carries a set of conditions (see them with kubectl describe node). Ready=True means healthy & schedulable; the four "pressure" conditions are early-warning flags.

ConditionProblem stateTypical cause
ReadyTrue = healthy · False/Unknown = problemkubelet down, lost heartbeat, runtime/CNI broken
MemoryPressureTrue = low memorynode RAM nearly exhausted → starts evicting pods
DiskPressureTrue = low diskfull disk / image cache → eviction + image GC
PIDPressureTrue = too many processesfork bomb / runaway workload
NetworkUnavailableTrue = node network not configuredCNI not installed / route missing

② Heartbeats, the node Lease & the eviction timeline

A node proves it's alive two ways: the kubelet renews a lightweight Lease in the kube-node-lease namespace (one per node, ~every 10s — the cheap, frequent heartbeat) and posts a fuller .status update whenever something changes (or periodically). When heartbeats stop, the node controller runs a fixed clock:

what happens when a node goes silent
   t = 0s     kubelet stops renewing its Lease / status   (node crashed, network cut)
   t ≈ 50s    node controller marks the node  Ready = Unknown   (node-monitor-grace-period)
              └─ adds taint  node.kubernetes.io/unreachable:NoExecute   (or …/not-ready)
   t ≈ 5min   pods without a matching toleration are EVICTED & rescheduled elsewhere
              └─ eviction is rate-limited so a big outage doesn't stampede the cluster
   kubectl get lease -n kube-node-lease     ← see each node's heartbeat

🔑 This is why "I rebooted a node and my pods vanished a few minutes later" is expected — the ~5-minute eviction timer fired. A pod's tolerations for node.kubernetes.io/unreachable / not-ready (with tolerationSeconds) control how quickly it's moved.

③ Capacity vs Allocatable — what the scheduler actually sees

A node's Capacity is its total hardware; Allocatable is what's left for your pods after reservations for the kubelet, the OS, and an eviction buffer. The scheduler only ever fills Allocatable — which is why a pod can sit Pending even though the node "looks" half-empty.

   NODE CAPACITY   (e.g. 4 CPU / 16Gi)
   ├─ kube-reserved       kubelet, container runtime
   ├─ system-reserved     OS, sshd, systemd
   ├─ eviction-threshold  safety buffer (e.g. memory.available < 100Mi)
   └─ ALLOCATABLE   ◀── the only slice the scheduler can place pods into
   kubectl describe node node-1     → shows Capacity and Allocatable side by side

④ Control-plane ↔ node communication — the trust asymmetry

Traffic from a node into the control plane is secured by default; traffic from the control plane out to nodes is the leg you must harden.

DirectionPathSecurity
Node → control planekubelet / kube-proxy → apiserver :6443✅ TLS + auth + RBAC by default — the one hub everything dials
CP → kubeletapiserver → kubelet :10250 (logs, exec, port-forward, metrics)⚠️ HTTPS, but the apiserver won't verify the kubelet's cert unless you set --kubelet-certificate-authority
CP → nodes / pods / servicesapiserver → cluster IPs⚠️ plain HTTP by default — unsafe over untrusted networks; use the Konnectivity service for a secured tunnel

💡 Mental model: everything dials the apiserver (secure, single front door); the apiserver dialing back out to nodes is the weaker leg — Konnectivity (the konnectivity-agent/server pair) wraps it in a managed tunnel for production.

Under the Hood — how the control plane stays consistent & highly available

The components in §3.2 are simple to name; the machinery that makes several copies of them cooperate without conflict is where real understanding lives. Four mechanisms do the heavy lifting.

① Leader election via Lease — how scheduler & controller-manager run HA

You can run 3 schedulers and 3 controller-managers for high availability, but if all of them acted at once they'd fight (three controllers each creating the "missing" pod). So they're active-passive: only one is the leader at a time, chosen by a Lease object the others watch.

   3 kube-scheduler replicas         🗄️ a Lease object in kube-system
   ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │ sched-1  │ │ sched-2  │ │ sched-3  │ ────▶ │ Lease "kube-scheduler"    │
   │ LEADER ✅ │ │ standby  │ │ standby  │      │ holder: sched-1           │
   └────┬─────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘      │ renewTime: …(every ~2s)   │
        │ only the leader schedules            └──────────────────────────┘
        └─ stops renewing (crash) → a standby grabs the Lease → becomes leader
   kubectl get lease -n kube-system   ← see who holds it
🔑 Why it matters: "I have 3 control-plane nodes but only one scheduler seems to work" is correct — the other two are hot standbys. Check kubectl get lease -n kube-system to see the current holder.
② The Binding subresource — how the scheduler actually places a pod

The scheduler doesn't "move" a pod. It computes the best node, then makes a tiny API call — a Binding — that sets the pod's nodeName. The kubelet on that node then notices "a pod is assigned to me" and runs it. Scheduling is just one field being written.

   scheduler picks node2  ──POST /api/v1/namespaces/easypj/pods/easypj-web-x/binding──▶ 📡 apiserver
   apiserver sets pod.spec.nodeName = "node2"  ──▶ 🗄️ etcd
   🤖 kubelet(node2) is watching pods where nodeName == its own → sees it → starts it
   💡 you can hand-schedule by setting nodeName yourself (bypasses the scheduler entirely)
③ API Priority & Fairness (APF) — keeping the apiserver alive under load

Because everything goes through the apiserver, a flood of requests (a buggy controller, a stampede of kubelets) could starve it. APF classifies incoming requests into priority levels and fair-queues them, so critical traffic (leader election, node heartbeats) isn't drowned out by bulk list calls.

ConceptWhat it does
FlowSchemaMatches requests (by user/verb/resource) → assigns them to a priority level
PriorityLevelConfigurationReserves concurrency shares + a fair queue per level
EffectA misbehaving client is throttled (HTTP 429) instead of taking down the API for everyone
④ The aggregation layer — extending the API itself

Beyond CRDs, you can register a second API server behind the main one via an APIService. The apiserver proxies a slice of the API path to it. That's how metrics-server serves metrics.k8s.io (powering kubectl top) — it's not a CRD, it's an aggregated apiserver.

⑤ REST + watch — the API machinery everything is built on

The apiserver is a RESTful server: every object is a URL, and the usual HTTP verbs act on it. The magic extra is WATCH — a long-lived stream of changes that lets components react instantly instead of polling. That single mechanism is how the scheduler, controllers, and kubelets all stay in sync.

   REST verbs on a resource:
     GET    /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/easypj/deployments/easypj-web   read one
     LIST   /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/easypj/deployments              read all
     POST / PUT / PATCH / DELETE                                     create / replace / modify / remove

   WATCH (the key to reactivity):
     GET …/deployments?watch=true&resourceVersion=4821
        ──▶ keeps the connection OPEN and streams events as they happen:
            ADDED {…}   MODIFIED {…rv:4822}   MODIFIED {…rv:4830}   DELETED {…}
     each event carries the new resourceVersion → a client can resume the stream
     after a disconnect from exactly where it left off (no missed & no duplicate work)
ConceptWhat it gives you
LIST then WATCHGet the full state once, then only the deltas — the pattern every informer uses
resourceVersionA cursor: "stream changes since here" + the basis of optimistic concurrency
watch cacheThe apiserver serves watches from memory, so thousands of watchers don't hammer etcd
kubectl get -wIs literally a watch stream you can see in your terminal
🔑 Why this is the whole design: components never call each other — they all watch the apiserver and react to changes. That's the loose coupling that makes Kubernetes resilient: a component that was briefly down just re-LISTs and resumes watching, catching up to current state automatically.
🔑 Tie it together: the apiserver isn't just a CRUD endpoint — it's a REST + watch hub (the API machinery), a consistency & fairness hub (APF), a placement coordinator (Binding), an HA arbiter (Leases), and an extensible surface (aggregation). Master these and "the control plane" stops being a black box.

🔬 Deeper (exam + beyond): reads can be served from the apiserver's watch cache (fast, slightly behind) or forced consistent; every object carries a resourceVersion for optimistic concurrency (Ch 1 UTH); controllers are built on informers (shared list-watch + cache) feeding workqueues with rate-limiting and retries; and the node controller's NotReady (~40s) → eviction (~5min) timers are why a briefly-down node doesn't instantly lose its pods.

⑥ The full pod-creation trace — what happens inside §3.4's 8 steps

§3.4 showed the journey; here is the internal trace — the named admission plugins, the scheduler's filter/score plugins, and the exact CRI calls the kubelet makes. This is the depth CKA troubleshooting questions live at.

kubectl run easypj-web --image=easypj:v1
   │
   ▼  STAGE 1 — apiserver: authN → authZ → admission → etcd
 📡 kube-apiserver
   ├─ a. AuthN      validate the bearer token (who are you?) → user: easypj-admin
   ├─ b. AuthZ      RBAC: may easypj-admin CREATE pods in ns easypj? → yes
   ├─ c. Admission chain (mutate, then validate):
   │       MutatingAdmissionWebhook   → inject sidecars / defaults
   │       LimitRanger                → apply default requests & limits
   │       PodSecurity                → enforce baseline / restricted
   │       ValidatingAdmissionWebhook → reject if a policy is violated
   ├─ d. WRITE      /registry/pods/easypj/easypj-web  → 🗄️ etcd (quorum write)
   └─ e. RETURN     201 Created → "pod/easypj-web created"
   │
   ▼  STAGE 2 — scheduler: watch → filter → score → bind
 📋 kube-scheduler  (watches pods where .spec.nodeName == "")
   ├─ FILTER (predicates) — drop nodes that CAN'T run it:
   │     NodeReady? · CPU/mem fits requests? · nodeSelector/affinity? · taints tolerated? · hostPort free?
   ├─ SCORE  (priorities) — rank the survivors 0–100:
   │     NodeResourcesFit(LeastAllocated) · NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation · ImageLocality · NodeAffinity
   └─ BIND: POST …/pods/easypj-web/binding → sets .spec.nodeName = "node-1" → 🗄️ etcd
   │
   ▼  STAGE 3 — kubelet → CRI → containerd → runc
 🤖 kubelet(node-1)  (watches pods assigned to it)
   └─ calls the CRI (gRPC), in order:
        RunPodSandbox   → create the pause container + network namespace (CNI assigns the IP)
        PullImage       → fetch easypj:v1 layers from the registry
        CreateContainer → set up namespaces + cgroups + overlay rootfs
        StartContainer  → exec the easypj process
      containerd builds the OCI bundle → runc create → runc start
        runc: clone() with namespace flags · write cgroups · pivot_root · exec
   └─ kubelet reports status → Running → Ready (once probes pass) → 🗄️ etcd
🔑 Map a failure to its stage: hangs at kubectl → Stage 1 (apiserver unreachable); stuck Pending → Stage 2 (nothing survived filtering — taints / resources / selector); stuck ContainerCreating → Stage 3 RunPodSandbox/PullImage (CNI, or image/registry); CrashLoopBackOff → Stage 3 StartContainer (the app itself — read kubectl logs).
⑦ Static pods — the bootstrap paradox solved

The control plane (apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) runs as pods — which is a chicken-and-egg problem: how do you run pods before the apiserver that schedules them even exists? The answer is the static pod — the kubelet reads manifests straight from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and runs them itself, with no apiserver and no scheduler involved.

   boot order on a control-plane node
   ① kubelet starts             (a systemd service — it does NOT need the API)
   ② reads /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
   ③ runs the apiserver static pod    (CRI → containerd → runc)
   ④ the apiserver is now up
   ⑤ kubelet registers a read-only MIRROR pod for it in the API
        → visible as kube-apiserver-<nodename>   (that's where the suffix comes from)
   ⑥ kubelet runs the remaining manifests: etcd, scheduler, controller-manager
   ⑦ control plane operational → normal, API-driven scheduling begins
🔁 Restarting a static pod (you can't kubectl delete it): move the manifest out and back — sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/ && sleep 20 && sudo mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — the kubelet sees the file vanish (stops the pod), then reappear (recreates it). Editing the manifest in place also triggers a restart.
🔑 CKA insight: if you SSH to a control-plane node and kubectl won't respond, the apiserver static pod may be down — there's no API to ask. Check it directly: sudo crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver (is the container running?) and sudo ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (is the manifest present?). A missing or corrupt manifest takes the entire control plane down.
⑧ A few more control-plane internals worth knowing
TopicWhat to know
Lease fieldsa leader-election Lease carries holderIdentity (who holds it), leaseDurationSeconds (TTL — ~15s for scheduler/controller-manager) and renewTime (the leader rewrites it every couple of seconds). If a renewal is missed past the TTL, a standby claims the Lease — so failover takes up to about one lease duration.
APF: 429 vs 503429 Too Many Requests = API Priority & Fairness fair-queued you and the queue/wait was exceeded → back off & retry. 503 = a priority level with no queueing, or the server is genuinely overloaded → investigate. exempt flows (e.g. system:masters, health checks) bypass APF so a misconfig can't lock you out of the API.
Admission failurePolicyif a webhook errors or times out: Fail (default) rejects the request — safe for policy/security; Ignore lets it through — for optional webhooks. Mutating runs before validating by design, so validators judge the final object (after sidecars/defaults are injected).

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Control plane decides, worker nodes run — sort every problem into "decision" vs "run" and you've found the half to look in.
  • Only the apiserver talks to etcd — and everything else talks only to the apiserver (the single choke point).
  • The kubelet is a systemd service, not a pod — debug it with systemctl / journalctl, never kubectl.
  • The control plane runs AS static pods in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — edit the YAML, the kubelet reloads.
  • CRI · CNI · CSI are the three plug points (runtime · network · storage).
  • Match symptom → component: NotReady=kubelet · Pending=scheduler · lost state=etcd · kubectl dead=apiserver.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Traps
  • kubelet ≠ pod. It's systemd — kubectl get pods won't show it; systemctl status kubelet will.
  • You can't kubectl delete a static pod — the kubelet recreates it. Remove the manifest file from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.
  • apiserver is the single choke point. If it's down, kubectl is useless — switch to crictl / journalctl on the node.
  • Static pod vs DaemonSet. Both = one pod per node, but static = kubelet-managed (mirror pod, -<nodename> suffix), DaemonSet = API object.
  • Scheduler vs controller-manager. Scheduler only places pods; the controller-manager handles replication, nodes, endpoints. Don't conflate.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • apiserver down? Debug from the node: crictl ps -a, crictl logs <apiserver-id>, journalctl -u kubelet.
  • Pods Pending? Suspect the scheduler — kubectl get pods -A | grep Pending then check the scheduler pod/logs.
  • Editing a control-plane component? Just edit its manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — the kubelet restarts it for you.
  • Find the HA leader: kubectl get lease -n kube-system.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 3)

inspect the cluster's anatomy
kubectl get pods -n kube-system            # control-plane + CNI + CoreDNS pods
kubectl get componentstatuses             # cs — control-plane health (older clusters)
kubectl get lease -n kube-system          # who holds leader election
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/             # the static-pod manifests
kubectl get nodes -o wide                 # node roles, versions, IPs

# node-level (when the apiserver is down)
crictl ps -a                              # containers via the CRI
crictl logs <container-id>
journalctl -u kubelet -f                  # live kubelet logs
🧪 Drill — Map the Control Plane

On a control-plane node — predict each output before running it:

  1. List the static-pod manifests.
  2. List the control-plane pods and note the -<nodename> suffix.
  3. Identify the leader of the scheduler/controller-manager.
  4. Tail the apiserver logs.
Show solution
terminal
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/              # etcd · kube-apiserver · kube-scheduler · kube-controller-manager
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep controlplane   # all 4 Running, -controlplane suffix (mirror pods)
kubectl get lease -n kube-system kube-scheduler kube-controller-manager   # HOLDER column = leader
kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-apiserver-controlplane | tail -20        # apiserver logs

What you proved: the control plane is just static pods the kubelet runs; their mirror pods carry the node-name suffix; HA components elect one leader via a Lease; and you can read any control-plane component's logs with kubectl logs (or crictl logs if the apiserver itself is down).

🧠 Chapter 3 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the architecture — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Which component is the ONLY one that reads/writes etcd?
Show Answer
Answer

The kube-apiserver. Every other component (scheduler, controller-manager, kubelet) reaches state through the apiserver, never etcd directly.

Explanation

This star topology is why an etcd backup = a cluster backup, and why securing/operating the apiserver is so critical.

Q2
A node shows NotReady. Which agent do you check first, and how?
Show Answer
Answer

The kubelet (it's a systemd service, not a pod), then the runtime and CNI:

node NotReady — first checks (on the node)
systemctl status kubelet        # is the agent even up?
journalctl -u kubelet -f        # why did it fail?
systemctl status containerd     # runtime alive?
ls /etc/cni/net.d/              # CNI configured?
Explanation

NotReady = the node can't report healthy. Usual causes: kubelet down, swap on, expired cert, missing CNI, cgroup-driver mismatch.

Q3
Trace what happens after kubectl apply -f easypj-deploy.yaml.
Show Answer
Answer

Each actor reconciles its own slice — no central script:

what kubectl apply sets in motion
 kubectl apply ─▶ 📡 apiserver (authN → authZ → admission) ─▶ 🗄️ etcd   (persist desired state)
                       │
                       ├─ 🔄 controller-manager:  Deployment ─▶ ReplicaSet ─▶ Pods
                       └─ 📋 scheduler:  filter → score → BIND (sets nodeName)
                              ▼
                    🤖 kubelet:  pull image → start container → 🌐 CNI assigns the pod IP
                              ▼
                    🔀 kube-proxy programs Service routing ─────▶ Running ✅
Explanation

No central script — each actor reconciles its own slice. Knowing the order lets you map any symptom to a step (§3.4).

Q4
The scheduler is down. What symptom appears, and on which objects?
Show Answer
Answer

New pods stay Pending (no node gets assigned). Existing pods keep running. Spot it: kubectl get pods -A | grep Pending, then check the scheduler pod/logs.

Explanation

The scheduler only sets nodeName; with it down, pods are created but never bound.

Q5
Create a static pod on a node, then delete it. Which files/commands?
Show Answer
Answer

The kubelet watches a directory; creating/deleting the file creates/deletes the pod:

static pod — create & delete (on the node)
# create: drop a manifest where the kubelet watches
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-easypj.yaml   # path = staticPodPath in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
# delete: remove the FILE — `kubectl delete` just gets recreated
sudo rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-easypj.yaml
Explanation

Static pods are owned by the kubelet, not the API; the API only shows a read-only mirror pod.

Q6
Name the network layers and what routes each.
Show Answer
Answer

Three layers, each programmed by a different actor (all riding on the node/infra network):

LayerAddressesWho programs it
Pod networkreal pod IPs (flat, no NAT)the CNI plugin
Service networkstable virtual IPs (ClusterIP)apiserver assigns the IP · EndpointSlice controller tracks Ready pods · kube-proxy programs the routing
ExternalNodePort · LoadBalancer · Ingress/Gatewaythe cluster edge
Explanation

Pods can fail to reach each other (CNI) independently of Services failing (kube-proxy) — keep the layers separate when debugging.

Q7
Which ports does etcd listen on, and for what?
Show Answer
Answer

Two ports, two jobs:

PortPurpose
2379client traffic — the apiserver (and etcdctl) connect here
2380peer traffic — etcd member ↔ member for Raft; only matters in multi-member HA
Explanation

etcdctl uses --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379; 2380 only matters in multi-member HA.

Q8
Why is the apiserver the cluster's single choke point?
Show Answer
Answer

Every read/write of state, every component's watch, and every kubectl call flows through it — and it's the only thing that touches etcd. Down apiserver → no scheduling, no reconciliation, no kubectl (though running pods continue).

Explanation

That's also why it gets HA replicas behind a load balancer and APF to stay alive under load (UTH).

Q9
Explain a controller's reconcile loop using the ReplicaSet example.
Show Answer
Answer

OBSERVE → COMPARE → ACT, forever — a deleted pod is just the next gap to close:

        ┌──────────── reconcile loop (runs forever) ───────────┐
        ▼                                                      │
   OBSERVE actual ──▶ COMPARE to desired ──▶ ACT to close gap ─┘
   (2 pods now)        (spec replicas: 3)     (create 1 pod)
   delete a pod → next pass sees 2 ≠ 3 again → recreates it
Explanation

Level-triggered: it reacts to current state, not events, so it self-heals even if an event is missed.

Q10
What is a "mirror pod" and why does its name end in -<nodename>?
Show Answer
Answer

When the kubelet runs a static pod, it creates a read-only mirror pod in the API so you can kubectl get it. The kubelet appends its node name (e.g. etcd-controlplane) to show which node owns it — and to keep names unique across nodes.

Explanation

You can view but not control a mirror pod via the API; the real lifecycle lives with the kubelet and the manifest file.

⚙️ Chapter 3 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — a broken state or a "trace it" question, with the real answer.

Q11
You SSH to the control-plane node and kubectl get nodes returns "The connection to the server …:6443 was refused." How do you diagnose it?
Show Answer
Answer

The apiserver (a static pod) isn't serving. kubectl can't help, so go node-level:

debug from the node
crictl ps -a | grep kube-apiserver        # is its container even up / crashlooping?
crictl logs <apiserver-container-id>       # why it won't start
journalctl -u kubelet | tail -30          # kubelet errors creating the static pod
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml   # a typo here = no apiserver
Explanation

A bad edit to the apiserver manifest is the classic cause — fix the YAML and the kubelet recreates the pod.

Q12
What are static pods — where defined, which component manages them, how distinguished from normal pods?
Show Answer
Answer

Pods defined as YAML in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (the staticPodPath), managed directly by the kubelet (not scheduler/apiserver). Distinguished by the -<nodename> suffix on their API mirror pod and by not being deletable via kubectl.

Explanation

This is how kubeadm runs the control plane — and a frequent exam task (create/repair one).

Q13
Explain the scheduler's decision process for a pod with no nodeName.
Show Answer
Answer

Filter (predicates): drop nodes that can't run it — insufficient CPU/mem, unsatisfied nodeSelector/affinity, untolerated taints, PV topology. Score (priorities): rank survivors by spread, resource balance, affinity preferences. Bind: write nodeName via the Binding subresource to the top node.

Explanation

If no node survives filtering, the pod stays Pending with a "FailedScheduling" event explaining why.

Q14
Name at least 5 controllers in the controller-manager and what each does.
Show Answer
Answer

Node (heartbeats → NotReady/eviction) · ReplicaSet (keep pod count) · Deployment (manage ReplicaSets / rollouts) · Endpoint/EndpointSlice (Service → pod IPs) · ServiceAccount (default SA per namespace) · Job (run-to-completion). Each watches one resource and reconciles drift.

Explanation

All run as goroutines in one process — kill the controller-manager and all of this self-healing stops.

Q15
How does the kubelet know which static-pod manifests to watch?
Show Answer
Answer

The staticPodPath setting in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (default /etc/kubernetes/manifests). The kubelet watches that directory and creates/updates/deletes pods as files appear/change/disappear.

Explanation

Change that path and you change where the kubelet looks — handy to know when manifests "aren't taking effect."

Q16
What is CoreDNS's role? If DNS fails inside a pod, what do you check?
Show Answer
Answer

CoreDNS provides in-cluster DNS — it resolves Service names (e.g. easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local) to ClusterIPs. If DNS fails: check the CoreDNS pods/logs in kube-system, the coredns ConfigMap (Corefile), and the kube-dns Service; test from a pod with nslookup kubernetes.default.

Explanation

CoreDNS runs as a Deployment (not DaemonSet). A bad Corefile can CrashLoop it and break name resolution cluster-wide (Ch 19).

Q17
Explain the apiserver's authentication vs authorization vs admission stages.
Show Answer
Answer

AuthN: who are you? (client cert / token / OIDC) → 401 if it fails. AuthZ: are you allowed this verb on this resource? (RBAC) → 403 if not. Admission: mutate (set defaults / inject) then validate (PodSecurity, webhooks, quota) → reject if a policy fails. Then persist to etcd.

Explanation

The error tells you the stage: "Unauthorized"=authN, "Forbidden"=authZ, "admission webhook denied"=admission.

Q18
A node's pod CIDR is 10.244.1.0/24. What does that mean?
Show Answer
Answer

That node hands out pod IPs from 10.244.1.0/24 (≈254 addresses) — so pods on it get 10.244.1.x. Each node gets a distinct slice of the cluster pod-CIDR (e.g. node2 = 10.244.2.0/24), and the CNI routes between slices so the pod network stays flat.

Explanation

If pods can't get IPs or cross-node traffic fails, suspect CNI / pod-CIDR misconfiguration.

Q19
kubectl get componentstatuses shows the scheduler Unhealthy. What could cause it, and how do you investigate?
Show Answer
Answer

The scheduler static pod is down or its health endpoint is unreachable — often a bad /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml edit. Investigate: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler, kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-scheduler-* (or crictl logs), and re-check the manifest.

Explanation

(Note: componentstatuses is deprecated/flaky on newer clusters — prefer checking the pods directly.)

Q20
Describe the complete communication flow between components when a user creates a resource.
Show Answer
Answer

User → apiserver (authN/authZ/admission) → etcd (persist). Controllers watch the apiserver and react (Deployment→RS→Pods); the scheduler watches for unbound pods and binds them; the target node's kubelet watches for its pods and runs them via the runtime; kube-proxy updates Service routing; status flows back kubelet → apiserver → etcd. Everything is apiserver-mediated watches — no direct component-to-component calls.

Explanation

This hub-and-watch design (loose coupling) is why the cluster is resilient: a briefly-down component just resumes from current state when it returns.

📌 Chapter 3 Visual Summary — the whole cluster, annotated
   ┌──────────────────────────────── ☸️ CLUSTER ───────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 🧠 CONTROL PLANE (decides)        every request & watch flows through apiserver │
   │   📡 apiserver :6443  ── the ONLY door, the ONLY etcd client                    │
   │        │  authN → authZ(RBAC) → admission                                       │
   │        ├── 🗄️ etcd :2379/2380   ALL state (Raft quorum)                          │
   │        ├── 📋 scheduler          filter → score → BIND (sets nodeName)           │
   │        └── 🔄 controller-mgr     reconcile loops (node·RS·endpoint·SA)           │
   │  ───────────────────────────── apiserver ⇅ nodes (watch) ──────────────────────│
   │ 💪 WORKER NODE                                                                   │
   │   🤖 kubelet (systemd, not a pod) · 🌐 kube-proxy (Service routing) · 🐋 runtime  │
   │   🌐 CNI gives each 📦 pod a flat IP   ·   💾 CSI attaches volumes                │
   │   ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐                                                 │
   │   │📦 easypj-web│ │🐘 postgres  │   the control plane itself = static pods in     │
   │   │  :8000      │ │  :5432      │   /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (kubelet-run)      │
   │   └────────────┘ └────────────┘                                                 │
   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   Decide (control plane) vs Run (nodes) · only apiserver→etcd · symptom→component = the exam.

In words: A cluster splits cleanly into two halves. The control plane decides; the worker nodes run. The apiserver (:6443) is the only way in and the only component that talks to etcd — every request first passes authentication → authorization (RBAC) → admission. etcd (:2379) holds all cluster state, kept consistent by Raft quorum.

Behind the apiserver, the scheduler filters and scores nodes then binds each pod (sets nodeName), and the controller-manager runs the reconcile loops (node, ReplicaSet, endpoint, service-account…). On each worker node, the kubelet runs the containers (it's a systemd service, not a pod), kube-proxy programs Service routing, the runtime executes containers, CNI gives each pod a flat IP, and CSI attaches storage. The control plane itself runs as static pods the kubelet starts from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.

The takeaway: hold the "decide vs run" split and "only the apiserver touches etcd" in your head, and troubleshooting becomes a lookup — match the symptom to the responsible component. That mapping is the heart of the exam's Architecture and Troubleshooting domains.

Chapter 4 · Core Kubernetes Objects — The Admin's Toolkit

These six objects are the nouns of every exam task and every easypj manifest: Pod, ReplicaSet, Deployment, Service, Namespace, and the labels that wire them together. Chapter 3 showed you the machines; this chapter shows you the things you actually create on them. Master how they nest and reference each other and you can read any manifest at a glance.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 📖 Core Objects 🎯 Workloads 15% · Services 20% 🐍 easypj / jobpost

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Pods — the smallest unit; single vs multi-container (sidecar)
  • ✅ ReplicaSets — self-healing by keeping a desired pod count
  • ✅ Deployments — rolling updates, rollback, the ownership chain
  • ✅ Services — stable networking for ephemeral pods (4 types)
  • ✅ Namespaces — what they isolate, and what they don't
  • ✅ Labels · Selectors · Annotations — the glue that connects everything
  • ✅ The full object relationship map — the one picture to memorize
🎓 CKA Relevance
Workloads & Scheduling 15% Services & Networking 20%
🧩 Object mastery = exam speed

Almost every CKA task is "create object X, wire it to Y, fix why Z isn't working." You'll create Deployments, expose them with Services, and chase down empty endpoints. Learn each object imperatively (fast kubectl create … $do) and declaratively (the YAML), and watch the labels — they're where most wiring bugs hide.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 4 Learning Arc

We climb the workload ladder (Pod → ReplicaSet → Deployment), add stable networking (Service) and isolation (Namespace), learn the glue (labels), then assemble everything into one relationship map.
