📋 One-shot environment readiness check

Paste this on any fresh cluster to verify the whole stack at once — kubectl, API reachability, nodes, control-plane pods, DNS, and metrics:

readiness-check.sh
#!/bin/bash
echo "── CKA environment readiness check ──"
echo -n "kubectl : "; kubectl version --client -o yaml >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo OK || echo "❌ not installed"
echo -n "cluster : "; kubectl cluster-info 2>/dev/null | head -1 || echo "❌ unreachable"
echo    "nodes   :"; kubectl get nodes -o wide 2>/dev/null || echo "  ❌ cannot list nodes"
echo    "control plane:"
kubectl get pods -n kube-system \
  -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -E "etcd|apiserver|scheduler|controller"
echo -n "CoreDNS : "; kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --no-headers 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $3}'
echo -n "metrics : "; kubectl top nodes 2>/dev/null | head -1 || echo "⚠️ enable metrics-server"
⚠️ Minikube convenience ≠ real cluster

Two timing/default traps when you graduate to kubeadm (Part 3): (1) metrics-server needs ~60 s after enabling before kubectl top works — it has to scrape a window of metrics first, so an immediate top errors with "metrics not available." (2) storage-provisioner is on by default in Minikube but absent on kubeadm — there a PersistentVolumeClaim stays Pending forever until you install a provisioner/StorageClass yourself (Ch 22). The convenience that makes Minikube great for learning is exactly what the exam's bare clusters won't give you.

✅ Chapter 5 done — your environment is ready

You have a working cluster, kubectl with completion + aliases, contexts under control, and the add-ons enabled. A one-line readiness check: kubectl version --client && kubectl get nodes && kubectl get pods -n kube-system && kubectl top nodes. Next (Ch 6): the kubectl fluency that multiplies your exam score.

Under the Hood — how kubectl finds, merges & authenticates with a cluster

"kubectl just connects" hides a precise resolution order. Knowing it turns "why am I on the wrong cluster?" into a two-second fix.

① Which kubeconfig wins — strict precedence
   1. --kubeconfig=FILE       ← explicit flag (highest priority)
   2. $KUBECONFIG=a:b:c       ← colon-separated list → MERGED (first file wins a clash)
   3. ~/.kube/config         ← the default
   chosen file → read clusters/users/contexts → act on current-context (or --context=X)
🔑 Merging: with $KUBECONFIG=a:b:c every context is visible at once and you switch with use-context — no single giant file needed. On a name clash the first file wins.
② Identity & auth tricks worth knowing
MechanismWhat it does
exec credential pluginkubeconfig calls an external binary for a short-lived token — how cloud auth works (aws eks get-token, gke-gcloud-auth-plugin)
impersonation--as=jane --as-group=dev acts as another identity (needs RBAC) — the fastest way to test "can this user do X?"
insecure-skip-tls-verifyskips the API server cert check — convenient in labs, a real risk in prod
kubectx / kubenscommunity tools for instant context/namespace switching (krew) — handy off-exam
③ How kubectl actually authenticates — the mutual-TLS handshake

Connecting isn't just "open a socket." kubectl and the apiserver run a mutual TLS handshake: the client verifies the server and the server verifies the client — and the client's certificate is its identity.

   kubectl (client)                                   📡 apiserver :6443
   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   ① TCP + ClientHello ────────────────────────────▶
   ② ◀─ server Certificate (CN=kube-apiserver, SANs)    client verifies it against
        certificate-authority(-data) from kubeconfig  ✅  (mismatch → connection refused)
   ③ client Certificate ───────────────────────────▶   apiserver verifies it was
        (CN=kubernetes-admin, O=system:masters)          signed by the cluster CA ✅
   ④ encrypted session ──── kubectl get pods ───────▶   authN done → authZ (RBAC) → respond
   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   🔑 the cert's  CN → your USERNAME  ·  O → your GROUP(s)
      RBAC RoleBindings then grant that username/group its permissions (Ch 24)
Auth methodIdentity comes fromUsed by
TLS client certificatecert CN → username · O → groupkubeadm admin (kubernetes-admin / system:masters), control-plane components
Bearer token (JWT)token subject & claimsServiceAccounts (pods), OIDC users, CI, managed clusters
🔑 The insight cka_1 only hints at: Kubernetes has no "User" objects — your identity is whatever the apiserver extracts from your cert or token at handshake time. That's why "creating a user" (Ch 26) really means issuing a client cert with the right CN/O, and why insecure-skip-tls-verify: true is dangerous — it disables step ②, so a spoofed apiserver would be trusted blindly.
④ Two facts that make it all click: switching context is local, auth is per-request

Two mechanics trip up almost everyone — and the moment they click, kubeconfig stops feeling like magic:

   SWITCHING CONTEXT = editing ONE local field — zero network, nothing in the cluster changes
     kubectl config use-context prod
        └─ just sets  current-context: prod  in ~/.kube/config
           no connection is opened; the NEXT command simply reads the new cluster + user + namespace

   EVERY API CALL re-authenticates from scratch — HTTP is stateless, there is NO login/session
     kubectl get pods   → TLS handshake → present cert/token → authN → authZ → response
     kubectl get svc    → TLS handshake → present cert/token → authN → authZ → response   (all over again)
        no cookie, no "logged-in" state — each request independently carries and proves its identity
🔑 Why this matters: because there is no session, a rotated or expired credential breaks the very next command (not "after you log out") — a classic "it worked five minutes ago" exam panic. And because switching context is purely local, you flip between the exam's ~6 clusters instantly with zero latency. An exec credential plugin (cloud auth) is also invoked per request, but it caches the token until expiry — which is why the first call after a token expires pauses briefly while it refreshes, then is fast again.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Minikube to learn, kubeadm to pass — the exam builds clusters with kubeadm (Part 3).
  • kubeconfig = clusters (where) + users (who) + contexts (the combo); current-context is active.
  • Switch context FIRST, verify, then act — the 4-beat rhythm of every exam task.
  • Set a default namespace with set-context --current --namespace=… so you stop typing -n.
  • Verify any cluster with cluster-info · get nodes · get pods -n kube-system; add-ons unlock top/ingress.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Traps
  • Wrong context = 0 marks. Every question names one — kubectl config use-context <name> before you touch anything.
  • Forgotten namespace. Miss -n (or a default ns) and your object lands in default — graded as missing.
  • Completion not loaded. If kubectl <TAB> is dead: source <(kubectl completion bash) (+ the complete … k line for your alias).
  • Minikube ≠ kubeadm. The exam's kubeadm clusters have real systemd kubelets, real certs, and real multi-node topology — practise on kubeadm too.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • First three lines of any shell: alias k=kubectl · export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml' · source <(kubectl completion bash).
  • One-key namespace: alias kns='kubectl config set-context --current --namespace' → kns easypj-dev.
  • Open every task with use-context then current-context — muscle memory beats memory.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 5)

environment & context essentials
minikube start --nodes=3 --driver=docker     # a multi-node practice cluster
minikube addons enable metrics-server ingress
kubectl config get-contexts | current-context | use-context <name>
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev
kubectl cluster-info ; kubectl get nodes -o wide ; kubectl get pods -n kube-system
kubectl top nodes                            # needs metrics-server
🧪 Drill — Own your contexts in under 3 minutes

Do it before peeking:

  1. From Minikube, create two contexts dev and ops (both → minikube), with namespaces easypj-dev and kube-system.
  2. Switch to dev, verify it's current, and confirm kubectl get pods defaults to easypj-dev.
  3. Switch to ops and list the control-plane pods without typing -n.
Show solution
terminal
kubectl config set-context dev --cluster=minikube --user=minikube --namespace=easypj-dev
kubectl config set-context ops --cluster=minikube --user=minikube --namespace=kube-system
kubectl config use-context dev && kubectl config current-context   # → dev
kubectl get pods                          # scoped to easypj-dev
kubectl config use-context ops
kubectl get pods                          # now lists kube-system control-plane pods

Why: the namespace is baked into the context, so switching context also switches your default scope — exactly the exam workflow.

🧠 Chapter 5 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of environment & context skills — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Name the three sections of a kubeconfig and what each holds.
Show Answer
Answer
SectionHoldsMeans
clustersserver URL + CA certWHERE to connect
usersclient cert/key or tokenWHO you are
contextscluster + user + namespacethe COMBO you switch to
Explanation

current-context names the active one; kubectl config view prints the whole file.

Q2
Switch to the context named prod (command).
Show Answer
Answer
switch context
kubectl config use-context prod
kubectl config current-context   # verify → prod
Explanation

This is the first action of nearly every exam task; always verify after switching.

Q3
Set the current context's default namespace to easypj.
Show Answer
Answer
set namespace
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj
Explanation

--current edits the active context, so you stop appending -n easypj to every command.

Q4
Use two kubeconfig files in one kubectl session.
Show Answer
Answer
list contexts
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/.kube/cfg-prod
kubectl config get-contexts            # all merged contexts now visible
Explanation

Colon-separated list (semicolon on Windows). On a name clash, the first file wins.

Q5
Verify a freshly-built cluster is healthy (three commands).
Show Answer
Answer
cluster health
kubectl cluster-info             # API reachable?
kubectl get nodes                # all Ready?
kubectl get pods -n kube-system  # control plane Running?
Explanation

Same three you run to orient yourself on any unfamiliar exam cluster; add get --raw='/readyz?verbose' for the API's own view.

Q6
What exactly is a "context"?
Show Answer
Answer

A named triple — cluster + user + namespace — that tells kubectl where to connect, who to be, and the default scope. Switching context switches all three at once.

Explanation

It's pure client-side config; switching context changes nothing in the cluster, only which cluster/identity your kubectl uses.

Q7
Enable metrics-server and prove kubectl top works.
Show Answer
Answer
enable addon
minikube addons enable metrics-server
sleep 60                          # give it time to collect
kubectl top nodes                 # CPU/memory per node
Explanation

kubectl top and the HorizontalPodAutoscaler both depend on metrics-server; it's not installed by default.

Q8
Start a 3-node local cluster (command).
Show Answer
Answer
start cluster
minikube start --nodes=3 --driver=docker --cpus=2 --memory=4096
Explanation

Multiple nodes unlock realistic practice for drain/cordon, taints, and affinity.

Q9
Print the current context in one command.
Show Answer
Answer
verify context
kubectl config current-context
Explanation

Run it reflexively before answering — it's the cheapest insurance against working on the wrong cluster.

Q10
KUBECONFIG precedence — flag vs env var vs ~/.kube/config: which wins?
Show Answer
Answer

1. --kubeconfig=FILE (flag) → 2. $KUBECONFIG (env, merged list) → 3. ~/.kube/config (default). Highest present wins.

Explanation

So a stray $KUBECONFIG in your shell silently overrides the default file — a classic "why can't I see my cluster?" gotcha.

⚙️ Chapter 5 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style "do it / fix it" tasks with the real commands.

Q11
The exam opens: "Use context cluster-prod; work in namespace finance." Write the exact commands.
Show Answer
Answer
switch context
kubectl config use-context cluster-prod
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=finance
kubectl config current-context                 # verify → cluster-prod
Explanation

The FIRST action of every question. Skip it and you do flawless work on the wrong cluster = zero marks.

Q12
A node shows NotReady. You SSH in — what are your first three checks?
Show Answer
Answer
diagnose node
kubectl describe node <n> | grep -A8 Conditions   # from control plane
ssh <n>
sudo systemctl status kubelet        # 1 is the agent up?
sudo journalctl -u kubelet | tail -30 # 2 why did it fail?
sudo systemctl status containerd     # 3 runtime alive?
Explanation

NotReady = no recent kubelet heartbeat. Usual causes: kubelet stopped, bad kubelet config/certs, or the runtime is down.

Q13
You only run Minikube but need to practise kubectl drain. What one change makes that possible?
Show Answer
Answer
start cluster
minikube start --nodes=3 --driver=docker
Explanation

drain evicts pods so they can reschedule elsewhere — that needs at least one other Ready node.

Q14
After a reboot, kubectl get nodes says "connection refused" on Minikube. Diagnose & fix.
Show Answer
Answer
start cluster
minikube status                  # host/apiserver state
minikube update-context          # repoint kubeconfig at the (new) IP
# still broken? recreate:
minikube stop && minikube start   # or: minikube delete && minikube start
Explanation

The Minikube IP/port can change across restarts, leaving kubeconfig pointing at a dead endpoint — update-context fixes the stale server URL.

Q15
Merge a teammate's kubeconfig and switch to their staging context.
Show Answer
Answer
switch context
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/Downloads/teammate.yaml
kubectl config get-contexts        # confirm 'staging' appears
kubectl config use-context staging
Explanation

To persist the merge into one file: kubectl config view --flatten > ~/.kube/merged && mv ~/.kube/merged ~/.kube/config.

Q16
Make kubectl top pods work in namespace easypj-dev.
Show Answer
Answer
set namespace
minikube addons enable metrics-server
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev
kubectl top pods                  # after ~60s
Explanation

No metrics-server → top errors with "Metrics API not available."

Q17
In one command, confirm WHICH cluster + namespace you're about to act on.
Show Answer
Answer
current context
kubectl config view --minify    # shows ONLY the current context: cluster, user, namespace
Explanation

--minify trims the view to the active context — faster than eyeballing the whole file.

Q18
Your object landed in default instead of easypj. Which two habits prevent this?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Set the context's default namespace up front: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj. (2) When in doubt, pass -n easypj explicitly on the command.

Explanation

Namespace is per-context; once set, every command defaults to it — fewer keystrokes, fewer misses.

Q19
A bare exam shell has no k alias or completion. Set both up.
Show Answer
Answer
shell setup
alias k=kubectl
source <(kubectl completion bash)
complete -o default -F __start_kubectl k    # completion for the alias too
Explanation

Completion + a short alias are the single biggest time-savers in a 2-hour terminal exam.

Q20
A freshly-joined kubeadm node is NotReady — but a Minikube node never is. Why, and the fix?
Show Answer
Answer

kubeadm does not install a CNI; until you apply one, the kubelet can't set up pod networking and reports NotReady. Minikube auto-installs a CNI, so you never see it there.

install CNI
kubectl apply -f https://.../calico.yaml   # install a CNI → node goes Ready
Explanation

This is the #1 "all nodes NotReady after kubeadm init/join" cause (Ch 9) — the fix is "install a CNI," not "restart kubelet."

📌 Chapter 5 Visual Summary — one laptop, many clusters, one context at a time
   💻 your laptop
      └─ kubectl ──reads──▶ ~/.kube/config   (or a $KUBECONFIG merge)
                             ├─ clusters (WHERE)  ├─ users (WHO)  └─ contexts (the COMBO)
                             current-context ─┐
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┐
        ▼                                      ▼                                  ▼
   ☸️ minikube                       ☸️ easypj-staging                  ☸️ easypj-prod
   use-context minikube              use-context dev (ns:easypj-dev)    use-context prod (ns:easypj-prod)
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   the rhythm:  use-context ▶ verify (current-context) ▶ act.  Switch FIRST — every time.  ☸️

In words: your laptop's kubectl reads one kubeconfig (or a merged set), which holds clusters (where), users (who) and contexts (the combo). The current-context decides which cluster, identity and namespace every command targets — so you point kubectl at a different cluster simply by switching context, no reconnect needed.

The takeaway: on the exam you'll hop between ~6 clusters; the discipline that saves you is the same three beats every time — use-context → verify → act, with a default namespace set so nothing lands in default by accident.

6.1 The kubectl Syntax Pattern

Every command is the same shape. Learn it once and you can construct any command from memory — even ones you've never used.

kubectl command anatomy
   kubectl    get      pods     easypj-web-x9k     -n easypj-dev   -o wide
   ───────   ─────   ───────   ───────────────   ─────────────   ───────
   binary    VERB    RESOURCE       NAME              FLAGS        (output)

   VERB     get · describe · create · apply · delete · edit · logs · exec ·
            scale · rollout · label · annotate · taint · drain · explain · top
   RESOURCE pods(po) · deploy · svc · no · ns · cm · secret · ing · pv · pvc · sa
   FLAGS    -n ns · -A (all-ns) · -o wide|yaml|json · -l labels · -w (watch) · -f file
💡 Short names save real seconds

po=pods · deploy=deployments · svc=services · no=nodes · ns=namespaces · cm=configmaps · ing=ingress · pv/pvc · sa=serviceaccounts · netpol=networkpolicies. See them all with kubectl api-resources.

6.2 Essential Admin Commands — by Intent

The commands you'll reach for every day, grouped by what you're trying to do:

📋 Get information & 🔍 inspect

look around
kubectl get nodes -o wide                       # IPs, OS, runtime
kubectl get pods -A                             # all pods, all namespaces
kubectl get pods -o yaml                        # the full YAML of each pod
kubectl get pods --sort-by=.status.startTime    # oldest → newest
kubectl get all -n easypj-dev                   # deploy/rs/pod/svc at a glance
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -n easypj-dev
kubectl describe pod easypj-web-x9k -n easypj-dev   # events, conditions, volumes
kubectl describe node worker-1                  # capacity, allocated, taints, conditions
kubectl top nodes ; kubectl top pods -n easypj-dev # needs metrics-server

✏️ Create & modify · 🗑️ delete

change things
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml ; kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
kubectl edit deployment easypj-web -n easypj-dev
kubectl patch deployment easypj-web -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}' -n easypj-dev
kubectl label node worker-1 disk=ssd ; kubectl taint node worker-1 gpu=true:NoSchedule
kubectl delete pod easypj-web-x9k -n easypj-dev
kubectl delete -f deploy.yaml                    # delete exactly what a manifest created
kubectl delete pods --field-selector status.phase=Failed -n easypj-dev   # bulk cleanup

🐛 Debug & troubleshoot

when something's broken
kubectl logs easypj-web-x9k -n easypj-dev
kubectl logs easypj-web-x9k --previous -n easypj-dev   # last crashed container
kubectl exec -it easypj-web-x9k -n easypj-dev -- /bin/sh
kubectl port-forward pod/easypj-web-x9k 8000:8000 -n easypj-dev
kubectl debug node/worker-1 --image=busybox            # ephemeral node-debug pod
📋
get

list resources; -o wide for detail

🔍
describe

📝

container output; --previous for a crash

🏷️ Labels & selectors — the glue of Kubernetes

Services find pods, Deployments manage pods, and Ingress targets a Service — all by matching labels. Master the selector syntax and most "it's not connected" bugs become obvious.

labels & selectors
# Add a label to a pod
kubectl label pod easypj-web-x9k app=easypj -n easypj-dev

# Show every pod's labels
kubectl get pods --show-labels -n easypj-dev
# NAME             READY   STATUS    LABELS
# easypj-web-x9k   1/1     Running   app=easypj,tier=web,version=v1

# Filter — equality
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj
kubectl get pods -l 'app=easypj,tier=web'        # AND (comma)

# Filter — set-based
kubectl get pods -l 'app in (easypj,nginx)'      # in the set
kubectl get pods -l 'tier notin (cache)'         # not in the set
kubectl get pods -l 'environment'                # HAS the label (any value)
kubectl get pods -l '!environment'               # does NOT have the label

# Remove a label (trailing minus) · overwrite an existing one
kubectl label pod easypj-web-x9k version- -n easypj-dev
kubectl label pod easypj-web-x9k version=v2 --overwrite -n easypj-dev
how labels wire everything together
   🚀 Deployment           🔌 Service            🌍 Ingress
   selector.matchLabels    selector              backend → easypj-svc
     app: easypj             app: easypj
         │                     │
         └──────────┬──────────┘   labels are the GLUE
                    ▼
              📦 Pod  labels: { app: easypj, version: v1 }  ◀── must match
   ⚠️ labels don't match → Service has 0 endpoints → app unreachable
📖 Equality vs set-based selectors — which to use

Equality (app=easypj, tier!=cache) is the everyday case and the only kind a Service's selector: field understands. Set-based (in, notin, exists) is richer and used by kubectl -l, plus Deployment/ReplicaSet/NetworkPolicy matchExpressions. Two traps worth memorising: tier notin (cache) also matches pods that have no tier label at all; and a plain Service cannot use set-based selectors — only controllers/policies can, via matchExpressions.

6.3 kubectl explain — Your Built-in API Manual

kubectl explain prints the exact fields for any resource, straight from the API server — usually faster than the docs tab and the perfect cure for "what's that field called again?"

explain — drill into any field
# Top-level fields of any resource — shows KIND, VERSION, and the field list
kubectl explain pod
# KIND:     Pod
# VERSION:  v1
# FIELDS:   apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec, status

# Drill down ONE level at a time — each dotted segment goes deeper
kubectl explain pod.spec
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources.limits

# --recursive dumps the WHOLE subtree of field names (the fastest field-finder)
kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy --recursive
# strategy              <Object>
#   rollingUpdate       <Object>
#     maxSurge          <string>
#     maxUnavailable    <string>
#   type                <string>

# Forgot the exact field name? recurse, then grep for it
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers --recursive | grep -i probe
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.livenessProbe --recursive

# Pin a specific API version's schema (output differs between versions)
kubectl explain deployment --api-version=apps/v1
explain — drill-down navigation
   kubectl explain pod
        └─ spec ─▶ kubectl explain pod.spec
                    └─ containers ─▶ kubectl explain pod.spec.containers
                                      ├─ image · ports · env
                                      ├─ resources ─▶ .resources.limits / .requests
                                      ├─ livenessProbe / readinessProbe / startupProbe
                                      └─ volumeMounts
   💡 add --recursive at any level to dump the whole subtree of field names
💡 explain + dry-run = speed

Forgot the path for resource limits? kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.resources --recursive (2 s), then scaffold with kubectl run web --image=easypj:v1 $do and drop the field in. Faster than any doc search.

📖 Reading explain's type annotations — the part most people skip

The <…> tag after every field name tells you exactly how to shape it in YAML. Learn these five and you'll stop guessing whether something is a list, a map, or a plain value:

You see in explainIt meansSo you write…
<string> · <integer> · <boolean>a leaf scalar value — stop herereplicas: 3
<Object>nest deeper — it's a map of sub-fieldsstrategy: then indented children
<[]Object>a YAML list of maps (dash items)containers: then - name: …
<map[string]string>arbitrary key/value pairslabels: → {app: easypj}
-required- (in the description)the field cannot be omittedthe apiserver rejects the object without it
🧭 Worked drill-down

To find where maxSurge lives: explain deployment.spec shows strategy <Object> → go deeper with explain deployment.spec.strategy → that shows rollingUpdate <Object> → explain deployment.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate finally shows maxSurge <string> (a leaf). Each <Object> is a signpost to add one more dotted segment.

6.4 Imperative vs Declarative — When to Use Each

Two ways to manage objects. Knowing which to reach for is worth real exam minutes — and real production safety.

imperative vs declarative
   🏃 IMPERATIVE — "do this NOW"            📝 DECLARATIVE — "make it look like THIS"
   ┌────────────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────────────┐
   │ kubectl create deploy easypj-web│      │ kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml    │
   │   --image=easypj:v1             │      │                                 │
   │ kubectl scale … --replicas=5    │      │ the file IS the desired state;  │
   │ kubectl expose … --port=80      │      │ K8s computes what to change     │
   │                                 │      │                                 │
   │ ✅ fast for one-offs            │      │ ✅ repeatable · version-control │
   │ ✅ exam speed                   │      │ ✅ GitOps · production standard │
   │ ❌ no record of what you did    │      │ ❌ slower for quick tests       │
   └────────────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────────────┘
ApproachWhenExamProduction
Imperativequick tasks · generate YAML✅ for speed❌ avoid
Declarativereal, repeatable changes✅ for complex tasks✅ always

🎯 The CKA power move: imperative + dry-run = a YAML generator

$do = --dry-run=client -o yaml
kubectl run easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --port=8000 $do > pod.yaml                     # Pod
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3 $do > deploy.yaml   # Deployment
kubectl expose deployment easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000 $do > svc.yaml        # Service
kubectl create namespace easypj-dev $do > ns.yaml                                       # Namespace
kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=False $do > cm.yaml         # ConfigMap
kubectl create secret generic easypj-secret --from-literal=SECRET_KEY=x $do > secret.yaml # Secret
# then edit the generated file and apply it:
vim deploy.yaml          # add resources, env, probes…
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
⚠️ --dry-run=client vs --dry-run=server

client validates locally (no API call) — use it to generate YAML. server runs the request through the apiserver (admission + "does it already exist?") without persisting — use it to validate before applying for real.

🎯 Real exam workflow — generate → edit → validate → apply → verify

~47 s vs 3+ min hand-writing YAML
# STEP 1 — generate the skeleton (≈5s)
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3 $do > web.yaml

# STEP 2 — edit to add the requirements (≈30s)
vim web.yaml                                # resource limits · labels · nodeSelector · env…

# STEP 3 — validate against the REAL cluster before applying (≈5s)
kubectl apply -f web.yaml --dry-run=server
# deployment.apps/easypj-web created (server dry run)

# STEP 4 — apply for real (≈2s)
kubectl apply -f web.yaml

# STEP 5 — verify (≈5s)
kubectl get deploy easypj-web -o wide
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-web
# Total ≈ 47 seconds — vs 3+ minutes hand-writing YAML from scratch
⚡ Generate ─▶ ✏️ Edit ─▶ ✅ Validate (server dry-run) ─▶ 🚀 Apply ─▶ 🔍 Verify

6.5 Output Formatting & Filtering

The exam constantly asks you to extract one value — a pod's node, a node's IP, every image — and often to save it to a file. Output flags are what separate fast solvers from slow ones.

FlagPurposeExample
-o wideextra columns (IP, node)kubectl get pods -o wide
-o yaml/jsonfull objectkubectl get pod web -o yaml
-o jsonpathextract a field… -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'
-o custom-columnscustom table… -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName
--sort-bysort by field… --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
-llabel filterkubectl get pods -l app=easypj
--field-selectorfield filter… --field-selector status.phase=Running

JSONPath — the CKA favourite

jsonpath examples
# All pod names
kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'

# Pod name + its node, one per line (a range/end loop with tab & newline)
kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.nodeName}{"\n"}{end}'

# Node internal IPs (a filter expression: only addresses of type InternalIP)
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}'

# Every container image across all namespaces, de-duplicated
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[*].image}' | tr ' ' '\n' | sort -u

# custom-columns — a clean table of exactly the fields you want
kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=\
NAME:.metadata.name,\
STATUS:.status.phase,\
NODE:.spec.nodeName,\
IP:.status.podIP
💡 JSONPath cheat-sheet

{.items[*]} all items · {.metadata.name} a field · {range …}{end} loop · {"\n"}/{"\t"} newline/tab · [?(@.type=="InternalIP")] filter. Always single-quote the expression (double quotes break in bash).

🎯 Common extraction patterns (muscle memory)

patterns that show up every exam
# ── Pattern 1: pod names sorted by creation time ──
kubectl get pods --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}'

# ── Pattern 2: which node each pod runs on ──
kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName

# ── Pattern 3: the internal IP of every node ──
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}'

# ── Pattern 4: every container image in the cluster (de-duped) ──
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' | sort -u

# ── Pattern 5: pods NOT in Running state (triage) ──
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase!=Running

# ── Pattern 6: count pods per namespace ──
kubectl get pods -A --no-headers | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

# ── Pattern 7: SAVE the answer to a file (the exam often requires this) ──
kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' > /opt/answers/pod-names.txt
📤
Output to file

Many tasks say "save to /opt/answers/x.txt." Use >, then cat to double-check you actually wrote it.

🔗
Pipe power

Combine with grep/awk/sort/wc -l — e.g. kubectl get po -A | grep -c Running.

6.6 Debugging Pods — logs, exec & ephemeral containers

When a pod misbehaves you climb a ladder: read its logs, then shell in, and — if the image has no shell or the container has already crashed — attach an ephemeral debug container with kubectl debug.

RungUse when…Command
logsthe container ran (even if it crashed)kubectl logs <pod> [--previous]
execit's running and the image has a shellkubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
debugdistroless (no shell) or crashedkubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<ctr>
logs & exec
kubectl logs easypj-web-x9k -c web --since=1h -f   # container · last hour · follow
kubectl logs easypj-web-x9k --previous             # the LAST crashed instance
kubectl exec -it easypj-web-x9k -- sh              # interactive shell (needs a shell in the image)

Ephemeral containers — kubectl debug

get a shell where there isn't one
kubectl debug -it easypj-web-x9k --image=busybox --target=web   # attach to a running pod
kubectl debug easypj-web-x9k -it --image=busybox --copy-to=dbg --share-processes  # debug a crashed pod via a copy
kubectl debug node/worker-1 -it --image=busybox                 # node shell (host fs at /host)
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/easypj-web-x9k --timeout=60s   # block in scripts
📖 What an ephemeral container is

A temporary debug container injected into a running pod — the only way to "get a shell" into a distroless image or a crashed pod. It shares the pod (optionally its PID namespace with --share-processes), but it can't be removed or restarted and takes no ports/probes/resources. It's not part of pod.spec — it's added through a special subresource.

Under the Hood — how a kubectl command becomes an HTTP API call

kubectl is just a REST client for the apiserver. Every command becomes one or more HTTP calls — and knowing the four stages explains "connection refused", RBAC "forbidden", stale-cache surprises, and why -v is your sharpest debugger.

🗺️ From a kubectl command to an HTTP request — the translation pipeline
   kubectl get pods -n easypj -l app=web -o yaml
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   ① PARSE — split the command into parts
        verb=get   resource=pods   -n easypj (namespace)   -l app=web (selector)   -o yaml (format)

   ② DISCOVER — find the URL path  (kubectl GETs /api & /apis once, then caches the resource→path map)
        core group   /api/v1 .............. pods → /api/v1/namespaces/easypj/pods
                                            services · configmaps · secrets · pvcs …
        named groups /apis/<grp>/<ver> ..... deployments → /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/easypj/deployments
                                            ingresses   → /apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/…
                                            cronjobs    → /apis/batch/v1/…
        cache: ~/.kube/cache/discovery/    (stale after a CRD/version change → `kubectl api-resources`
                                            to refresh, or --cache-dir=/tmp to dodge a bad cache)

   ③ BUILD — construct the HTTP request
        GET /api/v1/namespaces/easypj/pods?labelSelector=app%3Dweb
        Host: 10.0.1.100:6443                 Accept: application/yaml
        Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci…       User-Agent: kubectl/v1.34
        (token OR client cert — whichever your kubeconfig user holds)

   ④ APISERVER — process the request
        a. authN     validate the token/cert → username + groups
        b. authZ     RBAC: may this user LIST pods in easypj?      ◀── a 403 stops here
        c. admission GET needs none (mutating + validating run for writes)
        d. etcd      read /registry/pods/easypj/  (usually served from the watch cache)
        e. format    convert the stored object → the version & format you asked for (YAML)
        f. respond   200 OK + YAML body  →  kubectl prints it
🔑 See the raw calls: kubectl get pods -v=8 prints every request & response (URL, headers, body) — the fastest way to debug auth, discovery, or "why did that 403?" problems. Ladder: -v=6 one line/call · -v=8 full request/response · -v=9 adds the equivalent curl.
Every verb is an HTTP method on a resource URL

kubectl verbs map straight onto REST — which is why -v=8 shows real HTTP, and why a "forbidden" error names the exact verb RBAC blocked.

kubectlHTTPWhat it does
get / describeGETread one/all (describe = a GET + related GETs & events)
createPOSTcreate a new object
applyPATCHdeclarative merge (last-applied, or server-side)
editGET → PATCHfetch, you edit in $EDITOR, patch back
replacePUToverwrite the whole object
deleteDELETEremove it
logsGET …/loga pod subresource
exec / attach / port-forwardPOST …/exec (WebSocket/SPDY)streaming subresources
get -wGET ?watch=truea long-lived stream of change events
🔑 Why RBAC is verb-based: because the API is. "cannot get pods" literally means "you may not issue GET on …/pods." kubectl auth can-i get pods asks the apiserver that exact question — the fastest way to confirm a permission before (or after) a 403.
How --dry-run really works — client vs server

Same flag, two completely different machines do the work — which is exactly why a server dry-run catches errors a client one never can:

   --dry-run=client          (kubectl ONLY — no API call leaves your laptop)
   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      build the object in memory  →  serialize to YAML/JSON  →  print it.   that's all.
      ✅ generate a manifest fast, even offline
      ❌ checks NOTHING server-side: no schema, no admission, no quota, no "does it already exist?"

   --dry-run=server          (a REAL request the apiserver runs but does NOT persist)
   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      kubectl → apiserver runs the FULL write pipeline:
         authN ✅   authZ/RBAC ✅   mutating + validating admission ✅   schema validation ✅   defaulting ✅
      …then returns the object it WOULD have stored — and skips the etcd write.
      ✅ catches RBAC denials, admission/webhook rejects, quota breaches, unknown fields, type errors
      ⚠️ requires a live cluster connection (unlike client dry-run)
🔑 The exam workflow: --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate a manifest (no server needed) → edit it → --dry-run=server to validate it against the real cluster → apply. And kubectl explain <res> --recursive is the offline manual that always matches the cluster's exact API version — faster than the docs tab.
One more layer — get -w, --watch and how big lists are paged

A plain get is a single request/response, but two behaviours go deeper than that and explain things you'll actually see:

   WATCH — a long-lived stream, not polling
     kubectl get pods -w
       1. GET …/pods?resourceVersion=0      → the full current list (a snapshot + its resourceVersion)
       2. GET …/pods?watch=true&resourceVersion=N  → connection stays OPEN
            apiserver pushes ADDED / MODIFIED / DELETED events as they happen (chunked HTTP)
       3. periodic BOOKMARK events advance your resourceVersion cheaply (no data)
       • if the stream falls too far behind → 410 Gone → kubectl re-LISTs and resumes
       this is exactly how every controller & the kubelet keep up to date — efficiently, without polling

   PAGINATION — huge lists arrive in chunks
     kubectl get pods -A                    (10 000 pods)
       apiserver returns ~500 at a time with a `continue` token; kubectl fetches the next page
       automatically — which is why a big get streams in rather than hanging on one giant reply
🔑 Why it matters: resourceVersion is the cluster's optimistic-concurrency clock — every object carries one, watches resume from one, and apply/replace use it to reject a write if someone changed the object since you read it ("the object has been modified"). Understanding watch also demystifies controllers: they don't poll the apiserver, they watch it — the whole system is event-driven on top of these streams.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • verb + resource + name + flags builds any command; the short names save real seconds.
  • kubectl explain is the manual you're allowed to "memorise" — drill with --recursive.
  • Generate, don't hand-write: kubectl create … $do > f.yaml → edit → apply -f.
  • Extract anything with jsonpath / custom-columns / selectors; save with > when asked.
  • Debug ladder: logs --previous → exec → kubectl debug (distroless/crashed).
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Traps
  • apply vs create. create fails if the object exists; apply creates-or-updates. Use apply for files, create for imperative one-liners.
  • jsonpath quoting. Single-quote the expression: -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' — double quotes break in bash.
  • -A = --all-namespaces, but cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs, clusterroles) ignore it.
  • Forgot -n. Without a default namespace your object lands in default — set one per context (Ch 5).
  • Editing the live object instead of the manifest. A kubectl edit / kubectl scale / kubectl patch change is invisible to your YAML file — the next apply -f (or a GitOps sync) silently reverts it. Fine for a quick exam fix; in production change the file and re-apply, or your edit is "configuration drift" waiting to be undone.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • alias k=kubectl · export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml' · export now='--force --grace-period=0' · bash completion.
  • k get po -o wide to see the node · --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp for age · -l app=easypj to filter.
  • kubectl explain <res> --recursive for unknown fields · kubectl diff -f f.yaml to preview before apply.

🔬 Beyond the basics — power-user kubectl worth knowing

These aren't day-one commands, but each removes a reason to ever leave the terminal — from scripting waits to debugging the API itself:

ToolWhat it doesExample
-o go-templateformat output with a Go template — more powerful than jsonpath for conditionals/loopsk get po -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.name}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'
-o custom-columnsa quick table of exactly the fields you wantk get po -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName
kubectl waitblock in a script until a condition is met — no sleep guessingk wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app=easypj --timeout=120s
--rawhit a raw API path directly (health, metrics, custom endpoints)k get --raw='/readyz?verbose' · k get --raw='/metrics'
-v=6 … -v=9verbose logging — see the exact HTTP requests kubectl makes (debug auth/RBAC/TLS)k get po -v=8 (shows URL, headers, response)
krew pluginsthe kubectl plugin manager — ctx/ns/neat/tree (great for practice; not on the exam)kubectl krew install ctx ns → kubectl ctx

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 6)

the kubectl power set
k get|describe|logs|exec|apply|create|delete|edit|scale|rollout   # the verbs
k explain <res>.spec --recursive          # the in-exam manual
k create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 $do > d.yaml   # generate
k get po -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.podIP}'            # extract
k get po -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName
k debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<ctr>           # ephemeral shell
k get po -v=8                              # see the raw API calls
🧪 Drill — Generate, apply, extract (the exam loop)

Time yourself; aim for under two minutes before peeking:

  1. Generate a Deployment manifest for easypj-web (image easypj:v1, 3 replicas) with $do — don't create it yet.
  2. Edit it to add a container port 8000, then apply it.
  3. Extract the names of all its pods, one per line, into /opt/answers/pods.txt, and confirm with cat.
Show solution
terminal
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3 $do > d.yaml
vim d.yaml          # under containers: add  ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
kubectl apply -f d.yaml
kubectl get po -l app=easypj-web \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}' > /opt/answers/pods.txt
cat /opt/answers/pods.txt   # always verify the file landed

Why: generate → edit → apply → extract → verify is the loop behind most exam tasks; the $do alias is what makes it fast.

📌 Chapter 6 Visual Summary — one command, four parts, total fluency
   kubectl   VERB   RESOURCE   NAME   FLAGS
       │
       ├─ 🔎 explain <res>.field --recursive            ← what's the YAML? (the in-exam manual)
       ├─ ⚡ create … $do > f.yaml → edit → apply -f     ← generate, don't hand-write
       ├─ 📤 -o jsonpath / custom-columns / -l / --field-selector  → > file   ← extract
       └─ 🐛 logs --previous → exec → kubectl debug      ← climb the debug ladder
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   it's all REST: kubectl ─▶ apiserver (authN → authZ → admission) ─▶ etcd.  `-v=8` reveals it. ☸️

In words: every kubectl command is the same four parts — verb · resource · name · flags. From there, four moves cover almost everything: explain tells you a field's YAML, --dry-run=client -o yaml generates a manifest to edit and apply, the output flags (jsonpath / custom-columns / selectors) extract any value (and > saves it), and the debug ladder (logs → exec → kubectl debug) gets you inside a broken pod.

The takeaway: kubectl is a REST client — it parses your command, discovers the API path, authenticates, and renders the JSON back. Speed comes from aliases + completion + $do, and when anything is "forbidden" or "refused," kubectl … -v=8 shows you the exact call to fix.

Chapter 7 · YAML & Kubernetes Manifests

Every Kubernetes object is described in YAML, and the #1 cause of failed exam tasks is a stray indent — not missing knowledge. This chapter makes YAML automatic: the syntax that bites, the four required fields, finding the right apiVersion, multi-doc files, validation, and how apply actually manages objects.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📝 YAML 🎯 used in 100% of tasks

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ YAML syntax — key/value, lists, nested maps, and the rules that trip people up
  • ✅ The 4 required fields every manifest must have (and selector == template labels)
  • ✅ How to find the right apiVersion for any resource
  • ✅ Multi-resource files with ---, and applying a whole directory
  • ✅ Validating with --dry-run and kubectl diff before you apply
  • ✅ Object management (imperative vs declarative) & server-side apply
🎓 CKA Relevance
All Domains 100% YAML correctness PASS/FAIL
⚠️ YAML mistakes = failed tasks

A single wrong indent breaks the whole manifest — silently. Build the habit of generating with $do and validating with --dry-run=server before you apply.

  • Spaces only — a tab breaks YAML with a cryptic error.
  • 2-space indents — the Kubernetes convention.
  • Colon + space — key: value, never key:value.
