7.1 YAML Basics for Kubernetes

YAML ("YAML Ain't Markup Language") is how you describe desired state. Three building blocks — and a handful of rules that silently break manifests:

YAML building blocks & the rules that bite
   ① KEY–VALUE (scalar)        ② LIST (sequence)         ③ NESTED MAP (indent = depth)
   name: easypj                ports:                    metadata:        ◀ parent
   replicas: 3                 - 8000   ◀ item             name: easypj   ◀ child (2 spaces)
   debug: true                 - 8080                      labels:
   note: "a string"            - 443                         app: easypj  ◀ grandchild

   ⚠️ RULES:  ✅ spaces only (2/level)   ❌ NO tabs (breaks silently)
              ✅ colon + space  key: value     ❌ key:value
              ✅ dash + space   - item         ❌ -item
              ✅ ---  separates documents in one file
yaml syntax in one glance
name: easypj                 # scalar — string
replicas: 3                  # scalar — int
enabled: true                # scalar — bool

skills:                      # a list of strings
- Python
- Django
- Kubernetes

containers:                  # a list of OBJECTS (maps)
- name: web
  image: easypj:v1
  ports:
  - containerPort: 8000

args: ["runserver", "0.0.0.0:8000"]   # inline (flow) list — shorthand for the above

description: |               # block scalar: |  PRESERVES newlines
  easypj is a Django job board.
  It filters jobs by Skill, Location, and Author.

summary: >                   # folded scalar: >  JOINS lines into one paragraph
  This becomes a single line
  even though it spans several.

metadata:                    # a nested map
  name: easypj
  labels: { app: easypj, tier: web }   # inline (flow) map
Indentation matters — same words, different meaning
   ✅ CORRECT — ports is a field OF the container        ❌ WRONG — ports is a sibling, not a child
   containers:                                          containers:
   - name: web                                          - name: web
     ports:            ← indented under the list item   ports:              ← NOT indented = separate field!
     - containerPort: 8000                              - containerPort: 8000

   ✅ CORRECT — labels nested under metadata            ❌ WRONG — labels at the same level as metadata
   metadata:                                            metadata:
     name: easypj                                         name: easypj
     labels:                                            labels:               ← NOT nested = top-level field!
       app: easypj                                        app: easypj
🔄 Why YAML, not JSON

YAML is a friendlier superset of JSON — it allows comments, drops the braces/quotes clutter, and diffs cleanly in Git. Kubernetes accepts both, but every manifest you'll meet is YAML.

📝
YAML — what you write
# Pod definition
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: easypj:v1

✅ comments · ✅ readable · ✅ less typing

{ }
JSON — what K8s stores
{
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "kind": "Pod",
  "metadata": {"name": "easypj"},
  "spec": {
    "containers": [{
      "name": "web",
      "image": "easypj:v1"
    }]}}

❌ no comments · ❌ verbose · ✅ precise

📖 Both are valid for kubectl

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml and kubectl apply -f pod.json both work — the apiserver speaks JSON and kubectl converts YAML to it. Always write YAML (readable, comments); reach for JSON only with -o json when extracting data programmatically.

📏 | vs > — the two block scalars people mix up

| (literal) keeps every newline exactly — use it for multi-line scripts, certs, or config files inside a ConfigMap. > (folded) replaces single newlines with spaces, collapsing wrapped lines into one paragraph — use it for long prose. Add a - (|- / >-) to strip the trailing newline.

📋 The five YAML mistakes that break manifests

Every one of these is a real "error converting YAML" or a silent misparse. This is the reference to scan when a manifest won't apply:

MistakeWhat you wroteWhat Kubernetes seesFix
Tab character name: easypj (leading tab)parse error — the whole file fails to loadspaces only, 2 per level
No space after colonname:easypjname:easypj read as a single stringname: easypj
Wrong indent levellabels: at the roota top-level field instead of nested under metadataindent 2 spaces under its parent
String vs numberreplicas: "3"a string where an integer is required → type errorreplicas: 3 (no quotes)
Missing dash for a listcontainers: → name: web"expected a list, got a mapping"containers: → - name: web

🧪 The same snippet — broken vs fixed

Each error below is a real "did not find expected key" or a silent misparse. Train your eye on the pair:

❌ Broken
spec:
	containers:          # a TAB → breaks silently
  - name:web           # no space after colon
    image: easypj:v1
    ports:
    -containerPort: 8000 # no space after dash
    env:
    - name: DEBUG
      value: yes         # unquoted → becomes boolean true!
✅ Fixed
spec:
  containers:          # 2 spaces, never a tab
  - name: web          # space after the colon
    image: easypj:v1
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000 # space after the dash
    env:
    - name: DEBUG
      value: "yes"       # quoted → stays the string "yes"
🔍 Catch it before the apiserver does

cat -A file.yaml shows tabs as ^I and line-ends as $; in vim, :set list reveals hidden whitespace and gg=G re-indents the whole file. On the exam, --dry-run=server (§7.5) is your final gate.

🔬 Beyond the basics — anchors, null & quoting traps

Feature / trapWhat to know (so a doc is never needed)
Anchors & aliases &name / *namedefine a block once and reuse it: defaults: &def {cpu: 100m} … then resources: *def. Pure-YAML DRY — valid in manifests, though Kustomize/Helm usually do reuse better. You'll see it in CI configs and the odd manifest.
Null forms null · ~ · emptykey: (nothing after), key: null, and key: ~ are all the same null = "unset". That's different from key: "" (an empty string) and from omitting the key entirely — a distinction that matters when a patch clears a field vs leaves it alone.
The "Norway problem"unquoted yes/no/on/off/true/false become booleans; NO (Norway's country code) silently becomes false. Quote any country code, "true/false" config value, or version string.
Numbers that aren't numbers08000 may error (looks like invalid octal) and 1.20 drops its trailing zero. Quote ports, versions, and zip codes you want preserved as strings.

7.2 The 4 Required Fields — Every Manifest

Every object — Pod, Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret — needs exactly these four top-level fields. Burn them in:

🔌
apiVersion

which API group/version — v1, apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1

📦
kind

the object type — Pod, Deployment, Service

🏷️
metadata

identity — name, namespace, labels, annotations

⚙️
spec

desired state — THE MEAT; different shape per kind

easypj-pod.yaml — the 4 fields
apiVersion: v1                    # 1️⃣ which API group/version
kind: Pod                         # 2️⃣ the object type
metadata:                         # 3️⃣ identity
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj-dev
  labels:
    app: easypj
    tier: web
spec:                             # 4️⃣ desired state (the meat)
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: easypj:v1
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
    env:
    - name: DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE
      value: "easypj.settings"
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: "100m"
        memory: "128Mi"
      limits:
        cpu: "500m"
        memory: "256Mi"
Deployment structure — and the rule that breaks rollouts
   apiVersion: apps/v1
   kind: Deployment
   metadata: { name: easypj-web, namespace: easypj-dev }
   spec:
     replicas: 3
     selector:
       matchLabels: { app: easypj }   ───────────┐  these TWO
     template:                                    │  MUST be
       metadata:                                  │  identical
         labels: { app: easypj }   ◀──────────────┘
       spec:
         containers: [{ name: web, image: easypj:v1, ports: [{containerPort: 8000}] }]
⚠️ selector.matchLabels must equal template.metadata.labels

If they differ, the Deployment can't find the pods it created — the rollout errors or the Service ends up with 0 endpoints. This is the single most common manifest bug.

7.3 Finding the Right apiVersion

A wrong apiVersion = manifest rejected. Here's the reference plus the two commands that look it up live on any cluster.

ResourceapiVersionShort
Pod · Service · ConfigMap · Secret · Namespace · PV · PVC · ServiceAccountv1 (core)po·svc·cm·ns·pv·pvc·sa
Deployment · ReplicaSet · DaemonSet · StatefulSetapps/v1deploy·rs·ds·sts
Job · CronJobbatch/v1—·cj
Ingress · NetworkPolicy · IngressClassnetworking.k8s.io/v1ing·netpol
Role · RoleBinding · ClusterRole · ClusterRoleBindingrbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1—
StorageClass · CSIDriverstorage.k8s.io/v1sc
PodDisruptionBudgetpolicy/v1pdb
look it up — never guess
# List ALL resources with their apiVersion, short name, and scope
kubectl api-resources
# NAME          SHORTNAMES   APIVERSION             NAMESPACED   KIND
# pods          po           v1                     true         Pod
# services      svc          v1                     true         Service
# deployments   deploy       apps/v1                true         Deployment
# ingresses     ing          networking.k8s.io/v1   true         Ingress

# List every served API group/version
kubectl api-versions
# apps/v1
# networking.k8s.io/v1
# rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
# v1

# Quick lookup: what apiVersion does Ingress use?
kubectl api-resources | grep -i ingress
# ingresses   ing   networking.k8s.io/v1   true   Ingress
💡 Memory trick

Core = v1 (Pod/Service/ConfigMap/Secret/NS/PV/PVC/SA) · Workloads = apps/v1 (Deployment/RS/DS/STS) · Networking = networking.k8s.io/v1 · RBAC = rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 · Batch = batch/v1.

API group map — where each kind lives
   Kubernetes API
   ├─ core  /api/v1 ............ Pod · Service · ConfigMap · Secret · Namespace · PV · PVC · SA · Node
   ├─ apps/v1 ................. Deployment · ReplicaSet · DaemonSet · StatefulSet
   ├─ batch/v1 ................ Job · CronJob
   ├─ networking.k8s.io/v1 .... Ingress · NetworkPolicy · IngressClass
   ├─ rbac.authorization…/v1 .. Role · RoleBinding · ClusterRole · ClusterRoleBinding
   ├─ storage.k8s.io/v1 ....... StorageClass · CSIDriver · CSINode
   └─ policy/v1 .............. PodDisruptionBudget

7.4 Multi-Resource YAML Files

Bundle several objects in one file with --- between them — handy for shipping an app and its Service together.

easypj-complete.yaml
# ── 1. Namespace — created first so everything below has a home ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: easypj-dev
---
# ── 2. ConfigMap — non-secret config ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: easypj-config
  namespace: easypj-dev
data:
  DEBUG: "False"
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: "*"
  DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "easypj.settings"
---
# ── 3. Deployment — the workload ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj-dev
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj                  # ← must match template labels
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj                # ← must match selector
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: easypj:v1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: easypj-config
---
# ── 4. Service — stable address in front of the pods ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj-dev
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj                    # ← selects the Deployment's pods
  ports:
  - port: 80                       # Service port → 
    targetPort: 8000               # → container port
apply strategies
kubectl apply -f easypj-complete.yaml   # one multi-doc file
kubectl apply -f k8s/                    # every YAML in a directory
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod/          # a Kustomize overlay (Ch 37)
kubectl delete -f easypj-complete.yaml   # tear it all down
file organization — two approaches
   Approach A — ONE multi-doc file            Approach B — a DIRECTORY of files
   ┌──────────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │ easypj-complete.yaml      │              │ k8s/                      │
   │  ├─ Namespace             │              │  ├─ 01-namespace.yaml     │
   │  ├─ ---                   │              │  ├─ 02-configmap.yaml     │
   │  ├─ ConfigMap             │              │  ├─ 03-secret.yaml        │
   │  ├─ ---                   │              │  ├─ 04-deployment.yaml    │
   │  ├─ Secret                │              │  └─ 05-service.yaml       │
   │  ├─ ---                   │              │                           │
   │  ├─ Deployment            │              │  kubectl apply -f k8s/    │
   │  ├─ ---                   │              │  (applies every file)     │
   │  └─ Service               │              └──────────────────────────┘
   │  kubectl apply -f easypj-complete.yaml                               │
   └──────────────────────────┘
   ✅ simple, one command                     ✅ better organization
   ❌ unwieldy for large apps                  ✅ each file = one concern
⚠️ Ordering with -f dir/

A directory is applied in alphabetical order — if a Deployment references a ConfigMap that's applied later, it can fail. Number files (01-namespace.yaml, 02-configmap.yaml, …) or use one multi-doc file (created top-to-bottom). apply is idempotent, so re-running fixes most ordering hiccups anyway.

7.5 Validation & Dry Run

Never apply blind. Validate locally, then against the server, then preview the diff — then apply.

the validation workflow
# Step 1 — client-side validation (no API call): is the YAML well-formed?
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml --dry-run=client
# deployment.apps/easypj-web created (dry run)   ← YAML is valid

# Step 2 — server-side validation: does the apiserver accept it? (admission, no persist)
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml --dry-run=server
# deployment.apps/easypj-web created (server dry run)   ← API accepted it

# Step 3 — preview the exact change (like git diff)
kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml

# Step 4 — apply for real
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
# deployment.apps/easypj-web created
1
client dry-run

local syntax/schema check

2
server dry-run

full admission, nothing saved

3
diff

preview the live-vs-new delta

4
apply

commit the change

🩺 Decode the two errors you'll actually hit

error converting YAML to JSON: did not find expected key → a bad indent. error validating data: unknown field "X" → a typo'd/mis-placed field — confirm the path with kubectl explain.

🚨 The six errors you'll meet — message → fix

common manifest errors & fixes
# ERROR — wrong apiVersion
error: resource mapping not found for name: "easypj"  kind: Deployment  apiVersion: v1
# FIX: a Deployment is apps/v1, not v1

# ERROR — missing required field
error: error validating: ValidationError(Deployment.spec): missing required field "selector"
# FIX: add spec.selector.matchLabels

# ERROR — selector ≠ template labels
The Deployment "easypj" is invalid: spec.selector does not match template.metadata.labels
# FIX: make selector.matchLabels == template.metadata.labels

# ERROR — invalid YAML (indent/tab)
error: error parsing deploy.yaml: yaml: line 12: did not find expected key
# FIX: check indentation at line 12 (a tab, or wrong nesting)

# ERROR — unknown field (typo)
error: error validating data: ValidationError(Deployment.spec): unknown field "replica"
# FIX: it's "replicas" — confirm with kubectl explain deployment.spec

# ERROR — namespace doesn't exist
Error from server (NotFound): namespaces "easypj-dev" not found
# FIX: create it first — kubectl create namespace easypj-dev

🛠️ Editing YAML in vim — the exam's default editor

The exam gives you vim, and YAML is whitespace-sensitive — so the very first thing to do in a fresh exam shell is fix vim's indent behaviour. These settings prevent the indent disasters that eat exam minutes:

~/.vimrc — set this FIRST
# Add to ~/.vimrc the moment the exam starts:
set tabstop=2       " a tab shows as 2 spaces
set shiftwidth=2    " one indent level = 2 spaces
set expandtab       " the Tab key inserts spaces, never a real tab
set autoindent      " keep the indent level on the next line
set number          " line numbers — error messages cite them

# One-liner to set it all at once:
echo 'set ts=2 sw=2 et ai nu' >> ~/.vimrc
vim commandWhat it doesWhen to use
:set pasteturn OFF auto-indent so a paste isn't re-indentedbefore pasting YAML from the docs tab
:set nopasteturn auto-indent back onafter pasting, to resume normal editing
gg=Gre-indent the whole filewhen indentation got mangled
Shift+V then > / <visual-select lines, indent right / leftpush a YAML block deeper or shallower
/textsearchjump to a field in a big manifest
dd / yy / pdelete / yank / paste a linemove or duplicate list items
:set listreveal hidden whitespace (tabs as ^I)hunting an invisible tab
u / Ctrl-rundo / redorevert a mistake instantly
⚠️ The #1 paste disaster

Pasting indented YAML into vim without :set paste makes auto-indent compound every line's indentation into a staircase. Habit: :set paste → paste → :set nopaste. (With expandtab set, the Tab key is also safe — it inserts spaces.)

7.6 Object Management & Server-Side Apply

There are three ways to manage objects — don't mix them on the same object — and it pays to know how apply figures out what changed.

ApproachCommandIdempotent?Use for
imperative commandkubectl create/run/expose/scale/labelno (errors if it exists)exam speed, quick fixes
imperative configkubectl create -f / replace -fnorarely (whole-object replace)
declarativekubectl apply -f / -kyesproduction & GitOps — the default
how apply knows what changed — the 3-way merge
   ① last-applied-configuration     ② live object (cluster)     ③ your new file
   (annotation from last apply)        (may have drifted)          (what you want)
            └────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┘
                                          ▼
              apply SETS fields you set · CLEARS fields you removed ·
              LEAVES fields others wrote (e.g. a replica count from `kubectl scale`)
📖 Server-Side Apply (--server-side)

The apiserver does the merge and records field ownership in metadata.managedFields. Two managers writing the same field → a conflict (resolve with --force-conflicts). It's the modern choice for controllers, GitOps, and any object with several writers.

⚠️ Don't mix

Editing an apply-managed object with kubectl edit/scale can be reverted by the next apply. Pick one workflow per object.

🧮 The 3-way merge, with real numbers

Suppose you first applied replicas: 2, someone then ran kubectl scale --replicas=4, and now your file says replicas: 3 with image: easypj:v2. What does apply produce?

Sourcereplicasimage
① last-applied annotation (your previous apply)2easypj:v1
② live object (after scale drifted it)4easypj:v1
③ your new file3easypj:v2
→ result of apply3easypj:v2

Your file sets both fields, so your values win (3 overrides the drifted 4; v2 overrides v1). The two edge cases that surprise people:

  • You remove replicas from the file (and it was in last-applied) → apply clears it, so it reverts to the default 1. Pruning is why "the field I deleted came back to default."
  • A field you never managed (not in your file, not in last-applied — e.g. replicas owned by an HPA) → apply leaves it alone. This is exactly how an HPA and your manifest coexist without fighting.

🔧 Targeted edits: strategic-merge vs JSON patch

When you don't want to re-apply a whole file, kubectl patch edits one path. Three patch grammars, each for a different job:

Patch typeFlagBest forExample
strategic merge (default)--type=strategicK8s-aware — merges lists by key (patch one container by name without replacing the rest)kubectl patch deploy easypj-web -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}'
JSON merge (RFC 7386)--type=mergesimple object overwrite; replaces whole lists — also what CRDs use (no strategic metadata)… --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"labels":{"tier":"web"}}}'
JSON patch (RFC 6902)--type=jsonprecise op-by-op edits at an explicit path (add / remove / replace)… --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/replicas","value":5}]'
📖 Validate offline with kubeconform

kubeconform (the maintained successor to kubeval) checks manifests against the Kubernetes JSON schemas without a cluster — perfect for a CI gate before anything reaches the apiserver: kubeconform -strict -summary k8s/. It can't see RBAC/admission/quota (only --dry-run=server can), but it catches shape and type errors in a pipeline where no live cluster exists.

Under the Hood — what the apiserver does to your manifest before it's stored

apply isn't a file save — your YAML runs a gauntlet. Knowing it explains why server dry-run catches errors client dry-run can't.

   kubectl apply -f x.yaml
     ① DECODE              YAML → JSON   (a tab / bad indent dies HERE — client-side)
     ② AuthN → AuthZ       who are you? may you? (RBAC)
     ③ MUTATING admission  inject defaults (LimitRanger) · sidecars (webhooks)
     ④ SCHEMA validation   unknown field? wrong type? (needs the server's schema)
     ⑤ VALIDATING admission PodSecurity · ResourceQuota · policy webhooks
     ⑥ PERSIST → etcd      resourceVersion assigned
🔑 Why server dry-run is stronger: client dry-run stops at ① (local shape). Server dry-run runs ②–⑤ without ⑥ — so it catches RBAC, admission, quota, and unknown-field errors a client check never sees.
ConceptWhat to know
defaultingthe server fills omitted fields (e.g. a Service's type: ClusterIP) — why get -o yaml shows more than you wrote
pruningapply removes fields you deleted from the file (via last-applied) — declarative means the file is the source of truth
structural schemaCRDs validate against their OpenAPI schema too — a bad custom-resource field is rejected just like a built-in

② Defaulting, made concrete — what the server adds to a minimal manifest. This is why kubectl get deploy -o yaml always shows far more than you wrote. You submit the left; the apiserver stores the right:

You write
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: easypj:v1
The server stores (defaults added)
spec:
  replicas: 1                 # ← default
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate       # ← default
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%           # ← default
      maxUnavailable: 25%     # ← default
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10    # ← default
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: easypj:v1
        resources: {}                       # ← default
        terminationMessagePath: /dev/termination-log  # ← default
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent       # ← default (tag ≠ :latest)
      restartPolicy: Always   # ← default
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst # ← default
🔑 Why it matters: the LimitRanger admission plugin can also inject defaults here (e.g. a default CPU/memory request if your namespace has a LimitRange), and a mutating webhook like Istio injects a sidecar container — all before the object is stored. Stage 5 then writes the fully-defaulted object to etcd at key /registry/deployments/easypj/easypj-web (protobuf-encoded) and fires a watch event the Deployment controller is waiting on.

③ apiVersion resolution & the storage version — why what you GET isn't always what you PUT. A single kind (say Deployment) can be served at several versions at once. The apiserver never stores your YAML verbatim — it converts every object through an internal "hub" form, persists it as the one storage version, and converts again on read to whatever version you asked for. That is why you can submit an old beta object and read it back as apps/v1.

   WRITE PATH                                    READ PATH
   you submit  apps/v1beta1                       you ask for  apps/v1
        │  decode + convert                            ▲  convert from storage
        ▼                                              │
   internal "hub" version  ──────────────►  internal "hub" version
        │  convert to storage version                  ▲
        ▼                                              │  read from etcd
   STORAGE VERSION (apps/v1)  ──►  etcd  ──────────────┘
   key: /registry/deployments/<ns>/<name>   value: protobuf (or JSON)
🔑 Core idea: conversion between versions of the same kind is required to be lossless — round-tripping v1 → v1beta1 → v1 must give back the identical object. Exactly one served version is flagged storage: true; everything in etcd is written in that version. When the team bumps the storage version, the apiserver rewrites objects lazily (on next write) or via a one-off migration.
SymptomWhat's really happening
get -o yaml shows a different apiVersion than you appliedyou read back the preferred served version, converted from the storage version — not the literal text you submitted
a deprecation warning on apply (object still created)you used a still-served-but-deprecated version; the apiserver returns a Warning: header — fix the manifest before the version is removed
no matches for kind … in version … (hard error)that version is removed, not just deprecated — migrate the manifest (e.g. extensions/v1beta1 Ingress → networking.k8s.io/v1)
a CRD with two versions returning the same data in boththe CRD declares a conversion strategy — None (identical schema, relabel only) or Webhook (you run a conversion server); one version is storage: true

Practical levers: kubectl api-versions lists every served group/version; kubectl explain <kind> --api-version=apps/v1 pins the schema you're validating against; and the kubectl-convert plugin rewrites a manifest from a removed version to a current one. The deprecation lifecycle is fixed and worth memorising: GA/stable versions are supported for a long window, beta for a few releases after a successor ships, and alpha can break or vanish at any release — never run alpha in anything you care about.

④ Field validation — why a typo is sometimes a warning and sometimes a hard error. Since v1.27 the apiserver validates fields server-side against the OpenAPI schema, and you choose how strict via --validate:

--validate=An unknown/duplicate field…When you'd use it
strict (the default)is a hard error — the request is rejectedalways, on the exam — catches replicas→replica typos
warnis accepted but returns a Warning: headermigrating old manifests you can't fix yet
false / ignoreis silently droppedalmost never — it hides real mistakes
🔑 Field ownership (Server-Side Apply) goes one level deeper: the apiserver records which manager wrote each field in metadata.managedFields. When two managers (say your apply and an HPA) both try to own spec.replicas, you get a conflict — resolve it with --force-conflicts (you take ownership) or by removing the field from your manifest (you cede it). This is how a Deployment manifest and an HPA coexist on the same object without endlessly overwriting each other — they own different fields, and the apiserver enforces the boundary. Inspect it with kubectl get deploy easypj-web -o yaml --show-managed-fields.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • 4 required fields in every manifest: apiVersion · kind · metadata · spec.
  • Spaces, not tabs; 2-space indent; colon+space — indentation is the #1 failure cause.
  • selector == template labels, or the controller loses its pods.
  • Find apiVersion with kubectl api-resources — never guess.
  • Generate then validate: $do → --dry-run=server → diff → apply.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Traps
  • Tabs. A single tab breaks the file with a cryptic "did not find expected key." Set your editor to spaces.
  • Missing colon-space. key:value parses as one string — always key: value.
  • selector ≠ template labels. Rollout errors or 0 endpoints; make them identical.
  • Deprecated apiVersion. extensions/v1beta1 is long gone — Deployments are apps/v1.
  • Unquoted "yes"/numbers. enabled: yes becomes true; a port like "08000" needs quotes to stay a string.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Never hand-write — scaffold with kubectl create … $do > f.yaml, then edit.
  • kubectl explain <res>.spec --recursive when you forget a field path.
  • kubectl diff -f f.yaml before every apply in a real cluster.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 7)

manifests & validation
kubectl api-resources ; kubectl api-versions       # find apiVersion / kind / scope
kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 $do > d.yaml   # generate
kubectl explain deployment.spec --recursive        # field reference
kubectl apply -f d.yaml --dry-run=server           # validate
kubectl diff -f d.yaml                              # preview
kubectl apply -f k8s/                               # apply a directory
🧪 Drill — catch a YAML bug before it costs you

Do it before peeking:

  1. Generate a Deployment YAML for easypj-web with $do.
  2. Break it on purpose: change one indent (or set selector.matchLabels to app: wrong).
  3. Catch the error with a server dry-run, fix it, and confirm with diff before applying.
Show solution
terminal
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 $do > d.yaml
vim d.yaml                                  # introduce the bug
kubectl apply -f d.yaml --dry-run=server    # → error (selector mismatch / parse)
vim d.yaml                                  # fix: selector == template labels
kubectl diff -f d.yaml && kubectl apply -f d.yaml

Why: server dry-run runs admission + schema validation, so it catches the selector/label mismatch that a client check would pass.

🧠 Chapter 7 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Read/write/validate-YAML recall — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
A manifest won't parse — what are the two most likely YAML causes?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) A tab instead of spaces. (2) A missing space after a colon (key:value). Both throw "did not find expected key."

Explanation

Set the editor to 2-space indents; cat -A file.yaml reveals hidden tabs (shown as ^I).

Q2
Name the four required top-level fields of any manifest.
Show Answer
Answer

apiVersion · kind · metadata · spec.

Explanation

Omit one and the apiserver rejects it; metadata.name is itself required.

Q3
Find the apiVersion for an Ingress (command).
Show Answer
Answer
discover API
kubectl api-resources | grep -i ingress   # → networking.k8s.io/v1
Explanation

Always look it up rather than guess — versions drift between releases.

Q4
Turn kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 into a YAML file.
Show Answer
Answer
generate manifest
kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml
Explanation

The dry-run YAML generator — then edit and apply.

Q5
Put a Deployment + Service in one file and apply it.
Show Answer
Answer

Separate the two objects with a --- line in one file, then kubectl apply -f app.yaml.

Explanation

Multi-doc files are created top-to-bottom, so the Deployment's deps can precede it.

Q6
Validate a manifest against the apiserver WITHOUT creating it.
Show Answer
Answer
server validate
kubectl apply -f app.yaml --dry-run=server
Explanation

Runs admission + schema validation but doesn't persist — catches more than client dry-run.

Q7
Preview exactly what an apply would change.
Show Answer
Answer
preview changes
kubectl diff -f app.yaml
Explanation

Shows the live-vs-new delta (like git diff) using a server dry-run under the hood.

Q8
Why does a label typo leave a Service with no endpoints?
Show Answer
Answer

The Service's selector no longer matches any pod's labels, so the EndpointSlice is empty and traffic has nowhere to go.

Explanation

Check with kubectl get endpoints <svc> and compare selector to pod labels (--show-labels).

Q9
You get "expected map, got list" (or vice-versa). What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

A field that should be a map has a - list item under it (or a list field lacks -). Fix the shape to match kubectl explain.

Explanation

e.g. env: is a list (- name: …), while resources: is a map.

Q10
Why quote "true" or a port like "8080" in some fields?
Show Answer
Answer

YAML auto-types true→boolean and 8080→integer. If a field needs a string (e.g. a ConfigMap value, an annotation), quote it so it isn't coerced.

Explanation

ConfigMap data: values must be strings — DEBUG: "False", not DEBUG: False.

⚙️ Chapter 7 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Manifest "build it / fix it" tasks with the real answers.

Q11
Task: a Deployment easypj-web, image easypj:v1, 3 replicas, containerPort 8000, namespace easypj-dev. Fastest correct workflow?
Show Answer
Answer
generate manifest
kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=3 -n easypj-dev $do > d.yaml
# add ports: [{containerPort: 8000}] under the container
vim d.yaml ; kubectl apply -f d.yaml
Explanation

Generate the bulk imperatively, hand-edit only what the flags can't set.

Q12
apply fails: unknown field "spec.replica". Fix it.
Show Answer
Answer

Typo — it's replicas (plural). Confirm the field with kubectl explain deployment.spec.

Explanation

"unknown field" almost always = a misspelled or misplaced key; explain is the fastest check.

Q13
apply -f dir/ fails because the Deployment is applied before its ConfigMap. Two fixes.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Number the files (02-configmap.yaml before 04-deployment.yaml). (2) Or put everything in one multi-doc file (created top-to-bottom). Re-running apply also resolves it — it's idempotent.

Explanation

Directories apply alphabetically; ordering only matters for hard dependencies.

Q14
Capture a running Deployment as a clean, committable manifest.
Show Answer
Answer
inspect
kubectl get deploy easypj-web -o yaml | kubectl neat > clean.yaml   # or hand-strip status/managedFields
Explanation

The live object carries status + managedFields noise; strip them for a tidy source file.

Q15
Confirm the apiserver would accept a manifest without changing anything.
Show Answer
Answer
server validate
kubectl apply -f app.yaml --dry-run=server
Explanation

Full admission + schema validation, nothing persisted — the safest pre-flight.

Q16
A ConfigMap value is being read as a number, but the app needs a string. Fix the YAML.
Show Answer
Answer
configmap data
data:
  REPLICAS: "3"      # quote it — ConfigMap data values must be strings
Explanation

Unquoted 3 is an int and a ConfigMap rejects non-string data; quotes force a string.

Q17
Two controllers keep fighting over one field every time you apply. What fixes it cleanly?
Show Answer
Answer
apply
kubectl apply -f f.yaml --server-side [--force-conflicts]
Explanation

Server-side apply records field ownership in managedFields; a conflict is explicit, and --force-conflicts takes ownership deliberately.

Q18
Find the YAML path to set a Deployment's maxSurge.
Show Answer
Answer
field reference
kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate --recursive
Explanation

→ spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge (and maxUnavailable). Detailed in Ch 13.

Q19
Apply a Kustomize overlay for prod.
Show Answer
Answer
apply
kubectl apply -k overlays/prod/
Explanation

-k builds a kustomization (base + overlays/patches) then applies it; full treatment in Ch 37.

Q20
A manifest has a hidden tab. Pinpoint it.
Show Answer
Answer
reveal tabs
cat -A app.yaml | grep -n '\^I'    # tabs show as ^I
Explanation

cat -A renders tabs as ^I and line-ends as $ — instant indentation forensics.

📌 Chapter 7 Visual Summary — the manifest skeleton, colour-coded by the 4 fields
   apiVersion: apps/v1        ◀ ① which API group/version   (kubectl api-resources)
   kind: Deployment           ◀ ② what object
   metadata:                  ◀ ③ identity
     name: easypj-web
     namespace: easypj-dev
     labels: { app: easypj }
   spec:                      ◀ ④ desired state
     replicas: 3
     selector: { matchLabels: { app: easypj } } ─┐  MUST
     template:                                    │  match
       metadata: { labels: { app: easypj } } ◀────┘
       spec: { containers: [{ name: web, image: easypj:v1, ports: [{containerPort: 8000}] }] }
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   write it → $do generates it → --dry-run=server validates it → diff previews → apply. ☸️

In words: every object is the same four-field skeleton — apiVersion (which API), kind (what), metadata (identity) and spec (desired state). YAML is whitespace-significant: spaces only, 2-per-level, colon+space. The one rule that breaks rollouts is selector must equal the template labels.

The takeaway: don't hand-write — generate with --dry-run=client -o yaml, validate with --dry-run=server (it runs admission + schema, unlike client), preview with diff, then apply. apply tracks your last-applied config to add/clear/leave fields — that's declarative management.

Everything from Parts 1–2 fuses here into a running system you can open in a browser. You'll deploy the easypj Django web tier step by step — Namespace → ConfigMap → Secret → Deployment → Service — then port-forward to /jobs/ and understand every piece. (PostgreSQL joins in Part 6.)

Workloads & Scheduling 15% Services & Networking 20%
🎯 This is the pattern for every deployment task

The exam asks you to create Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps & Secrets again and again. This exact workflow is the answer — drill it to muscle memory.

  • Namespace → ConfigMap → Secret → Deployment → Service — this order avoids reference errors.
  • Generate with $do, edit for the specifics, then apply.
  • Always verify with kubectl get all -n <ns> and check the Service has endpoints.

8.1 The easypj Application Overview

We're deploying the easypj Django project (the jobpost app). Knowing the app shapes the Kubernetes objects we create.

🐍
Django project: easypj

Job board. Models: Skills · Author · Location · JobPost · User. Endpoints /jobs/, /jobs/<id>/, /skills/.

📦
Image: easypj:v1

Containerised Django on port 8000; needs env vars for settings, allowed hosts, DB host, and a secret key.

Target architecture — easypj-dev (web tier)
   NAMESPACE: easypj-dev
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  🚀 Deployment easypj-web (replicas: 1→3)                      │
   │     ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐                        │
   │     │📦 easypj-web  │  │📦 easypj-web  │  image easypj:v1 :8000 │
   │     └──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────┘                        │
   │            └────────┬─────────┘                                │
   │            🔌 Service easypj-web (ClusterIP)  80 ─▶ 8000        │
   │   ⚙️ ConfigMap easypj-config        🔒 Secret easypj-secret     │
   │      DEBUG·ALLOWED_HOSTS·DB_HOST       SECRET_KEY·DB_PASSWORD   │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   💻 you ──port-forward──▶ Service ──▶ Pod ──▶ Django /jobs/
📂 Namespace ─▶ ⚙️ ConfigMap ─▶ 🔐 Secret ─▶ 🚀 Deployment ─▶ 🌐 Service ─▶ ✅ Verify create in THIS order so nothing references an object that doesn't exist yet

8.2 Step 1 — Create the Namespace

Isolate the app in its own namespace — tidy, and trivial to tear down later.

namespace + make it your default
kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev   # stop typing -n
📖 Or declaratively

A 3-line manifest works too: apiVersion: v1 / kind: Namespace / metadata: {name: easypj-dev}. Every object below sets namespace: easypj-dev.

8.3 Step 2 — ConfigMap (non-secret config)

Plain, non-sensitive settings go in a ConfigMap so config lives outside the image.

easypj-config.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: easypj-config
  namespace: easypj-dev
data:                          # every value MUST be a string (quote it)
  DEBUG: "False"
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: "*"
  DB_HOST: "easypj-db"
  DB_PORT: "5432"
  DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "easypj.settings"
…or generate it imperatively
kubectl create configmap easypj-config -n easypj-dev \
  --from-literal=DEBUG=False --from-literal=ALLOWED_HOSTS='*' \
  --from-literal=DB_HOST=easypj-db --from-literal=DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=easypj.settings
⚠️ Values are strings

ConfigMap data: values must be strings — quote "False" so YAML doesn't coerce it to a boolean (Ch 7 §7.5).

8.4 Step 3 — Secret (sensitive config)

Credentials go in a Secret. Use stringData so you write plaintext and Kubernetes base64-encodes it for you.

easypj-secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: easypj-secret
  namespace: easypj-dev
type: Opaque                  # arbitrary key/value (the default Secret type)
stringData:                   # plaintext IN → apiserver base64-encodes it at rest
  SECRET_KEY: "change-me-in-prod"
  DB_PASSWORD: "supersecret"
…or imperatively
kubectl create secret generic easypj-secret -n easypj-dev \
  --from-literal=SECRET_KEY='change-me-in-prod' --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD='supersecret'
🚨 base64 ≠ encryption

Secrets are only base64-encoded and sit unencrypted in etcd by default. Never commit real Secrets to Git; protect them with encryption-at-rest + RBAC (Ch 11 / Ch 24). data: holds base64; stringData: takes plaintext and encodes it.

🔑 Creating the typed Secrets (not just generic)

Beyond generic Secrets, two typed ones come up constantly — registry pull creds and TLS certs. Memorise these imperative forms; they're far faster than hand-encoding the JSON/PEM:

typed secret creation
# docker-registry: private-image pull creds → reference via imagePullSecrets
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com \
  --docker-username=admin --docker-password='s3cret' \
  --docker-email=admin@example.com -n easypj-dev

# tls: a cert + key (for Ingress HTTPS / webhooks)
kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls \
  --cert=path/to/tls.crt --key=path/to/tls.key -n easypj-dev

8.5 Step 4 — The Deployment

The heart of it: pods from easypj:v1, configuration pulled from the ConfigMap + Secret via envFrom, resource bounds, and probes so traffic only flows when the app is ready.

easypj-deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj-dev
  labels:
    app: easypj
    tier: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj                       # ← MUST match the template labels below
      tier: web
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1                       # at most 1 EXTRA pod during a rollout
      maxUnavailable: 0                 # never drop below desired while rolling
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj                     # ← MUST match the selector above
        tier: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: easypj:v1
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          name: http
        envFrom:                        # inject ALL keys as env vars…
        - configMapRef:
            name: easypj-config         # ← every ConfigMap key
        - secretRef:
            name: easypj-secret         # ← every Secret key
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"                 # ← scheduling floor (0.1 core)
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"                 # ← hard ceiling (0.5 core)
            memory: "256Mi"
        readinessProbe:                 # gates traffic — only Ready pods get requests
          httpGet:
            path: /jobs/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:                  # restarts a wedged container
          httpGet:
            path: /jobs/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10

🔬 The deployment manifest — field by field

Every line above earns its place. Here's what each field does and why it's there:

FieldWhat it doesGet it wrong and…
replicas: 3run 3 identical pods; the ReplicaSet maintains this count, recreating any that dietoo few = no resilience; omitted = defaults to 1
selector.matchLabelsthe query that says "these pods are mine" — links the Deployment to its pods≠ template labels → apiserver rejects the manifest
strategy: RollingUpdatereplace pods gradually; maxSurge:1 adds one new pod before removing an old, maxUnavailable:0 keeps full capacityRecreate instead = brief full downtime during updates
template.metadata.labelsstamped on every pod; what the selector (and the Service) matches on≠ selector → rollout error; ≠ Service selector → 0 endpoints
image: easypj:v1the container image; a tag change here is what triggers a rolloutwrong tag/registry → ImagePullBackOff
envFrominjects every key of the ConfigMap + Secret as env vars at container startmissing CM/Secret → CreateContainerConfigError
resources.requeststhe guaranteed floor the scheduler reserves a node fortoo high → pod stuck Pending (no node fits)
resources.limitsthe hard ceiling; CPU is throttled, memory over-limit is OOMKilledtoo low memory → container killed & restarted in a loop
readinessProbe"can it serve traffic now?" — controls EndpointSlice membershipfails → pod silently dropped from the Service (no traffic)
livenessProbe"is it still alive?" — kubelet restarts the container on failuretoo aggressive → restart loop on a slow-starting app
🔢
replicas + selector

how many pods, and which pods are "mine" (by label)

📥
envFrom

inject every key of the ConfigMap & Secret as env vars

⚖️
resources

requests = scheduling floor · limits = hard ceiling (Ch 15)

❤️
probes

readiness gates traffic; liveness restarts a dead container

❤️ Readiness vs liveness — same endpoint, opposite jobs

Both probes can hit /jobs/, yet they react in completely different ways — and confusing them is one of the most common troubleshooting traps on the exam:

 readinessProbelivenessProbe
Question it asks"can it serve traffic right now?""is it alive, or wedged?"
On failurepod is removed from the Service endpoints — traffic stops, the container keeps runningthe kubelet restarts the container
Use it forwarm-up, temporary overload, waiting on a dependency (DB not up yet)deadlocks / hangs that only a restart can clear
easypj exampleapp slow under load → drops out of rotation, recovers, rejoins — no restart stormgunicorn worker deadlocks but the process stays up → restart to recover
what each probe failure does
   readiness FAILS ─▶ ❌ removed from EndpointSlice ─▶ Service stops routing ─▶ (container still running, may recover)
   liveness  FAILS ─▶ 🔁 kubelet kills + restarts the container ─▶ restartCount++ ─▶ back to readiness gate
⚠️ The classic restart-loop trap

A liveness probe that's too aggressive (tiny initialDelaySeconds/timeoutSeconds) on a slow-booting app becomes a restart loop — the app never finishes starting before liveness kills it. The fix: a startupProbe for slow boots (it suspends liveness until the app is up), generous readiness for warm-up, and a forgiving liveness reserved only for true hangs.

⚡ Scaffold then edit

kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 -n easypj-dev $do > d.yaml, then add envFrom, resources, and probes — far faster than hand-writing.

8.6 Step 5 — The Service

Pods come and go with new IPs; a Service gives easypj a stable VIP + DNS name and load-balances across the pods its selector matches.

easypj-svc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: easypj-dev
spec:
  type: ClusterIP             # default — in-cluster stable VIP (Part 5 covers NodePort/LB/Ingress)
  selector:                   # MUST match the pod labels, or 0 endpoints
    app: easypj
    tier: web
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80                  # the Service port (what clients call)
    targetPort: 8000          # the container port (where gunicorn listens)
    protocol: TCP
…or imperatively, then check endpoints
kubectl expose deployment easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000 -n easypj-dev
kubectl get svc,endpoints easypj-web -n easypj-dev   # endpoints should list pod IPs
Service → Pod traffic flow
   client request
        │
        ▼
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   │ 🔌 Service: easypj-web        │
   │    ClusterIP: 10.96.45.123    │
   │    port: 80                   │
   └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ selector: app=easypj, tier=web   (matches every Ready pod)
          ┌───────┴────────┐
          ▼                ▼
   ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐
   │ 📦 Pod 1     │ │ 📦 Pod 2     │   each listening on :8000
   │   :8000      │ │   :8000      │   labels: {app: easypj, tier: web}
   └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘
   kube-proxy load-balances (round-robin / random) across the EndpointSlice
⚠️ 0 endpoints?

Selector doesn't match pod labels, or no pod is Ready. Compare spec.selector with the pod labels, and check the readiness probe. (Types/ports in depth: Ch 4 §4.9 & Part 5.)

8.7 Step 6 — Access It

For a quick local test, forward a port straight to the Service — no external exposure needed.

port-forward → browser
kubectl -n easypj-dev port-forward svc/easypj-web 8000:80
# now open  http://localhost:8000/jobs/   ✅
port-forward — how it works
   your laptop                         Kubernetes cluster
   ┌─────────────────┐                ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   │ 🌐 browser       │                │                              │
   │ localhost:8000  │──kubectl tunnel─│─▶ 🔌 Service:80 ─▶ 📦 Pod:8000│
   │                 │                │      easypj-web      gunicorn │
   └─────────────────┘                └──────────────────────────────┘
   traffic path:  browser → kubectl → apiserver → pod   (a private, session-scoped tunnel)
MethodReachable fromUse when
port-forwardyour laptop only (kubectl tunnel)quick local test / debug — what we did here
ClusterIP (default)inside the cluster onlypod-to-pod / service-to-service traffic
NodePort<anyNodeIP>:30000–32767simple external access without a cloud LB
LoadBalancera cloud-provisioned external IPproduction on a cloud provider
ExternalNameno proxying — returns a DNS CNAME to an external hostalias an in-cluster name to an outside service (e.g. a managed DB)
Ingressone external IP, HTTP routing by host/pathmany services behind one entrypoint (easypj graduates here, Part 5)
📖 Port-forward is for testing only

It tunnels through your kubectl session. Real external access uses NodePort, LoadBalancer, or Ingress (Part 5) — easypj graduates to Ingress there.

resource dependency chain — and one-command cleanup
   🗂️ Namespace easypj-dev
      ├─ ⚙️ ConfigMap easypj-config ─┐
      ├─ 🔒 Secret easypj-secret    ─┤ envFrom
      ├─ 🚀 Deployment easypj-web ──▶ 🎛️ ReplicaSet ──▶ 📦 Pods
      └─ 🔌 Service easypj-web ──selector──▶ the Pods
   🧹 cleanup:  kubectl delete namespace easypj-dev   ← cascades, deletes ALL of the above

🩺 Pod not Running? — the troubleshooting decision tree

Start at kubectl get pods -n easypj-dev, read the STATUS, and follow it down to the exact fix. This single tree resolves the vast majority of "my pod won't start" exam tasks:

pod STATUS → cause → fix
   kubectl get pods -n easypj-dev
     │
     ├─ Pending ──────────────▶ kubectl describe pod <pod>   (read the Events)
     │     ├─ "Insufficient cpu/memory"   → lower requests, or add / free a node
     │     ├─ "node(s) didn't match …"    → check nodeSelector · affinity · taints/tolerations
     │     └─ node Unschedulable           → kubectl uncordon <node>
     │
     ├─ ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull ─▶ wrong image:tag, or the registry needs auth
     │     └─ fix the image name/tag, or add an imagePullSecret (Ch 2)
     │
     ├─ CreateContainerConfigError ──────▶ a referenced ConfigMap/Secret key is missing
     │     └─ create/fix it, then kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-web
     │
     ├─ CrashLoopBackOff ────▶ kubectl logs <pod> --previous   (last crashed container)
     │     ├─ app error          → fix the code / config
     │     ├─ missing env var      → check ConfigMap/Secret refs
     │     └─ permission denied    → check securityContext
     │
     ├─ Running, READY 0/1 ──▶ readiness probe failing → check probe path/port; needs more warm-up?
     │
     └─ Running, READY 1/1 ──▶ ✅ healthy
✅ Verify after each step (so you never debug the whole stack at once)

After Namespace → kubectl get ns. After ConfigMap/Secret → kubectl get cm,secret -n easypj-dev. After Deployment → kubectl get pods -n easypj-dev. After Service → kubectl get ep easypj-web -n easypj-dev (endpoints = the proof it found pods). Catching a failure at its own step is far faster than untangling it at the end.

8.9 What Just Happened? — The Full Flow

One apply set the whole reconciliation machine in motion. Here's the trace from Chapter 3, grounded on easypj — with where each step can fail.

apply → running easypj, step by step
   kubectl apply -f k8s/
     ─▶ 📡 apiserver (authN → authZ → admission)
            ─▶ 🗄️ etcd            persist desired state
            ─▶ 🔄 controller-mgr  Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods
            ─▶ 📋 scheduler       filter → score → BIND each pod to a node
                   ─▶ 🤖 kubelet  pull easypj:v1 → start container → 🌐 CNI gives a pod IP
                          ─▶ ❤️ readiness probe passes → pod joins endpoints
                          ─▶ 🔀 kube-proxy programs Service routing
     ─▶ ✅ easypj LIVE — reachable via the Service
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   where it breaks:  image not built/pushed → ImagePullBackOff  ·  targetPort≠8000 → refused
                     secret missing → env error  ·  selector≠labels → 0 endpoints
💡 Debug in flow order

Pod not Running? → describe pod (image/scheduling). Running but no traffic? → get endpoints + readiness. Endpoints empty? → selector vs labels. Each symptom maps to one step above.

8.10 ConfigMaps & Secrets — the Full Picture

You used both above; here's everything the exam (and real ops) expects you to know about how they're consumed and how they behave.

 ConfigMapSecret
Purposenon-sensitive config (URLs, flags)sensitive data (passwords, tokens, keys)
Stored asplain textbase64 (encoding, not encryption)
Size limit1 MiB1 MiB
Consume asenv vars or volume filesenv vars or volume files (kept in tmpfs RAM)
RBACless restricted by defaultshould be tightly RBAC-restricted
Create withkubectl create configmapkubectl create secret generic

🔌 How each is consumed

Consume viaHowLive-updates?
one key → envvalueFrom.configMapKeyRef / secretKeyRef❌ fixed at pod start
all keys → envenvFrom: [configMapRef|secretRef]❌ fixed at pod start
keys → files (volume)mount the CM/Secret as a volume✅ auto-updates (~kubelet sync)
one file (subPath)mount a single key with subPath❌ no live update
into command/argsreference an injected env var as $(VAR) in the container's command/args❌ fixed at pod start

🎚️ envFrom vs env — inject everything, or pick & rename

envFrom injects every key as an env var (the simplest path — what §8.5 used). env + valueFrom lets you inject individual keys and rename them to whatever the app expects:

env-vs-envFrom.yaml
# envFrom: inject ALL keys from a ConfigMap/Secret
envFrom:
- configMapRef:
    name: easypj-config
- secretRef:
    name: easypj-secret

# env: inject INDIVIDUAL keys — and optionally rename them
env:
- name: DJANGO_SECRET            # ← the name the container sees
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef: { name: easypj-secret, key: SECRET_KEY }            # ← key in the Secret
- name: SETTINGS_MODULE          # ← renamed from the ConfigMap key
  valueFrom:
    configMapKeyRef: { name: easypj-config, key: DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE }
📖 env-over-envFrom precedence

If the same variable name arrives from several sources, a later envFrom source overrides an earlier one, and an explicit env entry overrides any envFrom value. Pattern: set bulk defaults with envFrom, then override one specific key with env.

📖 Limits & immutability

Each ConfigMap/Secret is capped at 1 MiB. Set immutable: true (v1.19+) to forbid edits and cut apiserver/etcd watch load — change it by delete-and-recreate. When to use immutable: a config referenced by thousands of pods (every pod watches every mutable CM/Secret; marking it immutable removes that watch load) and to guarantee no accidental mid-rollout config change.

📝 data vs stringData — stop hand-encoding base64

In a Secret manifest, data: values must be base64-encoded; stringData: lets you write plaintext and the apiserver encodes it for you (write-only — it never shows up on read). Prefer stringData for hand-written manifests. If a key appears in both, stringData wins. kubectl create secret … --from-literal handles the encoding either way.

🔒 Built-in Secret types

TypeFor
Opaquearbitrary key/value (the default)
kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjsonprivate-registry pull creds — modern ~/.docker/config.json (imagePullSecrets)
kubernetes.io/dockercfglegacy registry creds — the older ~/.dockercfg format
kubernetes.io/tlsa TLS cert + key (Ingress, webhooks)
kubernetes.io/basic-authbasic-auth credentials (username/password keys)
kubernetes.io/ssh-authan SSH private key (ssh-privatekey key)
kubernetes.io/service-account-tokena ServiceAccount token (Ch 25)
bootstrap.kubernetes.io/tokena node-join bootstrap token (kubeadm, Ch 9)
🚨 Remember

base64 is encoding, not encryption — Secrets sit unencrypted in etcd by default. Lock them down with encryption-at-rest (apiserver --encryption-provider-config, Ch 11) + RBAC (limit who can get/patch secrets in the namespace, Ch 24), and never commit real values.

🧠 In plain English

A ConfigMap is the app's settings file; a Secret is the same idea for passwords (just base64'd, not locked). Inject as env vars and the values are printed once at startup (fixed); mount as a volume and it's a live noticeboard the app can re-read.

Under the Hood — how config reaches the container & how readiness gates traffic

Two mechanisms make this deploy "just work": envFrom injection at start, and the readiness gate on endpoints.

   CONFIG INJECTION (once, at container start)
     ⚙️ ConfigMap + 🔒 Secret ──envFrom──▶ kubelet builds the container's env block ──▶ Django reads os.environ
     precedence: a later envFrom source, or an explicit `env:` entry, OVERRIDES an earlier key

   READINESS GATE (continuous)
     readinessProbe GET /jobs/ → 200 → pod Ready → EndpointSlice includes its IP → 🔀 Service routes to it
     probe fails → pod DROPPED from endpoints (no restart) → traffic stops, the pod keeps running
🔑 env is fixed at start: edit a ConfigMap/Secret and the running pods don't see it until you kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-web. A volume-mounted ConfigMap updates live (Ch 8 §8.10).
PatternWhat it's for
initContainersrun manage.py migrate to completion before the web container starts (Ch 16)
downward APIexpose pod metadata (name, namespace, IP) to the app as env/files
minReadySecondsa new pod must stay Ready this long before the rollout proceeds — guards against flapping
Recreate vs Rollingschema-incompatible DB migrations may need strategy: Recreate to avoid two versions at once

③ One apply, a whole controller chain — what really happens when easypj goes live. Your single file is split on --- into separate API requests, each written to etcd. Nothing is "deployed" yet — a chain of independent controllers, each watching for work, then turns those records into running containers. Every link only knows its own job:

   kubectl apply -f easypj-all.yaml   (Namespace → ConfigMap → Secret → Deployment → Service)
        │  5 objects POSTed to etcd, in file order
        ▼
   Deployment Controller   sees Deployment, no ReplicaSet  ─▶ creates ReplicaSet  (adds pod-template-hash)
        ▼
   ReplicaSet Controller   sees RS wants 2, has 0 pods     ─▶ creates 2 Pods      (ownerReference → RS)
        ▼
   Scheduler               sees Pods with nodeName=""       ─▶ filter+score+bind   (PATCH spec.nodeName)
        ▼
   kubelet (on that node)  sees Pod bound to me             ─▶ pull image · CRI create/start · mount CM+Secret · probes ─▶ Ready
        ▼
   Endpoints Controller    sees Service + Ready pods        ─▶ writes EndpointSlice (pod IPs)
        ▼
   kube-proxy (every node) sees EndpointSlice change        ─▶ programs iptables/IPVS  ─▶ Service IP now routes
🔑 Each controller is blind to the others: the Deployment Controller never touches a Pod — it only makes a ReplicaSet and watches its status. This is why a stuck rollout is debugged top-down: describe deploy → describe rs → describe pod, following the ownerReferences chain down to whichever link is failing.
CreatedDepends onIf it's out of order…
Namespacenothingevery later create fails with "namespace not found"
ConfigMap / SecretNamespaceDeployment still creates, but pods sit in CreateContainerConfigError until the CM/Secret exists
DeploymentNamespace, CM, Secretworks; if config is added later, the broken pods need a restart to pick it up
ServiceNamespace onlyfine anytime — the Endpoints Controller adds pod IPs dynamically as they turn Ready

Two details worth locking in. The pod-template-hash the Deployment Controller stamps onto each ReplicaSet (and its pods) is how one Deployment can own several ReplicaSets during a rollout without their selectors colliding — the hash is computed from the pod template, so a template change makes a new hash, hence a new ReplicaSet. And CreateContainerConfigError is specifically the kubelet failing step "mount CM/Secret" — the pod was scheduled fine; it's a missing/renamed ConfigMap or Secret key. Fix the config, and because the Deployment owns the pods, you can just kubectl rollout restart (or delete a pod) and the chain re-runs from the kubelet down.

④ What actually drives the chain — the reconciliation loop, and how readiness gates more than traffic. Each controller in the chain runs the same loop, and it's level-triggered (it acts on current state, not on events) — which is why the system is so self-healing:

   THE LOOP every controller runs (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Endpoints…)
     watch → an event lands in a per-controller WORK QUEUE → reconcile(key):
        read DESIRED (spec)  vs  ACTUAL (status/world)  →  make ONE change toward desired  →  return
     • success → drop the key.   failure → RE-QUEUE with exponential backoff (think 1s,2s,4s…)
     • level-triggered: even if an event is missed or the controller restarts, the next
       reconcile still sees the gap and fixes it — events are hints, state is the truth

   READINESS gates TWO things, not one
     ① traffic — only Ready pods are written into the EndpointSlice (you saw this in §8.5)
     ② rollout — during a Deployment update, a NEW pod must report Ready before the rollout
        removes an OLD one; maxUnavailable/maxSurge bound how many can be down/extra meanwhile
        → a readiness probe that never passes STALLS the rollout (old pods stay up, new ones never count)
🔑 The debugging payoff: "my rollout is stuck at 1/3 updated" almost always means the new pods aren't passing readiness — not a Deployment bug. Check kubectl rollout status, then describe a new pod's readiness probe. And because reconcile is level-triggered with backoff, a transient failure (image registry briefly down) self-heals once the cause clears — you'll see RESTARTS/age climb, then the pod settle, with no manual intervention. (Rollout strategy mechanics in full: Ch 13.)

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • The order: Namespace → ConfigMap → Secret → Deployment → Service → port-forward.
  • envFrom injects every CM/Secret key as env vars (fixed at pod start).
  • Readiness gates traffic — only Ready pods appear in the Service's endpoints.
  • Verify with get all + endpoints; a Service with 0 endpoints = selector/label or readiness problem.
  • Cleanup is one command: kubectl delete namespace easypj-dev cascades.
⚠️ First-Deployment Traps
  • Image not built/pushed. Pod stuck ImagePullBackOff — build & push easypj:v1 (Ch 2), or check the registry/secret.
  • targetPort ≠ containerPort. Service says 80→8000 but the app listens elsewhere → "connection refused."
  • Secret values not base64. Use stringData (plaintext) or pre-encode for data.
  • selector ≠ pod labels. Service ends up with 0 endpoints — match them exactly.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Scaffold the Deployment: kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 -n easypj-dev $do, then add envFrom/probes.
  • Make the Service fast: kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000 -n easypj-dev.
  • First check after deploying: kubectl get endpoints easypj-web -n easypj-dev.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 8)

the deploy toolkit
kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=False -n easypj-dev
kubectl create secret generic easypj-secret --from-literal=SECRET_KEY=x -n easypj-dev
kubectl apply -f k8s/                                 # deploy + service
kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000 -n easypj-dev
kubectl get all,endpoints -n easypj-dev ; kubectl logs deploy/easypj-web -n easypj-dev
kubectl -n easypj-dev port-forward svc/easypj-web 8000:80
🧪 Drill — Deploy easypj from scratch in under 10 minutes

No peeking — this is the capstone of Part 2:

  1. Create namespace easypj-dev and make it your default.
  2. Create a ConfigMap (DEBUG=False, ALLOWED_HOSTS=*) and a Secret (SECRET_KEY).
  3. Deploy easypj:v1 (1 replica, port 8000, envFrom both, a readiness probe on /jobs/).
  4. Expose it (80→8000), confirm endpoints, port-forward, and hit /jobs/.
Show solution
terminal
kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev
kubectl create configmap easypj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=False --from-literal=ALLOWED_HOSTS='*'
kubectl create secret generic easypj-secret --from-literal=SECRET_KEY='change-me'
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 $do > d.yaml
# edit d.yaml: ports 8000 · envFrom configMapRef+secretRef · readinessProbe httpGet /jobs/:8000
kubectl apply -f d.yaml
kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000
kubectl get endpoints easypj-web        # pod IPs listed?
kubectl port-forward svc/easypj-web 8000:80   # → http://localhost:8000/jobs/

Why: this exact ns→CM→Secret→Deployment→Service→verify loop is the template behind most Workloads/Services exam tasks.

🧠 Chapter 8 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

The deploy workflow, recalled — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Create a namespace, Deployment, and Service for easypj imperatively.
Show Answer
Answer
generate manifest
kubectl create namespace easypj-dev
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 -n easypj-dev
kubectl expose deploy easypj-web --port=80 --target-port=8000 -n easypj-dev
Explanation

Imperative is fastest for simple objects; add $do > f.yaml when you need to tweak fields the flags can't set.

Q2
Inject DB_HOST into the pod from a ConfigMap.
Show Answer
Answer
configMap → env
env:
- name: DB_HOST
  valueFrom:
    configMapKeyRef:
      name: easypj-config
      key: DB_HOST
Explanation

One key → one env var. For ALL keys use envFrom: [configMapRef: {name: easypj-config}].

Q3
Expose SECRET_KEY from a Secret as an env var.
Show Answer
Answer
secret → env
env:
- name: SECRET_KEY
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef:
      name: easypj-secret
      key: SECRET_KEY
Explanation

Same shape as a ConfigMap, but secretKeyRef. envFrom: [secretRef: …] injects every key.

Q4
The pod is ImagePullBackOff. Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
read pod events
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n easypj-dev | grep -A6 Events   # exact pull error
Explanation

"not found" → wrong name/tag · "unauthorized" → add imagePullSecrets · timeout → registry/network. Build & push easypj:v1 if it doesn't exist.

Port-forward the Service and hit /jobs/.

access locally
kubectl -n easypj-dev port-forward svc/easypj-web 8000:80   # → localhost:8000/jobs/

Q6
Scale easypj-web to 3 replicas.
Show Answer
Answer
scale
kubectl scale deploy easypj-web --replicas=3 -n easypj-dev
Explanation

The ReplicaSet reconciles to the new count; verify with get deploy (3/3) and get endpoints (3 IPs).

Q7
Add a readiness probe so traffic only flows when /jobs/ responds.
Show Answer
Answer
readiness probe
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /jobs/, port: 8000 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
Explanation

A failing readiness probe removes the pod from endpoints (no restart) — clients never hit a not-yet-ready pod.

Q8
Confirm the Service has endpoints — and what if it doesn't?
Show Answer
Answer
check endpoints
kubectl get endpoints easypj-web -n easypj-dev
Explanation

Empty = selector doesn't match pod labels OR no pod is Ready. Compare selector vs labels and check the readiness probe.

Roll the image to easypj:v2 and watch the rollout.

Answer
rollout
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web web=easypj:v2 -n easypj-dev
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web -n easypj-dev   # undo: kubectl rollout undo …
Explanation

Rolling update by default; the old ReplicaSet is kept at 0 for instant rollback (Ch 13).

Q10
A pod is Pending — which command shows why, and where do you look?
Show Answer
Answer
read pod events

"FailedScheduling" → no node fits (resources/taints/selector). Pending also covers image pulls — Events tells you which.

Show Answer

rollout

Explanation

Init containers run to completion, in order, before app containers — perfect for migrations (Ch 16).

Pod is CrashLoopBackOff right after deploy. First two checks?

      💻 you ──port-forward 8000:80──▶ http://localhost:8000/jobs/  ✅
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   ns → ConfigMap → Secret → Deployment → Service → port-forward → /jobs/. That's Part 2. ☸️

In words: you isolated easypj in a Namespace, put plain settings in a ConfigMap and credentials in a Secret, ran the app as a Deployment (pulling both via envFrom, gated by a readiness probe), fronted it with a Service (80→8000), and reached /jobs/ through a port-forward.

The takeaway: this exact order — ns → ConfigMap → Secret → Deployment → Service → verify — is the template behind most Workloads & Services exam tasks. Generate with $do, wire labels/selectors carefully, and always confirm the Service has endpoints.

🟢 Part 2 · Recap · Complete

Hands-On Basics — What You Now Know

You arrived with a mental model; you leave with a cluster you built, kubectl in your fingers, YAML you can read & validate, and easypj running and reachable at /jobs/. Everything in Parts 3–14 operates on this foundation.

🔑 Part 2 — Key Takeaways

  • Environment (Ch 5): kubeconfig = clusters + users + contexts; switch context & set the namespace first, every single task.
  • kubectl (Ch 6): verb + resource + name + flags; explain is your manual; generate with $do (never hand-write); jsonpath/custom-columns extract anything; climb the debug ladder logs→exec→debug.
  • YAML (Ch 7): the 4 required fields; spaces not tabs; selector == template labels; validate with --dry-run=server + diff before applying.
  • Deploy (Ch 8): Namespace → ConfigMap → Secret → Deployment → Service → port-forward → /jobs/; envFrom injects config; readiness gates traffic.
  • 🎯 Exam: kubectl speed + correct context/namespace + clean YAML = passing.
  • 🔑 config use-context · k get/desc/logs/exec/apply · explain · $do · port-forward

In words: Part 2 turned theory into hands. You stand up a cluster and point kubectl at it through a context; you generate and validate YAML instead of hand-writing it; and you assemble easypj from the five core objects in dependency order, then prove it works.

The takeaway: the loop is always the same — set context → generate with $do → validate (--dry-run=server/diff) → apply → verify (get all + endpoints). Master that rhythm and the rest of the guide is variations on it.

Build & Own the Cluster

Chapters 9–12 · Intermediate → Advanced · "Build it, configure it, protect it"

Part 2 drove a cluster someone else built. Part 3 is where you become the administrator: stand up a multi-node cluster from bare Linux nodes with kubeadm, configure the control plane and kubelet, back up and restore etcd (the one skill that can save a cluster), and manage the control plane's static pods. This is the heart of the CKA's Cluster Architecture (25%) domain.

🎯 What you'll be able to do by the end: build a 3-node cluster from scratch, recover a lost join token, snapshot & restore etcd, safely edit a control-plane component, and reason about every required port — the exact tasks the exam sets.

Chapter 9 · Installing Kubernetes with kubeadm

A cluster doesn't appear by magic — kubeadm builds one from ordinary Linux machines: it generates the certificates, launches the control plane, and hands you a command to join workers. The exam may give you a half-built or broken cluster and expect you to finish or fix it, so you must know every step cold.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~3 hours 🎯 Heavily Tested 🔧 kubeadm

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What kubeadm does for you — and what it deliberately leaves to you

🎯 Why this chapter is exam gold

"Prepare infra" and "create a cluster with kubeadm" are explicit CKA competencies — and a broken cluster is a favourite troubleshooting scenario. The five moves below are a script you should be able to run from memory; the exam rewards muscle memory here more than almost anywhere else.

  • Order is everything: prep all nodes → init the CP → install a CNI → join workers. Skip a step and nothing works.
  • The #1 gotcha: all nodes NotReady after init = no CNI installed yet (not a kubelet bug).
  • Save the join command — and know how to regenerate it when you didn't.
