9.1 What is kubeadm?

kubeadm is the official cluster bootstrapper. Point it at a freshly-installed Linux machine and it does the genuinely hard, error-prone parts of standing up Kubernetes: it generates a whole PKI (a CA plus certs for every component), writes the control-plane static-pod manifests, brings up etcd, configures the kubelet, and prints a join command that lets workers enrol securely. What it deliberately does not do is provision machines or choose your networking — those stay your call.

🧠 In plain English

Think of kubeadm as the contractor who builds the house, not the one who buys the land or picks the paint. You supply the plot (VMs, OS, runtime); kubeadm pours the foundation and frames the structure (certs, control plane, etcd); you still choose the "plumbing" (the CNI network plugin) and move in the furniture (your apps). That division is exactly why a fresh kubeadm init cluster sits NotReady until you install a CNI.

kubeadm — what it does vs what it leaves to you
   🖥️ YOU provide (the infra)          🔧 kubeadm handles (the hard parts)        ❌ NOT kubeadm's job
   ─────────────────────────────      ──────────────────────────────────        ─────────────────────────
   VMs / bare metal                   ✅ bootstrap the control plane             VM provisioning
   OS installed (Ubuntu/etc.)         ✅ generate the TLS PKI (CA + certs)       (Terraform / cloud console)
   network connectivity               ✅ create the etcd member                  OS install & patching
   swap disabled                      ✅ configure & start the kubelet           CNI install (you choose it)
   container runtime (containerd)     ✅ render static-pod manifests             LoadBalancer for HA CP
   kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl installed  ✅ issue the bootstrap join token          app deployment (kubectl's job)
🔧
kubeadm init

Run once, on the control-plane node. Generates the PKI, brings up apiserver + etcd + scheduler + controller-manager as static pods, and prints the join command.

🔗
kubeadm join

Run on every worker (and extra control-plane nodes). Uses a token + CA cert hash to authenticate to the cluster and register the node.

the build pipeline — six moves, in order
   🖥️ provision    ⚙️ prerequisites   🔧 kubeadm init    🌐 install CNI     🔗 kubeadm join    ✅ cluster Ready
      VMs/OS    ─▶  swap·modules   ─▶  (control plane) ─▶ (pod network)  ─▶  (each worker)  ─▶  all nodes Ready
                    ·containerd                            nodes Ready                          → run easypj
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   skip a step and the next one fails — this exact order is what the exam tests.
📖 kubeadm vs the alternatives

kubeadm = the CKA-tested, do-it-yourself bootstrapper (you own upgrades, etcd, certs). Managed services (EKS/GKE/AKS) hide the control plane entirely. kops/kubespray wrap kubeadm with infra automation. The exam uses kubeadm precisely because it makes you the administrator of every layer.

9.2 Pre-requisites for All Nodes

Before kubeadm will run, every node — control plane and workers — must be prepared identically. Each of these five steps fixes a specific way the kubelet or runtime would otherwise refuse to work, and each is a classic "broken node" the exam asks you to repair. Do all five on every machine.

🖥️
Hardware

2+ CPUs · 2 GB+ RAM · a unique hostname & MAC per node · full network connectivity

🚫
Swap OFF

the kubelet refuses to start with swap on — disable it now and in /etc/fstab

🐳
Container runtime

containerd (recommended) with the systemd cgroup driver

📦
Toolchain

kubeadm + kubelet + kubectl, same version, held

Step A — disable swap

all nodes · swap
sudo swapoff -a                              # off right now (this boot)
sudo sed -i '/ swap / s/^/#/' /etc/fstab     # and permanently (comment the fstab line)
free -h | grep Swap                          # verify
# Swap:            0B          0B          0B
📖 Why swap must be off

Kubernetes schedules by memory requests/limits and assumes a pod that hits its memory limit is OOM-killed deterministically. Swap breaks that contract (a "full" node could limp along on disk), so the kubelet refuses to start unless swap is off (or you explicitly opt into the newer, still-niche swap support). On the exam: a node NotReady with the kubelet crash-looping → check swapoff first.

Step B — load kernel modules

all nodes · /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf   # load on every boot
overlay
br_netfilter
EOF
sudo modprobe overlay        # overlay = the overlayfs storage driver containers use
sudo modprobe br_netfilter   # br_netfilter = lets iptables see bridged pod traffic
lsmod | grep -E "overlay|br_netfilter"   # verify both are loaded

Step C — sysctl for bridged pod traffic

all nodes · /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables  = 1   # iptables sees IPv4 bridge traffic
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables = 1   # …and IPv6
net.ipv4.ip_forward                 = 1   # route packets between pods/nodes
EOF
sudo sysctl --system                       # apply without a reboot
sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables  # → ... = 1
📖 Why these two settings exist

Pods talk over a Linux bridge. Without bridge-nf-call-iptables=1, packets crossing that bridge bypass iptables — so kube-proxy's Service rules and NetworkPolicies silently don't apply. Without ip_forward=1, the node won't route packets between pods and other nodes at all. Symptom of missing these: pods schedule but can't reach Services or each other.

Step D — containerd with the systemd cgroup driver

all nodes · containerd
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y containerd
sudo mkdir -p /etc/containerd
containerd config default | sudo tee /etc/containerd/config.toml   # write a default config

# CRITICAL — switch the cgroup driver to systemd (must match the kubelet)
sudo sed -i 's/SystemdCgroup = false/SystemdCgroup = true/' /etc/containerd/config.toml

sudo systemctl restart containerd && sudo systemctl enable containerd
sudo systemctl status containerd      # Active: active (running)
🚨 The #1 hidden "broken node": SystemdCgroup mismatch

Modern Linux uses systemd to manage cgroups. The kubelet and the runtime must agree on the driver — both systemd. If containerd is left on the default SystemdCgroup = false (cgroupfs) while the kubelet uses systemd, you get two competing cgroup managers: pods fail to start, the kubelet logs cgroup errors, and the node flaps. This is a favourite exam trap because the node looks "almost" healthy. Always verify this one line.

Step E — install & pin the toolchain

all nodes · kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl
sudo apt-get install -y apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl gpg
# add the Kubernetes apt repo (one minor-version stream, e.g. v1.34)
curl -fsSL https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.34/deb/Release.key \
  | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg
echo 'deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg] \
  https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.34/deb/ /' \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y kubelet kubeadm kubectl
sudo apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl   # ← pin: an apt upgrade must NOT break the node
kubeadm version                              # kubeadm version: ...Major:"1", Minor:"34"...
⚠️ Why apt-mark hold matters

Without a hold, a routine apt upgrade could jump the kubelet a minor version ahead of the control plane — violating the version-skew policy and breaking the node. To upgrade deliberately (Ch 23) you unhold → upgrade → hold again. The apt-repo URL is also per-minor (…/v1.34/…), so upgrading minors means editing that URL too.

A
Swap off

swapoff -a + fstab

B
Modules

overlay · br_netfilter

C
Sysctl

bridge-nf-call · ip_forward

D
containerd

SystemdCgroup = true

E
Toolchain

install + hold

9.3 Initialize the Control Plane

With every node prepared, run kubeadm init on the control-plane node only. This single command generates the cluster's entire PKI, writes the control-plane static-pod manifests, brings up etcd and the apiserver, and prints the command workers use to join. It's the most important command in cluster creation — and the exam expects you to know its key flags and what to do immediately after.

control plane only · kubeadm init
sudo kubeadm init \
  --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16 \        # must match your CNI (Flannel uses this)
  --apiserver-advertise-address=192.168.56.10 \  # this node's IP
  --kubernetes-version=v1.34.0

# ── abbreviated output ──
# [init] Using Kubernetes version: v1.34.0
# [certs] Generating "ca", "apiserver", "etcd/ca", "etcd/server" …
# [kubeconfig] Writing "admin.conf", "kubelet.conf" …
# [control-plane] Creating static Pod manifests for apiserver/scheduler/controller-manager
# [etcd] Creating static Pod manifest for local etcd
# [mark-control-plane] Marking the node as control-plane
#
# Your Kubernetes control-plane has initialized successfully!
#
# To start using your cluster:
#   mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
#   sudo cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
#   sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config
#
# Then you can join any number of worker nodes by running:
# kubeadm join 192.168.56.10:6443 --token abcdef.0123456789abcdef \
#   --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:1a2b3c…

🔧 kubeadm init flags — what each one does

🌐 --pod-network-cidr
the IP range pods get. Must match the CNI you'll install — Flannel expects 10.244.0.0/16, Calico defaults to 192.168.0.0/16. Mismatch = pods never get usable IPs.
📡 --apiserver-advertise-address
the IP the apiserver advertises to other nodes. Use the control-plane node's real (routable) IP, or workers can't reach :6443.
📌 --kubernetes-version
pin the exact version so all components match; otherwise kubeadm picks "latest stable," which may skew from your held packages.
🔒 --control-plane-endpoint
for HA: a shared DNS name / load-balancer fronting all control-plane nodes. Set it even for a single CP if you might add more later (it can't be added afterwards without pain).
📤 --upload-certs
stores the control-plane certs in a Secret so extra CP nodes can join with --control-plane (HA). Covered in Ch 33.

Right after init — wire up kubectl (the 3 commands)

control plane · as your normal user (not root)
mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
sudo cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config

kubectl get nodes
# NAME            STATUS     ROLES           AGE   VERSION
# control-plane   NotReady   control-plane   30s   v1.34.0
# ↑ NotReady is EXPECTED here — there's no CNI yet (§9.4 fixes it)
🚨 SAVE THE JOIN COMMAND — right now

The kubeadm join … line printed at the end of init carries a bootstrap token that expires in 24 hours. Copy it somewhere safe immediately. Lost it (or it expired)? Regenerate any time with kubeadm token create --print-join-command (§9.5) — but on the exam clock, saving it up front is one less thing to fix.

what kubeadm init actually creates on disk
   sudo kubeadm init
     │
     ├─ 🔐 PKI  → /etc/kubernetes/pki/
     │     ca.crt / ca.key ................ the cluster Certificate Authority (root of trust)
     │     apiserver.crt ................... apiserver's TLS serving cert
     │     apiserver-kubelet-client.crt .... apiserver → kubelet auth
     │     etcd/ca.crt · etcd/server.crt ... etcd's own TLS
     │     sa.key / sa.pub ................. signs ServiceAccount tokens
     │
     ├─ 📋 kubeconfigs → /etc/kubernetes/
     │     admin.conf (cluster-admin) · kubelet.conf · controller-manager.conf · scheduler.conf
     │
     ├─ 📦 static-pod manifests → /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
     │     etcd.yaml · kube-apiserver.yaml · kube-controller-manager.yaml · kube-scheduler.yaml
     │
     └─ 🚀 starts everything
           kubelet (systemd) watches that manifests dir → brings up etcd + apiserver +
           scheduler + controller-manager as STATIC PODS; kube-proxy runs as a DaemonSet
📖 This is why Ch 11 & 12 work the way they do

Everything above lives on the control-plane node's filesystem, managed by the kubelet — not by the scheduler. That's why you fix a broken apiserver by editing a file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (Ch 12), and why an etcd snapshot (Ch 11) plus /etc/kubernetes/pki is enough to rebuild a control plane.

9.4 Install a CNI Plugin (Pod Networking)

A fresh kubeadm cluster has no pod network — so every node sits NotReady and CoreDNS stays Pending. The CNI plugin is the missing piece: it gives each pod an IP, wires up pod-to-pod routing across nodes, and (depending on the plugin) enforces NetworkPolicies. Install exactly one, on the control plane, and the nodes flip to Ready within a minute.

📖 KEY TERM — CNI (Container Network Interface)

A standard plug-point: the kubelet calls a CNI plugin each time a pod is created, and the plugin sets up that pod's network namespace, IP, and routes. Kubernetes ships no built-in pod network on purpose — you choose a CNI that fits your needs. This is one of the three big "interfaces" (CRI for runtime, CNI for network, CSI for storage — §12.5).

CNI pluginWhat it's known forNetworkPolicy?ComplexityCKA choice?
CalicoBGP/IP-in-IP routing, mature policy engine✅ full🟡 medium✅ the most common pick
Flanneldead-simple VXLAN overlay❌ none🟢 low✅ great for learning
CiliumeBPF — high performance & deep observability/security✅ rich (L3-L7)🔴 high⚠️ advanced
Weave Netsimple encrypted mesh✅ basic🟢 low⚠️ less common now
control plane · install ONE CNI
# Option A — Calico (default pod CIDR 192.168.0.0/16)
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/calico.yaml

# Option B — Flannel (expects --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16 from init)
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/flannel-io/flannel/releases/latest/download/kube-flannel.yml

# watch the nodes flip NotReady → Ready as the CNI pods come up
kubectl get nodes -w
# control-plane   NotReady → Ready   (≈30-60s after the CNI pods are Running)
why nodes are NotReady until the CNI is up
   kubeadm init done            kubectl apply -f <cni>            CNI pods Running
   ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────┐
   │ node: NotReady   │  ──▶    │ CNI DaemonSet     │   ──▶      │ node: Ready ✅    │
   │ CoreDNS: Pending │         │ lands on each node │            │ CoreDNS: Running │
   │ (no pod network) │         │ sets up CNI config │            │ pods get IPs     │
   └──────────────────┘         └──────────────────┘            └──────────────────┘
   the kubelet reports NotReady while its NetworkReady condition is false —
   i.e. until a CNI has written /etc/cni/net.d/ and its pods are healthy.
🚨 The pod-CIDR must match

The --pod-network-cidr you gave kubeadm init must match what the CNI expects (Flannel → 10.244.0.0/16). Mismatch = pods get IPs the routing doesn't know about → cross-node pod traffic silently fails. With Calico's manifest you either use its default 192.168.0.0/16 or edit the manifest's CIDR to match your init value.

9.5 Join Worker Nodes

With the control plane Ready, each prepared worker joins with the kubeadm join command init printed. The token authenticates the node to the apiserver; the CA cert hash lets the worker verify it's talking to the real control plane (not an impostor) before trusting it.

each worker · kubeadm join
sudo kubeadm join 192.168.56.10:6443 \
  --token abcdef.0123456789abcdef \
  --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:1a2b3c…

# ── output ──
# [preflight] Running pre-flight checks
# [kubelet-start] Starting the kubelet
# This node has joined the cluster.
# → back on the control plane, the node appears and goes Ready once the CNI pod lands

🔑 Lost or expired the join command? Regenerate it

The bootstrap token expires after 24 hours. On the control plane, mint a fresh one — or rebuild the full command (token + correct CA hash) in a single shot:

control plane · token recovery (memorise this)
# the one-liner that rebuilds the WHOLE join command (token + ca-cert-hash)
kubeadm token create --print-join-command
# kubeadm join 192.168.56.10:6443 --token 9z8y7x… --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:1a2b3c…

# …or do it by hand:
kubeadm token create                         # a fresh token
kubeadm token list                           # see tokens + their TTLs
openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt -noout -pubkey \
  | openssl rsa -pubin -outform DER 2>/dev/null | sha256sum | awk '{print $1}'   # the ca-cert-hash
the complete kubeadm build — one flow, the order that matters
   ALL NODES (prep)                          swap off · overlay+br_netfilter · sysctl bridge+ip_forward
   ─────────────────                         · containerd (SystemdCgroup=true) · install kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl + hold
         │
         ▼   CONTROL PLANE only
   kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16   ─►  generates PKI + static-pod manifests + etcd
         │   then: mkdir ~/.kube · cp admin.conf · chown      (+ SAVE the join command!)
         ▼
   kubectl apply -f <CNI>   (Calico / Flannel)     ─►  nodes go Ready (NOT before this!)
         │
         ▼   EACH WORKER
   kubeadm join <cp>:6443 --token <t> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<h>
         │   (lost it? kubeadm token create --print-join-command)
         ▼
   ✅ kubectl get nodes → all Ready   ─►  deploy easypj as the smoke test
   ⚠️ NotReady everywhere = no CNI · token expired = regenerate · swap on = init/join refuses
🏷️
Workers show ROLES <none>

Normal. Label one for cosmetics: kubectl label node worker-1 node-role.kubernetes.io/worker= — it changes nothing functionally.

🧹
Remove a worker cleanly

From the CP: kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data → kubectl delete node worker-1. On the worker: sudo kubeadm reset to wipe its state.

📖 Why a CA cert hash, not just a token?

The token proves the node to the apiserver. The --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash works the other way — it lets the joining node verify the apiserver's CA before sending credentials, defeating a man-in-the-middle. Skipping verification (--discovery-token-unsafe-skip-ca-verification) exists but is exactly as dangerous as it sounds.

9.6 Verifying the Cluster

Once every node has joined, four checks confirm the cluster is genuinely operational — not just "up." The last one (a real scheduled pod) is the proof that scheduling, networking, and the runtime all work end-to-end.

control plane · verify the cluster
# 1. All nodes Ready?
kubectl get nodes -o wide
# NAME            STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION   INTERNAL-IP
# control-plane   Ready    control-plane   10m   v1.34.0   192.168.56.10
# worker-1        Ready    <none>          5m    v1.34.0   192.168.56.11
# worker-2        Ready    <none>          3m    v1.34.0   192.168.56.12

# 2. All system pods Running? (CNI pods, CoreDNS, control plane)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
# calico-node-xxxxx (one per node)        1/1   Running
# coredns-… (x2)                          1/1   Running   ← Running, not Pending
# etcd-control-plane                      1/1   Running
# kube-apiserver-control-plane            1/1   Running
# kube-controller-manager-control-plane   1/1   Running
# kube-proxy-xxxxx (one per node)         1/1   Running
# kube-scheduler-control-plane            1/1   Running

# 3. Where is the API server?
kubectl cluster-info
# Kubernetes control plane is running at https://192.168.56.10:6443

# 4. The real test — deploy easypj and confirm it schedules to a WORKER
kubectl create deployment easypj-web --image=easypj:v1 --replicas=2
kubectl get pods -o wide
# easypj-web-…-abcde   1/1   Running   worker-1   ← scheduled off the control plane ✅
✅
Healthy cluster checklist
  • all nodes STATUS=Ready
  • every kube-system pod Running
  • CoreDNS Running (not Pending)
  • a test pod schedules to a worker
❌
If something's off
  • node NotReady → kubelet down or CNI missing
  • CoreDNS Pending → CNI not installed
  • pods only on the CP → no workers joined
  • ImagePullBackOff → registry/image (Ch 2)

🩺 kubeadm troubleshooting decision tree

When a freshly-built cluster misbehaves, follow the symptom down to the fix — this single tree resolves the vast majority of "my kubeadm cluster is broken" tasks:

symptom → cause → fix
   kubectl get nodes
     │
     ├─ a node is NotReady ─────────────▶ on that node:
     │     ├─ CNI installed?        no ─▶ kubectl apply -f <calico|flannel>
     │     ├─ containerd running?   no ─▶ sudo systemctl restart containerd
     │     ├─ kubelet running?      no ─▶ journalctl -u kubelet  (swap? cgroup driver?)
     │     └─ swap off?             no ─▶ swapoff -a + fstab
     │
     ├─ kubectl can't connect ─────────▶
     │     ├─ kubeconfig set?       no ─▶ cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config
     │     ├─ apiserver running?    no ─▶ crictl ps -a | grep apiserver ; crictl logs (Ch 12)
     │     └─ firewall blocking 6443? yes ─▶ open 6443 between nodes (§9.8)
     │
     └─ pods stuck Pending ────────────▶
           ├─ workers joined?       no ─▶ kubeadm join (or token create --print-join-command)
           ├─ enough cpu/memory?    no ─▶ lower requests / add a node
           └─ taints blocking?     yes ─▶ tolerate or remove the taint (Ch 14)

9.7 Practice Exercises

Building clusters is a muscle-memory skill — the exam gives you minutes, not hours. Drill these until Exercise 1 takes under 30 minutes and the recovery moves are reflex.

🏋️
1 · Build a 3-node cluster

3 VMs → prereqs on all → kubeadm init → install Calico → join 2 workers → deploy easypj and verify. ⏱️ target: 30 min.

🔑
2 · Token recovery

Assume the join token expired. Regenerate with kubeadm token create --print-join-command and join a fresh worker with it.

🔧
3 · Fix a broken node

Deliberately break a worker (turn swap on, stop containerd, flip SystemdCgroup=false). Diagnose via journalctl -u kubelet and restore it to Ready.

🎯
4 · Add a control-plane node

Re-init with --control-plane-endpoint + --upload-certs, then join a second CP with --control-plane (HA preview, Ch 33).

🧪 Capstone drill — rebuild from scratch in < 30 minutes

The single best Part-3 exercise: tear a cluster down with kubeadm reset on every node, then rebuild it end-to-end against the §9.5 flow without looking. When that's comfortable, the kubeadm exam questions become free marks.

📦
Vagrant quick setup for practice

The fastest way to get throwaway multi-node VMs locally: a Vagrantfile defining control-plane + worker-1/2 on a private network → vagrant up → SSH in and run the prereqs + kubeadm. Cheaper than cloud and resets in seconds with vagrant destroy.

🆘
The 3-command debugging lifeline

When anything in a kubeadm build is broken, these three answer 90% of it: kubectl get nodes (what's NotReady?) → kubectl get pods -n kube-system (which control-plane/CNI pod is unhealthy?) → sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 (the node-level reason).

9.8 Required Ports (open these between nodes)

A cluster only works if its components can reach each other. On a real install (and in firewall-troubleshooting exam tasks) you must know which inbound ports each node type needs. A blocked port produces a specific failure — memorise the mapping and you can diagnose "joins fail" or "kubectl logs hangs" in seconds.

NodePort(s)ComponentWho connects
Control plane (inbound)6443kube-apiserverevery client, kubelet & node
2379-2380etcd: client (2379) + peer/Raft (2380)apiserver → etcd; etcd ↔ etcd
10259kube-schedulerlocalhost (health/metrics)
10257kube-controller-managerlocalhost (health/metrics)
10250kubelet APIcontrol plane → kubelet
Worker (inbound)10250kubelet APIcontrol plane → kubelet (logs/exec/metrics)
10256kube-proxy healthload balancers / health checks
30000-32767NodePort Service rangeexternal clients → NodePort Services
who dials whom — the ports that must be open
        🧑 kubectl / clients ───────────────6443──────────────▶ 📡 apiserver ─┐
                                                                              │ 2379-2380
   🤖 worker kubelet ◀──10250── apiserver        🗄️ etcd ◀────────────────────┘
   🌐 external user ──30000-32767──▶ 🔀 NodePort (worker)      📋 scheduler :10259  🔄 ctrl-mgr :10257
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   control-plane inbound: 6443 · 2379-2380 · 10259 · 10257 · 10250
   worker inbound:        10250 · 10256 · 30000-32767
🚨 Blocked port → exact symptom
  • 6443 blocked → kubeadm join fails & kubectl can't reach the cluster ("connection refused" to :6443).
  • 10250 blocked → kubectl logs/exec hang and kubectl top/metrics fail (apiserver can't reach the kubelet).
  • 2379-2380 blocked → etcd can't form/keep quorum → apiserver errors, cluster effectively down.
  • 30000-32767 blocked → NodePort Services unreachable from outside.
Under the Hood — what kubeadm init actually does, phase by phase

kubeadm init isn't one action — it's an ordered pipeline of phases, each of which you can run (or skip) individually with kubeadm init phase <name>. Knowing the order explains every "init failed at step X" message and is the key to repairing a half-built control plane.

   kubeadm init
     ① preflight ............ check swap/cgroups/ports/CRI; pull images   (fails fast & loud)
     ② certs ................ generate the PKI in /etc/kubernetes/pki  (CA, apiserver, etcd, sa keys)
     ③ kubeconfig .......... write admin/kubelet/controller-manager/scheduler .conf
     ④ etcd ................ render the local etcd static-pod manifest
     ⑤ control-plane ....... render apiserver + controller-manager + scheduler static-pod manifests
     ⑥ kubelet-start ....... write kubelet config + start the kubelet (it then runs the static pods)
     ⑦ upload-config ....... store kubeadm & kubelet config in the kubeadm-config ConfigMap
     ⑧ upload-certs ........ (HA, optional) stash CP certs in a Secret for other CP nodes
     ⑨ mark-control-plane .. taint & label this node as control-plane
     ⑩ bootstrap-token ..... create the join token + RBAC so nodes can bootstrap
     ⑪ kubelet-finalize .... point the kubelet at its rotated, cluster-issued cert
     ⑫ addons .............. deploy CoreDNS + kube-proxy
🔑 Why phases matter on the exam: a broken control plane rarely needs a full re-init. If certs expired you re-run just kubeadm init phase certs (or kubeadm certs renew); if the apiserver manifest is gone you regenerate just kubeadm init phase control-plane apiserver. And kubeadm reset undoes the lot. The phase list is also the troubleshooting order — an init that dies at "preflight" is swap/cgroup/port; one that dies later is usually certs or the kubelet.
Beyond the basicsWhat to know (so you never need the docs)
the kubeadm-config ConfigMapphase ⑦ stores your cluster's config in kube-system/kubeadm-config; upgrades & new node joins read it. Inspect with kubectl -n kube-system get cm kubeadm-config -o yaml.
declarative --configinstead of flags, pass a kubeadm init --config=cfg.yaml (a ClusterConfiguration + InitConfiguration) — reproducible, version-controllable installs.
TLS bootstrapping & bootstrap tokensa joining kubelet uses the short-lived bootstrap token to submit a CSR; the cluster auto-approves it and issues the kubelet a real cert (which then auto-rotates). That's why a token, not a permanent credential, is enough to join.
--upload-certs (HA)uploads CP certs (encrypted) so additional control-plane nodes join with --control-plane --certificate-key … instead of hand-copying /etc/kubernetes/pki.
air-gapped installskubeadm config images pull pre-pulls every control-plane image; point it at a private registry with --image-repository.
--ignore-preflight-errors & CRI socketbypass a specific preflight check when you know better; --cri-socket unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock when multiple runtimes are present.

Going deeper than the phase list — the PKI is one trust chain, and it explains everything. Phase ② doesn't just "make certs"; it builds a certificate hierarchy rooted in a self-signed cluster CA. Every component proves its identity with a cert that traces back to that root — which is why one CA can authenticate the whole cluster, and why an expired cert breaks things in predictable ways.

   /etc/kubernetes/pki/
   🔱 ca.crt + ca.key  ── the CLUSTER root CA (self-signed, valid 10 years) ── signs ▼
        ├─ apiserver.crt ................ apiserver's TLS serving cert (SANs: every cluster IP/DNS)
        ├─ apiserver-kubelet-client.crt . lets the apiserver authenticate TO each kubelet (logs/exec)
        └─ (kubelet client certs) ....... each kubelet's identity, auto-issued via the CSR flow
   🔱 etcd/ca.crt ───── a SEPARATE CA just for etcd ── signs ▼
        ├─ etcd/server.crt ............. etcd's serving + peer cert (:2379 client, :2380 peer)
        └─ apiserver-etcd-client.crt ... lets the apiserver authenticate to etcd
   🔑 sa.key / sa.pub ─ NOT a cert — the keypair that SIGNS & verifies ServiceAccount tokens
   front-proxy-ca.crt ─ a third CA for the aggregation layer (extension apiservers, metrics-server)
🔑 Why this is the "to the core" view: there are two CAs on purpose — compromising the etcd CA shouldn't let you mint apiserver certs, and vice-versa. The certs default to a 1-year life (the CA lasts 10) — that's why kubeadm certs check-expiration/renew all exist and why a kubeadm upgrade (which auto-renews) keeps long-lived clusters healthy. And because identity is entirely these files, a working control plane can be rebuilt from just /etc/kubernetes/pki + an etcd snapshot — lose the PKI and even a perfect etcd backup can't re-establish trust. This is the deep reason Ch 11 (etcd) and the PKI together are the cluster.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Prep every node first: swap off · overlay+br_netfilter · sysctl bridge+ip_forward · containerd SystemdCgroup=true · install + hold the toolchain.
  • kubeadm init on the control plane → copy admin.conf to ~/.kube/config → save the join command.
  • Install a CNI — nodes stay NotReady and CoreDNS Pending until you do.
  • kubeadm join the workers with token + ca-cert-hash; regenerate with kubeadm token create --print-join-command.
  • Ports: CP needs 6443 · 2379-2380 · 10259/10257 · 10250; workers need 10250 · 10256 · 30000-32767.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Traps
  • Swap on. kubeadm init/join refuses outright — swapoff -a + comment fstab.
  • No CNI. All nodes NotReady after init is expected until you apply a network plugin — not a kubelet bug.
  • cgroup-driver mismatch. containerd SystemdCgroup=false vs systemd kubelet → pods won't start; the subtlest "broken node."
  • Expired join token. Tokens last 24h — regenerate, don't panic.
  • pod-CIDR mismatch. --pod-network-cidr must match the CNI's expectation.
  • Forgot apt-mark hold. A later apt upgrade skews the kubelet and breaks the node.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • kubeadm token create --print-join-command rebuilds a lost join in one line.
  • kubeadm config images pull before init = faster init (and works air-gapped).
  • kubeadm reset -f on a node to undo everything and start clean.
  • journalctl -u kubelet -f is your first stop for any "node won't come up."

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 9)

the kubeadm toolkit
kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16 --apiserver-advertise-address=<ip>
kubeadm join <cp>:6443 --token <t> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<h>
kubeadm token create --print-join-command     # regenerate a lost join
kubeadm config images pull                    # pre-pull control-plane images
kubeadm reset -f                              # undo init/join on a node
kubeadm certs check-expiration ; kubeadm certs renew all   # cert lifecycle
systemctl status kubelet ; journalctl -u kubelet -f        # the node agent
kubectl get nodes -o wide ; kubectl get pods -n kube-system
🧪 Drill — bootstrap a control plane & join a worker (from memory)

No peeking — this is the core CKA build:

  1. On all nodes: disable swap, load modules, set sysctls, install containerd with SystemdCgroup=true, install & hold the toolchain.
  2. On the CP: kubeadm init with a pod-CIDR, then configure ~/.kube/config.
  3. Install a CNI and confirm the node goes Ready.
  4. Regenerate the join command and join one worker; verify get nodes shows both Ready.
Show solution
terminal
# every node
sudo swapoff -a; sudo sed -i '/ swap / s/^/#/' /etc/fstab
sudo modprobe overlay br_netfilter
echo -e "net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1\nnet.ipv4.ip_forward=1" | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf; sudo sysctl --system
sudo sed -i 's/SystemdCgroup = false/SystemdCgroup = true/' /etc/containerd/config.toml; sudo systemctl restart containerd

# control plane
sudo kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
mkdir -p ~/.kube; sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config; sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) ~/.kube/config
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/flannel-io/flannel/releases/latest/download/kube-flannel.yml
kubeadm token create --print-join-command      # copy this

# worker (paste the printed join command)
sudo kubeadm join <cp>:6443 --token <t> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<h>
kubectl get nodes        # both Ready ✅

🧠 Chapter 9 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

kubeadm build & recovery recall — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Disable swap permanently on a node (commands).
Show Answer
Answer
swap off
sudo swapoff -a                            # now
sudo sed -i '/ swap / s/^/#/' /etc/fstab   # and across reboots
Explanation

swapoff -a only lasts until reboot; commenting the swap line in /etc/fstab makes it stick. The kubelet refuses to start with swap on (unless you explicitly enable the newer swap feature-gate).

Q2
Name the 3 commands you run right after kubeadm init.
Show Answer
Answer
configure kubectl
mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
sudo cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config
Explanation

They copy the cluster-admin kubeconfig (admin.conf) into your home dir so kubectl works as your normal user. Run them as that user, not root. (And immediately save the printed join command.)

Q3
All nodes are NotReady right after init — most likely cause and fix?
Show Answer
Answer

No CNI installed. The kubelet's NetworkReady condition is false until a pod-network plugin is applied. Fix: kubectl apply -f <calico|flannel>; nodes go Ready in ~30-60s.

Explanation

This is expected behaviour, not a bug — kubeadm intentionally ships no pod network. CoreDNS staying Pending is the corroborating symptom.

Q4
The join token expired — add a new worker anyway (commands).
Show Answer
Answer
control plane → then worker
kubeadm token create --print-join-command   # CP: prints a fresh full join command
# on the worker, paste it:
sudo kubeadm join <cp>:6443 --token <new> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<h>
Explanation

--print-join-command bundles a new token with the correct CA hash in one step — far faster than minting a token and computing the hash by hand.

Q5
Why must --pod-network-cidr match the CNI's expectation?
Show Answer
Answer

Because the CNI hands pods IPs from, and programs routes for, a specific CIDR. If kubeadm advertises one range and the CNI uses another, pods get IPs the routing fabric doesn't know about → cross-node pod traffic silently fails.

Explanation

Flannel expects 10.244.0.0/16; Calico defaults to 192.168.0.0/16. Either pass the matching --pod-network-cidr at init or edit the CNI manifest's CIDR.

Q6
The kubelet is crash-looping on a fresh node — where do you look?
Show Answer
Answer
on the node
sudo systemctl status kubelet
sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager   # the actual error
Explanation

Top suspects in order: swap still on, containerd SystemdCgroup mismatch, container runtime down, or a bad /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml. The journal names which one.

Q7
Which kernel modules & sysctls are required, and why?
Show Answer
Answer

Modules: overlay (overlayfs container storage) and br_netfilter (so iptables sees bridged traffic). Sysctls: net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 (kube-proxy/NetworkPolicy apply to bridged pod traffic) and net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 (route packets between pods/nodes).

Explanation

Without them, pods may schedule but can't reach Services or other nodes — a confusing "networking just doesn't work" failure.

Q8
Cleanly remove a worker (drain + delete + reset).
Show Answer
Answer
CP, then the worker
kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data   # evict workloads
kubectl delete node worker-1                                        # remove from the API
# on worker-1 itself:
sudo kubeadm reset -f                                               # wipe cluster state
Explanation

Drain first so pods reschedule elsewhere; delete removes the node object; reset cleans certs/manifests/CNI config off the machine so it could rejoin fresh.

Q9
Which ports must be open between the control plane and workers?
Show Answer
Answer

Control plane (inbound): 6443 (apiserver), 2379-2380 (etcd), 10259 (scheduler), 10257 (controller-manager), 10250 (kubelet). Workers (inbound): 10250 (kubelet), 10256 (kube-proxy), 30000-32767 (NodePort).

Explanation

Memorise by symptom: 6443 down = joins/kubectl fail; 10250 down = logs/exec/metrics fail; 2379-2380 down = etcd loses quorum.

Q10
Pin the toolchain so an apt upgrade can't break the node.
Show Answer
Answer
pin versions
sudo apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl
apt-mark showhold        # verify they're held
Explanation

A hold freezes the package version so a routine upgrade can't skew the kubelet ahead of the control plane. To upgrade deliberately (Ch 23): unhold → upgrade → hold again.

⚙️ Chapter 9 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style "build it / fix it" tasks with the real commands.

Q11
A worker fails to join with couldn't validate the identity of the API Server. Diagnose & fix.
Show Answer
Answer

The token expired or the CA hash is wrong/stale. On the control plane, mint a fresh full command and rejoin:

fix
kubeadm token create --print-join-command   # CP: fresh token + correct hash
sudo kubeadm join … --token <new> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<h>
Explanation

The CA hash lets the worker verify the apiserver; a mismatch (or expired token) aborts the join before any credentials are sent.

Q12
kubeadm init aborts at preflight: [ERROR Swap]: running with swap on is not supported. Fix and retry.
Show Answer
Answer
fix
sudo swapoff -a; sudo sed -i '/ swap / s/^/#/' /etc/fstab
sudo kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
Explanation

Preflight catches this loudly. Don't paper over it with --ignore-preflight-errors=Swap in the exam — actually disable swap.

Q13
After init, kubectl get nodes says connection refused / localhost:8080. Cause & fix.
Show Answer
Answer

No kubeconfig in scope — kubectl is falling back to the legacy localhost:8080. Set it up:

fix
mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
sudo cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config
Explanation

Without ~/.kube/config (or $KUBECONFIG), kubectl has no server URL or creds and defaults to the old insecure port that no longer exists.

Q14
Nodes are Ready but new pods stick in ContainerCreating with failed to set up sandbox … cni. Likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer

A broken/misconfigured CNI — often a pod-CIDR mismatch or a half-applied plugin. Check the CNI pods and the init CIDR:

diagnose
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|flannel|cilium'
kubectl -n kube-system logs ds/kube-flannel-ds   # or the calico-node DaemonSet
Explanation

If CNI pods are CrashLooping, fix the CIDR (must match --pod-network-cidr) or re-apply the correct manifest; the kubelet can't create pod sandboxes until the CNI config in /etc/cni/net.d is valid.

Q15
Prepare for an air-gapped install — pre-pull all control-plane images.
Show Answer
Answer
pre-pull
kubeadm config images list                    # what's needed
kubeadm config images pull                    # pull them all
kubeadm config images pull --image-repository registry.local:5000   # from a private mirror
Explanation

Pre-pulling makes init fast and works without internet; --image-repository (also valid on init) points everything at your mirror.

Q16
A year-old cluster's control plane fails with x509 "certificate has expired." Renew the certs.
Show Answer
Answer
cert renewal
kubeadm certs check-expiration            # see what expired
sudo kubeadm certs renew all              # renew every cert
# restart the control-plane static pods (move-and-return the manifests, or reboot kubelet)
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
# refresh your admin kubeconfig too:
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
Explanation

kubeadm certs are valid ~1 year; a kubeadm upgrade auto-renews them, which is why regularly-upgraded clusters rarely hit this.

Q17
Outline adding a second control-plane node for HA.
Show Answer
Answer

Init the first CP with a shared endpoint and uploaded certs, then join the second with --control-plane:

HA control plane
# first CP
sudo kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint "lb.example:6443" --upload-certs --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
# second CP (kubeadm prints this join, note --control-plane + --certificate-key)
sudo kubeadm join lb.example:6443 --token … --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:… \
  --control-plane --certificate-key <key>
Explanation

HA needs an odd number of CP/etcd members behind a load balancer (the --control-plane-endpoint). Full HA topologies are Ch 33.

Q18
A node is NotReady; the kubelet logs show cgroup driver errors. Fix it.
Show Answer
Answer
align cgroup drivers
sudo sed -i 's/SystemdCgroup = false/SystemdCgroup = true/' /etc/containerd/config.toml
sudo systemctl restart containerd kubelet
sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 20 --no-pager   # confirm the errors stop
Explanation

The kubelet and containerd must use the same cgroup driver (systemd). A mismatch is the classic "almost healthy" broken node.

Q19
kubeadm init fails: [ERROR Port-6443]: Port 6443 is in use. Cause & fix.
Show Answer
Answer

A previous init/join left state behind. Reset, then init again:

reset & retry
sudo kubeadm reset -f
sudo rm -rf /etc/cni/net.d ~/.kube/config
sudo kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
Explanation

reset tears down the existing control-plane pods/etcd holding those ports; clearing CNI config and the stale kubeconfig avoids leftovers.

Q20
Confirm a node's kubelet is healthy and which config file it uses.
Show Answer
Answer
kubelet health & config
systemctl status kubelet                       # active (running)?
sudo cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml          # the kubelet's config (cgroupDriver, etc.)
sudo cat /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf          # its kubeconfig (how it reaches the apiserver)
Explanation

/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml holds runtime settings (cgroup driver, eviction thresholds); kubelet.conf is its kubeconfig. The systemd drop-in under /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/ shows the flags kubeadm set.

📌 Chapter 9 Visual Summary — bare nodes to a verified cluster, one flow
   🖥️ EVERY NODE (prep)   swapoff · overlay+br_netfilter · sysctl · containerd(SystemdCgroup=true) · kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl+hold
        │
        ▼  CONTROL PLANE
   🔧 kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=…  ─►  PKI + static-pod manifests + etcd + join token
        │   mkdir ~/.kube · cp admin.conf · chown      (SAVE the join command!)
        ▼
   🌐 kubectl apply -f <CNI>   ─►  nodes flip NotReady → Ready, CoreDNS Runs
        │
        ▼  EACH WORKER
   🔗 kubeadm join <cp>:6443 --token … --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash …   (lost? token create --print-join-command)
        ▼
   ✅ kubectl get nodes → all Ready  ─►  deploy easypj as the smoke test
   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   ports: CP 6443·2379-2380·10259·10257·10250 │ worker 10250·10256·30000-32767     ☸️

In words: you prepare every node identically (swap off, kernel modules, sysctls, containerd on the systemd cgroup driver, the held toolchain). On the control plane, kubeadm init generates the PKI, writes the static-pod manifests, starts etcd, and prints a join command — then you wire up kubectl and save that join command. Nodes stay NotReady until you apply a CNI; then workers kubeadm join with a token + CA hash.

The takeaway: the order is the exam — prep all → init CP → install CNI → join workers → verify — and the two recovery reflexes that save you are kubeadm token create --print-join-command (lost join) and journalctl -u kubelet (broken node). Get the right firewall ports open and the cluster simply works.

Chapter 10 · Cluster Configuration & kubeconfig

A running cluster is a configured cluster. This chapter is where you learn to bend Kubernetes to requirements — read and merge kubeconfig, tune the apiserver and kubelet by editing their config, enable admission controllers, and navigate API groups — and, just as importantly, how to recover when an edit breaks the control plane.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🎯 Heavily Tested ⚙️ Configuration

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Read a kubeconfig to the bottom — clusters, users, contexts, and how files merge
  • ✅ Manage many clusters from one machine and switch safely between them
  • ✅ Configure the kube-apiserver via its static-pod manifest (and recover a bad edit)
  • ✅ Configure the kubelet via /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml + its systemd unit
  • ✅ Understand & enable admission controllers — where they run and why order matters
  • ✅ Navigate API groups & versioning — core vs named groups
🎓 CKA Relevance
Cluster Architecture 25% apiserver/kubelet config CORE TASK Troubleshooting 30%
🎯 The one habit that saves your cluster

Configuring the control plane means editing files — and a single typo in kube-apiserver.yaml takes the apiserver (and your kubectl) offline. The exam loves this scenario.

  • Always back up first: sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/ before any edit.
  • The kubelet auto-restarts the component when you save the manifest — no kubectl needed (which is good, because it may be down).
  • Recovery = fix the file. If the apiserver won't come back, your edit is wrong — restore from /tmp.

10.1 kubeconfig — the Deep Dive

You met kubeconfig in Ch 5; now we read it to the bottom. A kubeconfig is three lists plus a pointer: clusters (where to connect), users (who you are), and contexts (a named pairing of cluster + user + default namespace), with current-context selecting the active one. Every field below is something the exam can ask you to read or change.

the three lists, joined by a context
   ~/.kube/config
   ├─ clusters[]   WHERE   { server: https://10.0.0.1:6443 , certificate-authority(-data): CA }
   ├─ users[]      WHO     { client-certificate(-data)+client-key(-data) | token | exec: <plugin> }
   └─ contexts[]   COMBO   { cluster: prod , user: admin , namespace: easypj-prod }
   current-context: prod   ◀── kubectl acts as THIS (cluster + user + namespace) until you switch
        🖥️ Cluster (WHERE)  +  👤 User (WHO)  +  📂 Namespace (SCOPE)  =  📋 Context
~/.kube/config — fully annotated
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
current-context: easypj-prod          # the active context
clusters:
- name: easypj-prod
  cluster:
    server: https://10.0.0.1:6443      # WHERE — apiserver URL
    certificate-authority-data: LS0t…  # the cluster CA (base64) — verifies the server
users:
- name: admin
  user:
    client-certificate-data: LS0t…     # WHO — your client cert (base64)…
    client-key-data: LS0t…             # …and its private key
    # OR a token:        token: eyJhbGci…
    # OR an exec plugin: exec: { command: aws, args: [eks, get-token, …] }  (cloud auth)
contexts:
- name: easypj-prod
  context:
    cluster: easypj-prod               # ties a cluster…
    user: admin                        # …to a user…
    namespace: easypj-prod             # …and a default namespace
SectionHoldsAnswers
clustersserver URL + CA certWHERE do I connect?
usersclient cert/key, token, or exec pluginWHO am I?
contextscluster + user + namespacethe COMBO I switch to

📋 kubeconfig — field by field

📍 clusters[].server
the apiserver URL — https://<ip>:6443 (6443 is the default API port)
🔐 clusters[].certificate-authority(-data)
the cluster CA — kubectl uses it to verify the apiserver's TLS cert (defeats a spoofed server)
👤 users[].client-certificate(-data) + client-key
your client cert + key — the apiserver verifies these to authenticate you (CN→username, O→group)
🎟️ users[].token / exec
an alternative identity — a bearer token (ServiceAccounts, OIDC) or an exec plugin (cloud auth)
🔗 contexts[].cluster + user + namespace
a named triple binding a cluster to a user, with an optional default namespace
⭐ current-context
which context is active now — changed with kubectl config use-context <name>
📖 Embedded vs file-path credentials

The -data suffix means the cert/CA is base64-embedded in the file; without it (certificate-authority: /path/ca.crt) it's a file reference. kubeadm's admin.conf embeds everything (portable); Minikube uses file paths (so the file is short but not self-contained). Decode an embedded cert with … | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -text.

10.2 Managing Multiple Clusters

Admins juggle several clusters from one laptop — exactly like the exam's ~6 contexts. Four commands cover everything, and the discipline is always the same: switch → verify → act.

context management
kubectl config get-contexts                 # list all (★ = current)
# CURRENT   NAME          CLUSTER      AUTHINFO   NAMESPACE
# *         easypj-prod   easypj-prod  admin      easypj-prod
#           easypj-dev    easypj-dev   dev-user   easypj-dev

kubectl config use-context easypj-dev       # SWITCH
kubectl config current-context             # verify → easypj-dev
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj   # change default ns
kubectl config view --minify               # show ONLY the active context (cluster/user/ns)
how $KUBECONFIG merges files (precedence)
   export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/work/dev.yaml:~/work/prod.yaml
                         │              │             │
                         └── highest ──┘  (on a name clash, the FIRST file wins)
   kubectl config get-contexts   ─►  shows the UNION of contexts from all files
   kubectl config view --flatten > merged && mv merged ~/.kube/config   ─►  bake the merge into one file
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   ⚠️ a stray $KUBECONFIG in your shell silently overrides ~/.kube/config — the #1 "where's my cluster?" bug
💡 Precedence, top to bottom

--kubeconfig=FILE (flag) > $KUBECONFIG (colon-separated list, first-wins on clashes) > ~/.kube/config (default). --flatten resolves a merged set into one self-contained file — handy after combining a teammate's config.

10.3 API Server Configuration

The kube-apiserver is configured by its static-pod manifest at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml. There is no "apiserver config UI" — you edit that file's command: flags, save, and the kubelet (which watches the directory) restarts the apiserver pod with the new flags. Powerful, and dangerous: a typo means the apiserver — and your kubectl — won't come back.

control plane — who talks to whom (the apiserver is the hub)
                              CONTROL PLANE NODE
   ┌──────────────────┐                          ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │ 📋 kube-scheduler │──────HTTPS :6443────────▶│ 📡 kube-apiserver         │
   │ "where should     │                          │  the CENTRAL hub —        │
   │  this pod run?"   │                          │  EVERY component talks    │
   └──────────────────┘                          │  through me               │
   ┌──────────────────┐                          │                           │
   │ 🔄 controller-mgr │──────HTTPS :6443────────▶│  :6443 HTTPS API          │
   │ "actual == desired?"                         └─────────────┬─────────────┘
   └──────────────────┘                                        │ HTTPS :2379
   ┌──────────────────┐                                        ▼
   │ 🤖 kubelet (nodes)│──────HTTPS :6443────────▶      ┌──────────────┐
   └──────────────────┘                                  │ 🗄️ etcd       │  ONLY the apiserver
   🧑 kubectl ─────────────HTTPS :6443──────────▶         │ :2379 client  │  talks to etcd
                                                          │ :2380 peer    │
                                                          └──────────────┘
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   it's a STAR: scheduler, controller-manager, kubelets & kubectl all go through the apiserver;
   the apiserver alone reads/writes etcd. Configure the hub → you configure how the cluster behaves.
how an apiserver flag change propagates
   you edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml   (add/change a --flag)
        │  save
        ▼
   🤖 kubelet (watching that dir) notices the change
        │  kills the old apiserver static pod, starts a new one with the new flags
        ▼
   📡 new kube-apiserver running   ──►  kubectl works again   (≈15-40s)
   ⚠️ bad flag / YAML typo → the new pod crash-loops → apiserver down → kubectl "connection refused"
      RECOVER: fix the file (or restore your /tmp backup); the kubelet keeps retrying until it's valid.
control plane · the SAFE edit workflow
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/   # 1. BACK UP first, always
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml        # 2. edit a --flag under command:
# 3. watch it restart (kubectl may briefly fail — that's expected)
sudo crictl ps | grep apiserver        # the container restarts with a new ID
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -w | grep apiserver
# broke it? restore and wait:
sudo cp /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
Key flagWhat it controls
--authorization-modethe authorizers, in order — typically Node,RBAC
--enable-admission-pluginswhich admission controllers run (e.g. NodeRestriction,PodSecurity) — §10.5
--etcd-serversthe etcd endpoint(s) the apiserver reads/writes (https://127.0.0.1:2379)
--service-cluster-ip-rangethe CIDR ClusterIPs are allocated from (e.g. 10.96.0.0/12)
--advertise-addressthe IP the apiserver advertises to the cluster
--encryption-provider-configenables encryption-at-rest for Secrets (Ch 11 §11.5)
🚨 Recovering a dead apiserver

If kubectl dies after your edit, the apiserver pod is crash-looping on your change. You can't use kubectl — work on the node: sudo crictl ps -a | grep apiserver and sudo crictl logs <id> show why (e.g. "unknown flag," "no such file"). Fix the YAML (or restore the /tmp backup); the kubelet relaunches it within ~20s. This exact recovery is a classic exam task — the backup is what makes it a non-event.

10.4 kubelet Configuration

The kubelet is a systemd service, not a pod, so it's configured differently from the control plane. Its settings live in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (a KubeletConfiguration object), and the flags kubeadm set live in a systemd drop-in. After a change you reload systemd and restart the service.

node · /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (excerpt)
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
clusterDNS:                 # the in-cluster DNS Service IP (CoreDNS)
- 10.96.0.10
clusterDomain: cluster.local  # the DNS suffix for Services/pods
cgroupDriver: systemd       # MUST match containerd (§9.2)
evictionHard:               # when the kubelet starts evicting pods
  memory.available: "100Mi"
  nodefs.available: "10%"
authentication:             # how the apiserver authenticates to this kubelet
  x509: { clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt }
node · apply a kubelet change
sudo vim /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml          # edit clusterDNS, evictionHard, etc.
# the kubelet's systemd flags live here:
sudo cat /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload                   # REQUIRED after a unit/drop-in change
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
sudo journalctl -u kubelet -f                  # watch it come back cleanly
⚠️ daemon-reload before restart

If you change the systemd unit or a drop-in (*.conf), you must systemctl daemon-reload before restart — otherwise systemd runs the old definition and your change appears to do nothing. (Editing only config.yaml needs just a restart.) When a node misbehaves, journalctl -u kubelet is always the first place to look.

10.5 Admission Controllers

Admission controllers are gatekeepers the apiserver runs after authentication & authorization, but before the object is persisted to etcd. They come in two waves: mutating ones can change the object (inject defaults, sidecars), then schema validation runs, then validating ones can only accept or reject it. This is where cluster policy lives.

the API request pipeline — every write travels this
   kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
        ▼
   🔐 AUTHENTICATION    who are you?     (client cert / token / OIDC)        ← reject → 401
        ▼
   🛂 AUTHORIZATION     are you allowed? (RBAC: verb + resource)             ← reject → 403
        ▼
   🧪 ADMISSION
        ├─ MUTATING controllers + webhooks   (ADD/CHANGE: LimitRanger defaults, sidecars)
        ├─ schema validation                 (OpenAPI: types, required fields)
        └─ VALIDATING controllers + webhooks (ACCEPT/REJECT only: PodSecurity, ResourceQuota)
        ▼
   🗄️ PERSIST to etcd   ─►  controllers + scheduler take over
   💡 mutating ALWAYS runs before validating — defaults are applied, THEN the final object is judged.
PluginTypeWhat it does
NamespaceLifecyclevalidatingblocks creating objects in a terminating/absent namespace
LimitRangermutatinginjects default CPU/memory requests/limits from a LimitRange
ResourceQuotavalidatingrejects a create that would exceed a namespace's quota
PodSecurityvalidatingenforces Pod Security Standards (privileged/baseline/restricted) — Ch 26
NodeRestrictionvalidatinglimits what a kubelet can modify (only its own node/pods) — key security default
DefaultStorageClassmutatingstamps the default StorageClass onto a PVC that omits one
Mutating/ValidatingAdmissionWebhookbothcall your external webhooks (Kyverno, OPA, Istio injection) — Ch 38
control plane · enable a plugin
# edit the apiserver manifest's command: flags (back up first!)
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity,ResourceQuota
# (kubelet restarts the apiserver on save)
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-control-plane -o yaml \
  | grep enable-admission-plugins        # verify it took
📖 Why "mutating before validating" matters

If validation ran first, a default injected by a mutating controller (say a LimitRanger memory request) could be rejected before it was ever added — or, worse, a sidecar webhook's container would dodge policy checks. Running all mutations first means the final object is the one that's validated. --disable-admission-plugins turns built-ins off; several (like NamespaceLifecycle, NodeRestriction) are on by default.

10.6 API Groups & Versioning

Every Kubernetes object lives in an API group at a version. There are two shapes: the original core group served at /api/v1 (Pods, Services, ConfigMaps…), and named groups served at /apis/<group>/<version> (apps, batch, networking…). The apiVersion field in every manifest is exactly this group/version string.

the API surface — core vs named groups
   kube-apiserver
   ├─ /api/v1                       ← the CORE group (no group name): apiVersion: v1
   │     Pod · Service · ConfigMap · Secret · Namespace · Node · PersistentVolumeClaim
   │
   └─ /apis/<group>/<version>        ← NAMED groups: apiVersion: <group>/<version>
         apps/v1 .................. Deployment · ReplicaSet · DaemonSet · StatefulSet
         batch/v1 ................. Job · CronJob
         networking.k8s.io/v1 ..... Ingress · NetworkPolicy
         rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1  Role · RoleBinding · ClusterRole…
         storage.k8s.io/v1 ........ StorageClass · CSIDriver
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   version maturity:  v1alpha1 (may vanish) → v1beta1 (usually safe) → v1 (stable, GA)
discover the API
kubectl api-resources                 # every kind → short name, APIVERSION, namespaced?, KIND
# NAME          SHORTNAMES   APIVERSION   NAMESPACED   KIND
# pods          po           v1           true         Pod
# deployments   deploy       apps/v1      true         Deployment
# nodes         no           v1           false        Node

kubectl api-resources --api-group=apps   # just one group's kinds
# deployments · replicasets · daemonsets · statefulsets   (all apps/v1)

kubectl api-versions                  # every served group/version
# apps/v1 · batch/v1 · networking.k8s.io/v1 · rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 · v1 (core)

kubectl api-resources | grep -i ingress
# ingresses   ing   networking.k8s.io/v1   true   Ingress
kubectl explain ingress --api-version=networking.k8s.io/v1   # pin the schema (shows KIND + VERSION)
📖 Why groups exist

Splitting the API into versioned groups lets Kubernetes evolve features independently and deprecate cleanly — batch can ship a new CronJob version without touching apps. It's also the extension model: a CRD (Ch 38) adds your own named group (easypj.example.com/v1) that behaves exactly like a built-in. Full deprecation/conversion mechanics were covered in Ch 7's "Under the Hood."

Under the Hood — how a config change reaches a running control-plane component

Editing a file and having the apiserver restart "by magic" is really the kubelet's static-pod reconcile loop. The kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and treats each YAML there as a pod it must keep running — so a file change is a redeploy.

   /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml   (you save an edit)
        │
        ▼   the kubelet watches this directory (inotify + periodic resync)
   🤖 kubelet sees the manifest's spec changed
        │  → terminates the OLD apiserver static pod
        │  → creates a NEW one from the updated manifest (via the CRI)
        ▼
   📡 new kube-apiserver Running   (its pod is "mirror"-reflected into kube-system, read-only)
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   the kubelet (a systemd service) configures itself differently: edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml,
   then systemctl daemon-reload (if the unit changed) + restart kubelet — there's no manifest to watch.
🔑 Two config models, one chapter: control-plane components are static pods → configure by editing a file the kubelet watches (auto-restart). The kubelet itself is a systemd service → configure via config.yaml + systemctl. Mixing them up ("why didn't my kubelet change apply?") is a common stumble — the kubelet has no one watching it.
Beyond the basicsWhat to know
API Priority & Fairness (APF)the apiserver fair-queues concurrent requests by FlowSchema/PriorityLevelConfiguration so a noisy client can't starve others; a 429 with a Retry-After is APF shedding load.
KMS v2 encryption providers--encryption-provider-config can wrap etcd Secrets with an external KMS (envelope encryption) instead of a local key — Ch 11 §11.5.
audit logging--audit-policy-file + --audit-log-path record who did what; a webhook backend ships audit events to an external SIEM.
aggregation layerthe front-proxy certs let extension apiservers (e.g. metrics-server, custom APIs) plug into the main API surface under /apis.
--feature-gates & OIDCtoggle alpha/beta features per component; --oidc-* flags wire the apiserver to an identity provider for human SSO.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • kubeconfig = clusters (where) + users (who) + contexts (combo); files merge via $KUBECONFIG (first-wins), flatten with --flatten.
  • Configure the control plane by editing its static-pod manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — the kubelet auto-restarts the component on save. Back up first.
  • Configure the kubelet via /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml + systemd (daemon-reload → restart).
  • Admission runs after authZ: mutating → schema → validating → persist; enable via --enable-admission-plugins.
  • API groups: core /api/v1 vs named /apis/<group>/<ver>; discover with api-resources/api-versions.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Traps
  • Manifest typo kills the apiserver. kubectl dies too — recover by fixing the file on the node (crictl logs shows why).
  • No backup. Always cp … /tmp before editing a control-plane manifest.
  • Forgot daemon-reload. A kubelet unit change won't apply until you reload systemd, then restart.
  • Stray $KUBECONFIG. Silently overrides ~/.kube/config — "where's my cluster?"
  • Wrong admission order assumption. Mutating always precedes validating.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Back up, always: sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/ before any edit.
  • Watch it return: crictl ps | grep apiserver (the container ID changes) or get pods -n kube-system -w.
  • kubectl config view --minify to confirm cluster/user/namespace fast.
  • kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-<node> -o yaml | grep <flag> to verify a flag took.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 10)

config & control-plane toolkit
kubectl config view --minify ; kubectl config get-contexts ; kubectl config use-context <c>
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns>
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/   # back up before editing
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml       # edit flags → kubelet restarts it
sudo crictl ps | grep apiserver ; sudo crictl logs <id>       # when kubectl is down
sudo vim /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml ; sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl api-resources ; kubectl api-versions ; journalctl -u kubelet -f
🧪 Drill — enable an admission plugin, verify, then revert

No peeking — practise the back-up-edit-recover loop safely:

  1. Back up kube-apiserver.yaml to /tmp.
  2. Add NamespaceAutoProvision (or NodeRestriction) to --enable-admission-plugins and save.
  3. Wait for the apiserver to restart, then verify the flag is live.
  4. Revert by restoring the backup; confirm kubectl still works.
Show solution
terminal (on the control-plane node)
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# edit:  - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity
watch -n2 'sudo crictl ps | grep apiserver'      # wait for a new container ID
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$(hostname) -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins
# revert
sudo cp /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
kubectl get nodes        # kubectl works again ✅

Cluster-config recall — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Name the 3 kubeconfig sections and what each holds.
Show Answer
Answer
SectionHolds
clustersserver URL + CA cert (WHERE)
usersclient cert/key, token, or exec plugin (WHO)
contextscluster + user + namespace (the COMBO)
Explanation

current-context selects the active context; kubectl config view --minify shows only it.

Q2
Merge two kubeconfig files into one session.
Show Answer
Answer
merge
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/work/dev.yaml
kubectl config get-contexts                    # union of both
kubectl config view --flatten > ~/.kube/merged  # bake into one file
Explanation

Colon-separated (semicolon on Windows); on a name clash the first file wins. --flatten embeds all certs into one self-contained file.

Q3
Enable the NodeRestriction admission plugin — which file, which flag?
Show Answer
Answer

Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml and add it to --enable-admission-plugins: - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity. Save; the kubelet restarts the apiserver.

Explanation

Back up first. Verify with kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-<node> -o yaml | grep enable-admission.

Q4
Find the current --service-cluster-ip-range of the apiserver.
Show Answer
Answer
find a flag
grep service-cluster-ip-range /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# - --service-cluster-ip-range=10.96.0.0/12
Explanation

All apiserver flags live in its static-pod manifest's command: list — grep the file, or read the live pod's spec.

Q5
The apiserver won't start after an edit — how do you recover?
Show Answer
Answer

kubectl is down, so work on the node: sudo crictl ps -a | grep apiserver then sudo crictl logs <id> to see the error. Fix the YAML (or restore the /tmp backup); the kubelet relaunches it within ~20s.

Explanation

The component is a static pod the kubelet keeps retrying — you never "start" it manually; you just make the manifest valid.

Q6
Core API group vs a named group — give an example apiVersion of each.
Show Answer
Answer

Core: apiVersion: v1 (Pod, Service, ConfigMap) — served at /api/v1. Named: apiVersion: apps/v1 (Deployment) — served at /apis/apps/v1.

Explanation

The core group has no group name (just v1); every other group is <group>/<version>.

Q7
Change the kubelet's clusterDNS and apply it.
Show Answer
Answer
node
sudo vim /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml      # edit clusterDNS: [10.96.0.10]
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 20 --no-pager
Explanation

It's a config-file change (not a unit change), so a plain restart suffices — no daemon-reload needed.

Q8
Set a context's default namespace to easypj.
Show Answer
Answer
set namespace
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj
Explanation

--current edits the active context so every command defaults to easypj — no more -n.

Q9
Where do mutating vs validating webhooks run in the request flow?
Show Answer
Answer

Both run in the admission phase, after authN+authZ and before etcd. Order: mutating (can change the object) → schema validation → validating (accept/reject only).

Explanation

Mutating-first guarantees the final, defaulted object is the one judged by validation.

Q10
Discover which API version serves Ingress.
Show Answer
Answer
discover
kubectl api-resources | grep -i ingress
# ingresses   ing   networking.k8s.io/v1   true   Ingress
Explanation

Always look it up rather than guess — versions drift between releases. api-resources is the source of truth for your cluster.

⚙️ Chapter 10 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style "configure it / fix it" tasks with the real commands.

Q11
You edited kube-apiserver.yaml; now kubectl says "connection refused." Recover.
Show Answer
Answer
on the node
sudo crictl ps -a | grep apiserver
sudo crictl logs <id>        # shows the bad flag / parse error
sudo cp /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/   # restore backup
# …or fix the offending line; kubelet relaunches within ~20s
Explanation

No kubectl needed — the fix is on the filesystem. This is why backing up to /tmp first turns a crisis into a one-liner.

Q12
Find which etcd endpoints the apiserver talks to.
Show Answer
Answer
grep the manifest
grep etcd-servers /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# - --etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379
Explanation

Useful before an etcd backup (Ch 11) — you also need the cert flags (--etcd-cafile, --etcd-certfile, --etcd-keyfile) from the same file.

Q13
Your current context defaults to default but you want easypj-dev. Fix it for this context only.
Show Answer
Answer
set ns
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev
kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace   # verify
Explanation

--current scopes the change to the active context, leaving your other contexts untouched.

Q14
Enable the PodSecurity admission controller and confirm it's active.
Show Answer
Answer
enable + verify
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,PodSecurity
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$(hostname) -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins
Explanation

PodSecurity enforces Pod Security Standards via namespace labels (Ch 26). It's on by default in recent versions but the exam may ask you to confirm/add it.

Q15
You changed the kubelet's systemd drop-in but restart didn't apply it. What did you forget?
Show Answer
Answer
fix
sudo systemctl daemon-reload   # reload unit definitions FIRST
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
Explanation

systemd caches unit files; without daemon-reload it restarts using the old definition. (A change to config.yaml alone needs only a restart.)

Q16
Widen the NodePort range to start at 30000 (it already does) — show where you'd change it.
Show Answer
Answer

Add/edit - --service-node-port-range=30000-32767 in kube-apiserver.yaml (back up first), save, and let the apiserver restart.

Explanation

The default is 30000-32767; you'd only change it to widen/shift the externally-exposed port window — same back-up-edit-verify loop as any apiserver flag.

Q17
Decode the embedded CA cert from your kubeconfig to inspect it.
Show Answer
Answer
inspect a cert
kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}' \
  | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates
Explanation

--raw keeps the base64 data (normally redacted); decode it and pipe to openssl x509 to read subject/validity — handy for cert-expiry troubleshooting.

Q18
A teammate sent staging.yaml. Use their staging context without clobbering your config.
Show Answer
Answer
temporary merge
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/Downloads/staging.yaml
kubectl config get-contexts            # staging now appears
kubectl config use-context staging
Explanation

The env-var merge is non-destructive — unset $KUBECONFIG and your original config is untouched. --flatten only if you want to persist the merge.

Q19
Pods in easypj-prod are rejected: violates PodSecurity "restricted". Where's the policy set?
Show Answer
Answer
check namespace labels
kubectl get ns easypj-prod --show-labels
# pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted   ← the gate
Explanation

PodSecurity is configured per-namespace via pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce labels — relax it (baseline) or fix the pod's securityContext (Ch 26).

Q20
List which admission plugins the running apiserver currently has enabled.
Show Answer
Answer
verify
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$(hostname) \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].command}' | tr ',' '\n' | grep admission
Explanation

Reading the live pod's command shows exactly what's running (some plugins are on by default even without the flag). Grepping the manifest file works too.

📌 Chapter 10 Visual Summary — request pipeline + the two config models
   THE REQUEST PIPELINE (every write)
   kubectl ─▶ 🔐 authN ─▶ 🛂 authZ(RBAC) ─▶ 🧪 admission(mutating ▶ schema ▶ validating) ─▶ 🗄️ etcd ─▶ controllers/scheduler
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   CONFIGURING THE CLUSTER — two models
   control-plane components (apiserver/scheduler/etcd)   →  edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/*.yaml  →  kubelet auto-restarts (BACK UP!)
   the kubelet itself (a systemd service)                →  edit /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml      →  daemon-reload + restart
   kubeconfig:  clusters(WHERE) + users(WHO) + contexts(COMBO);  merge via $KUBECONFIG (first-wins)
   API surface:  core /api/v1  vs  named /apis/<group>/<ver>   (api-resources · api-versions)            ☸️

In words: every write runs the gauntlet — authenticate, authorize, then admission (mutating defaults first, then validation), then it's stored. You shape the cluster by configuring two different kinds of thing: control-plane components, which are static pods you reconfigure by editing files the kubelet watches; and the kubelet itself, a systemd service you configure with config.yaml + systemctl.

The takeaway: the single habit that protects you is back up before you edit a control-plane manifest — then recovery is just restoring a file. Know the admission order (mutating → validating), where each config lives, and how to read the API surface, and Chapter 10's tasks are routine.

Chapter 11 · etcd — Backup & Restore

etcd is the cluster's entire memory — every object you've ever created lives there. Lose it without a backup and the cluster is gone. That makes etcd snapshot & restore the single highest-value skill an administrator has, and an almost-guaranteed CKA task. This chapter makes the backup/restore dance automatic.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🎯 Almost-Guaranteed Task 🗄️ etcd

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ What etcd is, what it stores (/registry/*), and why losing it loses the cluster
  • ✅ etcd's Raft consensus — leader/follower, quorum math, why members are odd
  • ✅ Take a verified snapshot with etcdctl snapshot save + the 3 TLS flags
  • ✅ Restore to a new data-dir and repoint the etcd static pod (both places!)
  • ✅ Secure etcd: TLS (default) + encryption at rest for Secrets
  • ✅ Automate nightly backups and check cluster health
🎓 CKA Relevance
Cluster Architecture 25% etcd backup/restore ALMOST GUARANTEED
🎯 The task you will almost certainly get

"Back up etcd to /opt/backup.db" and "restore etcd from this snapshot" are among the most common CKA tasks — and they're free marks once the muscle memory is there.

  • Memorise the 4 inputs: --endpoints + --cacert + --cert + --key. The cert paths live in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml.
  • Restore to a NEW data-dir — never the live one — and update etcd.yaml in two places (the --data-dir flag AND the hostPath volume).
  • ETCDCTL_API=3 is required for the snapshot commands.
🧭 Chapter 11 Roadmap — the cluster's memory, backed up & restorable
   11.1 WHAT is etcd ──▶ 11.2 Raft & quorum ──▶ 11.3 BACKUP (snapshot save) ──▶ 11.4 RESTORE ──▶ 11.5 SECURE
   KV store · /registry   leader/follower         the 3 TLS flags + verify        new data-dir       TLS + encryption
   Secrets unencrypted    quorum = N/2+1                                          repoint etcd.yaml   at rest
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   the through-line: snapshot save ▶ 💥 disaster ▶ snapshot restore ▶ repoint static pod ▶ cluster back.
SectionQuestion it answersTakeaway
11.1 What is etcd?What holds all cluster state?a distributed KV store at /registry/*; Secrets unencrypted by default.
11.2 Architecture & RaftHow does it stay consistent & HA?Raft leader/follower; quorum = N/2+1; odd members (3,5,7).
11.3 BackupHow do I snapshot it?etcdctl snapshot save + endpoint + 3 TLS flags; verify with status.
11.4 RestoreHow do I bring it back?restore to a NEW data-dir; repoint etcd.yaml (flag + hostPath).
