11.1 What is etcd?

etcd is a distributed, strongly-consistent key-value store — and it is the only place Kubernetes keeps state. Every node, pod, Deployment, Secret, ConfigMap, and RBAC rule is a key under /registry/. The apiserver is the sole component that talks to it; everything else goes through the apiserver. That's the whole reason an etcd snapshot is a cluster backup.

🗝️
Key-Value Store

data is keys → values under /registry/… — simple, fast, and easy to snapshot whole.

🌐
Distributed

runs as a cluster of members (Raft) so it survives a node loss — no single point of failure.

🎯
Strongly Consistent

every member agrees on every committed write — reads never return stale, contradictory state.

👁️
Watch API

clients watch key ranges and are pushed changes — the engine behind every K8s controller.

🧠 In plain English

etcd is the cluster's memory. The control plane is the brain that thinks, but every thought — every object's desired and current state — is written in etcd. Wipe etcd with no backup and the cluster has total amnesia: the nodes and containers may still be running, but Kubernetes no longer knows they exist. That's why this chapter is the most important in Part 3.

what's inside etcd — the /registry keyspace
   etcd  (key → value, value = the object as protobuf/JSON)
   /registry/
     ├─ namespaces/easypj-dev
     ├─ pods/easypj-dev/easypj-web-7d8f9-abcde
     ├─ deployments/easypj-dev/easypj-web
     ├─ replicasets/easypj-dev/easypj-web-7d8f9
     ├─ services/easypj-dev/easypj-web
     ├─ configmaps/easypj-dev/easypj-config
     ├─ secrets/easypj-dev/easypj-secret        ⚠️ stored UNENCRYPTED by default (§11.5)
     ├─ clusterroles/… · rolebindings/…
     └─ … every object in the cluster
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   only the kube-apiserver reads/writes etcd → one snapshot of etcd = the entire cluster's state
🚨 Secrets sit unencrypted in etcd by default

A Secret's value is only base64-encoded in etcd — anyone who can read the etcd data files (or a snapshot) can read your Secrets in plaintext. That's why §11.5 (encryption at rest) and tight file permissions on snapshots matter, and why a leaked etcd-backup.db is a full credential breach.

📖 What etcd does NOT back up

An etcd snapshot captures Kubernetes objects — not the data inside your PersistentVolumes. A restored cluster knows the PVC exists, but the actual disk contents are the storage backend's responsibility (Ch 22). Back up app data separately.

11.2 etcd Architecture & Raft

For high availability, etcd runs as a cluster of members that stay consistent using the Raft consensus algorithm. One member is elected leader and handles all writes; the rest are followers. A write is only committed once a majority (quorum) of members has acknowledged it — which is why etcd never loses a committed write but also why it needs an odd number of members.

3-member etcd — Raft keeps the memory consistent
   ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────┐
   │ etcd-0   │◄────►│ etcd-1   │◄────►│ etcd-2   │     3 members
   │ LEADER   │      │ follower │      │ follower │     quorum = N/2+1 = 2
   │ :2379 cli│      │          │      │          │     tolerates 1 failure
   │ :2380 peer│     │          │      │          │
   └──────────┘      └──────────┘      └──────────┘
   WRITE: client ─► LEADER ─► replicate to followers ─► commit once a MAJORITY ack ─► ✅ ack client
   READ:  served from any member (linearizable reads go via the leader)
MembersQuorum (N/2+1)Failures toleratedVerdict
110dev only — no HA
321✅ the common HA choice
532✅ large/critical clusters
2 or 42 / 30 / 1❌ even = no extra tolerance, just more risk
⚠️ Always odd, and beware quorum loss

Even counts are pointless: a 4-member cluster tolerates the same 1 failure as a 3-member one but has more to go wrong. If a cluster loses quorum (e.g. 2 of 3 members down), etcd goes read-only / unavailable and the whole control plane stalls — recovery means restoring members or a snapshot. This is why production etcd is 3 or 5 members across failure domains.

📖 Stacked vs external etcd

kubeadm's default is stacked: etcd runs as a static pod on each control-plane node, alongside the apiserver. The alternative is external etcd on dedicated machines (better isolation, independent scaling). The backup/restore commands are identical; the operational difference is that with external etcd you stop the apiservers manually during a restore (Ch 33).

11.3 etcd Backup — the Snapshot

A backup is a single etcdctl snapshot save call. The catch is that etcd is TLS-protected, so etcdctl must authenticate with three certs plus the endpoint — four inputs you'll memorise. Get the cert paths from the etcd static-pod manifest, run the snapshot, then always verify it.

control plane · snapshot save
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# Snapshot saved at /opt/etcd-backup.db

🔑 The 4 inputs every snapshot save needs

🎯 --endpoints
https://127.0.0.1:2379 — etcd's client port on the local control-plane node
🔐 --cacert
/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt — verifies etcd's server cert
📄 --cert
/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt — etcdctl's client cert
🗝️ --key
/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key — its private key
💡 Don't remember the cert paths? Read them off etcd.yaml

The exact flags etcd uses are in its manifest — copy them straight into your command:

find the cert paths
grep -E 'cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca|listen-client' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
# --cert-file, --key-file, --trusted-ca-file → those are your --cert/--key/--cacert

✅ Always verify the snapshot before you trust it

verify
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /opt/etcd-backup.db --write-table
# +----------+----------+------------+------------+
# |   HASH   | REVISION | TOTAL KEYS | TOTAL SIZE |
# +----------+----------+------------+------------+
# | fe01c2ab |    95620 |       1480 |     4.6 MB |
# +----------+----------+------------+------------+
⚡ Speed: alias the TLS flags

Save typing all session: alias e='sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key' → then just e snapshot save /opt/backup.db and e endpoint health.

11.4 etcd Restore

Restore reads a snapshot into a fresh data directory, then you repoint the etcd static pod at it. Two rules save you: restore to a new dir (never the live /var/lib/etcd), and update etcd.yaml in two places — the --data-dir flag and the hostPath volume that mounts it.

control plane · restore
# 1. Restore the snapshot into a NEW data directory
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored

# 2. Repoint the etcd static pod — edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml:
#    (a) the flag:        - --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored
#    (b) the hostPath volume that mounts the data-dir:
#        volumes: - name: etcd-data
#            hostPath: { path: /var/lib/etcd-restored , type: DirectoryOrCreate }
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml

# 3. The kubelet restarts etcd from the restored data; the apiserver reconnects.
kubectl get nodes        # cluster is back at the snapshot's point-in-time ✅
BACKUP ▶ 💥 DISASTER ▶ RESTORE — the #1 admin skill
   etcdctl snapshot save ──► 💾 /opt/etcd-backup.db        (needs --endpoints --cacert --cert --key)
        │  verify: snapshot status --write-table
        │
   ─ ─ ─│─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ 💥 DISASTER (someone deleted prod / etcd corrupted) ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
        ▼
   etcdctl snapshot restore ──► 📁 /var/lib/etcd-RESTORED   (a NEW dir — never the live one!)
        ▼
   edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
        change  --data-dir   AND   the hostPath volume    ──► BOTH, or etcd starts on old/empty data
        ▼
   🤖 kubelet auto-restarts etcd ──► ✅ cluster restored to the snapshot's moment
🚨 The three restore mistakes that cost marks
  • Restoring into the live data-dir while etcd is running → corruption. Always a new dir.
  • Updating only the flag, not the hostPath (or vice-versa) → etcd mounts the wrong directory and your restore "didn't work."
  • Forgetting ETCDCTL_API=3 → the v2 API doesn't understand snapshots.
📖 What about HA (multiple etcd members)?

On a multi-member cluster you restore the snapshot on one node, then either re-add the others as fresh members or restore the same snapshot to each with matching --initial-cluster settings. For the CKA's single stacked control plane, the steps above are all you need.

📋 The one-glance etcd backup & restore cheat sheet

Everything you need for the exam task, in one place — copy the pattern, swap the paths:

CKA etcd — complete backup & restore cheat sheet
   ┌─ BACKUP ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/backup.db \                       │
   │   --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \                                     │
   │   --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \                               │
   │   --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \                             │
   │   --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key                                │
   │ VERIFY:  etcdctl snapshot status /opt/backup.db -w table                   │
   ├─ RESTORE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/backup.db \                    │
   │   --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored        ← a NEW dir                     │
   │ THEN edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml — BOTH:                      │
   │   1) - --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored                                   │
   │   2) volumes → hostPath.path: /var/lib/etcd-restored                       │
   │ WAIT: kubelet auto-restarts etcd · VERIFY: kubectl get pods -n kube-system │
   ├─ FORGOT THE CERT PATHS? ─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ grep -E 'cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🏥 Checking etcd health & status

Before (and after) a backup/restore, confirm etcd is healthy — these show the leader, DB size, members, and write latency:

etcd health & status (alias the TLS flags as $CERTS)
# is it alive?
etcdctl endpoint health $CERTS
# https://127.0.0.1:2379 is healthy: successfully committed proposal: took = 2.3ms

# leader · version · DB size (the <2 GB quota lives here)
etcdctl endpoint status $CERTS --write-out=table
# +------------------------+--------+---------+---------+-----------+
# |        ENDPOINT        |   ID   | VERSION | DB SIZE | IS LEADER |
# | https://127.0.0.1:2379 | abc123 | 3.5.x   | 4.2 MB  |   true    |
# +------------------------+--------+---------+---------+-----------+

# the members & their roles (who's the leader, are all started?)
etcdctl member list $CERTS --write-out=table

# write-latency benchmark (etcd is fsync-bound — slow disks = a sick cluster)
etcdctl check perf $CERTS

11.5 etcd Security & Encryption at Rest

etcd is protected on the wire by TLS already (that's why backups need certs). But the data at rest — including Secrets — is only base64-encoded on disk. Encryption at rest closes that gap: you give the apiserver an EncryptionConfiguration and it encrypts Secret values before writing them to etcd.

two layers of etcd security
   🔒 IN TRANSIT (default)        client ──TLS (certs)──▶ etcd        ✅ already on in kubeadm
   🔐 AT REST (you enable)        apiserver ──encrypt Secret──▶ etcd  ❌ OFF by default → Secrets readable on disk
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   threat: anyone with the etcd data files or a snapshot can read every Secret in plaintext.
/etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources:
  - secrets                       # encrypt Secret objects…
  providers:
  - aescbc:                       # …with AES-CBC (a 32-byte key, base64)
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: <base64-32-byte-key>
  - identity: {}                  # fallback so EXISTING (unencrypted) reads still work
control plane · enable + re-encrypt
# 1. point the apiserver at the config (back up the manifest first!)
# in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml add:
#   - --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml
#   + a hostPath volume mounting /etc/kubernetes/enc into the pod

# 2. re-write every existing Secret so it gets encrypted with the new key
kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
⚠️ identity first vs second matters

The provider list is tried in order for writes (first provider encrypts), and all providers are tried for reads. Putting aescbc first means new writes are encrypted; keeping identity in the list lets the apiserver still read the old plaintext Secrets until you re-encrypt them. Step 2's get … | replace forces a re-write so everything ends up encrypted. Verify by reading the raw key directly from etcd — an encrypted value starts with k8s:enc:aescbc:…, not readable text.

📖 Beyond aescbc — KMS v2

aescbc keeps the key in the config file on the node (better than nothing). Production uses a KMS provider (kms: v2): the apiserver asks an external key-management service (cloud KMS, Vault) to wrap a per-object data key — so the master key never touches the node. Same --encryption-provider-config flag, a different provider block.

Under the Hood — how etcd actually stores & commits your data

etcd's durability and consistency come from three pieces working together: a WAL (write-ahead log) for crash safety, a BoltDB B+tree for the keyspace, and MVCC revisions so every change is versioned. Understanding them explains snapshots, "database space exceeded" alarms, and why defrag exists.

   A WRITE (e.g. kubectl scale → apiserver → etcd)
     ① leader appends the change to its WAL (write-ahead log) on disk      ← crash-safe
     ② leader replicates the log entry to followers (Raft)
     ③ once a MAJORITY have persisted it → the entry is COMMITTED
     ④ each member applies it to its BoltDB B+tree (the keyspace) under a NEW revision
     ⑤ leader acks the client
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   MVCC: every write bumps a global revision; old revisions are kept (history) until COMPACTION
   COMPACTION drops old revisions (frees logical space) · DEFRAG returns freed space to the disk
   a SNAPSHOT = a consistent copy of the BoltDB file at one revision (what `snapshot save` writes)
🔑 Why "database space exceeded" happens: etcd has a quota (--quota-backend-bytes, default ~2 GB). MVCC history + a busy cluster fill it; etcd then raises a NOSPACE alarm and goes read-only — the control plane freezes. Recovery: compact to an old revision, defrag to reclaim disk, then etcdctl alarm disarm. This is the deep version of "etcd is full and my cluster won't take writes."
Beyond the basicsWhat to know
compaction & defragetcdctl compact <rev> drops old MVCC revisions; etcdctl defrag returns the freed pages to the filesystem. --auto-compaction-mode=periodic --auto-compaction-retention=8h automates it.
NOSPACE alarm recoveryetcdctl alarm list → compact + defrag → etcdctl alarm disarm to take writes again.
member & learner managementetcdctl member add/remove/list; a learner joins read-only and catches up before voting — safer HA growth.
quorum-loss recoverylost majority? restore a snapshot with --force-new-cluster on one survivor, then re-add members.
performance tuning--heartbeat-interval/--election-timeout for high-latency networks; etcd wants fast disks (it's fsync-bound).

④ The deepest connection — how an etcd write becomes a cluster-wide event. MVCC revisions aren't just history; they're the engine behind everything reactive in Kubernetes. This is where Ch 11 (etcd), Ch 6 (get -w) and Ch 1 (controllers/informers) join up:

   kubectl scale deploy easypj-web --replicas=5
        ▼
   apiserver writes the new spec to etcd  →  etcd bumps the global REVISION (say 95620 → 95621)
        ▼
   etcd WATCH: every client watching that key range is pushed the change AT that revision
        ▼
   the apiserver is etcd's watcher → it fans the event out to ITS watchers:
        ReplicaSet controller (informer) sees replicas 3→5  →  creates 2 pods
        scheduler sees the new pods (nodeName="")           →  binds them
        kubelet on each node sees its bound pod             →  starts containers
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   resourceVersion (Ch 6) IS the etcd revision. A watch resumes from one; a stale watcher gets
   410 Gone and re-lists. The whole control loop is event-driven on top of etcd's MVCC watch stream.
🔑 Why this is the "to the core" insight: nothing in Kubernetes polls. One etcd write at a new revision ripples — via the apiserver's watch — to every controller, the scheduler, and the kubelets, each reacting and writing their change back as a further revision. etcd isn't a passive database the cluster reads; it's the heartbeat whose every tick drives the next reconciliation. That's why losing it (this chapter) loses not just data but the cluster's ability to act.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • etcd holds ALL cluster state at /registry/* — one snapshot = the whole cluster. Secrets are unencrypted by default.
  • Backup: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save + --endpoints + the 3 TLS flags; verify with snapshot status --write-table.
  • Restore into a new data-dir, then repoint etcd.yaml in two places (--data-dir flag AND the hostPath volume).
  • Quorum = N/2+1; odd members (3 → tolerate 1, 5 → tolerate 2).
  • Encryption at rest = EncryptionConfiguration + --encryption-provider-config; re-encrypt with get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Traps
  • Missing TLS flags. snapshot save without --cacert/--cert/--key = "context deadline exceeded."
  • Restoring into the live data-dir. Always a NEW dir, or you corrupt running etcd.
  • Updating only one of the two places in etcd.yaml (flag vs hostPath) → restore appears to fail.
  • Forgetting ETCDCTL_API=3 → snapshot commands don't exist in v2.
  • Assuming etcd backs up PV data. It backs up objects, not volume contents.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Alias the TLS flags (see §11.3) so every etcdctl call is two words.
  • Cert paths are always in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml — grep it instead of guessing.
  • Always take a fresh snapshot before a restore — your current state is itself worth saving.
  • etcdctl endpoint health / endpoint status --write-table for a one-line health check.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 11)

the etcdctl toolkit (ETCDCTL_API=3)
# with the TLS flags (alias them):  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=… --cert=… --key=…
etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db        # BACK UP
etcdctl snapshot status /opt/etcd-backup.db --write-table   # verify
etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored   # RESTORE
etcdctl member list -w table                     # cluster members
etcdctl endpoint health ; etcdctl endpoint status -w table   # health
etcdctl alarm list ; etcdctl defrag ; etcdctl alarm disarm   # NOSPACE recovery
🧪 Drill — back up, "lose" a Deployment, restore it

The exact CKA disaster-recovery loop. No peeking:

  1. Snapshot etcd to /opt/etcd-backup.db and verify it.
  2. Delete the easypj-web Deployment (the "disaster").
  3. Restore the snapshot into a new data-dir and repoint etcd.yaml.
  4. Confirm the Deployment is back.
Show solution
terminal (control-plane node)
alias e='sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key'
e snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db ; e snapshot status /opt/etcd-backup.db --write-table

kubectl delete deploy easypj-web -n easypj-dev          # 💥 disaster

sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml            # --data-dir + hostPath → /var/lib/etcd-restored
# wait for etcd + apiserver to restart…
kubectl get deploy easypj-web -n easypj-dev             # it's back ✅

🧠 Chapter 11 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

etcd backup/restore recall — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Write the full etcdctl snapshot save command with TLS flags.
Show Answer
Answer
snapshot save
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-backup.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
Explanation

Four inputs: endpoint + the three certs. Without them etcdctl can't authenticate to the TLS-protected etcd and times out.

Q2
Restore a snapshot and repoint the static pod — every step.
Show Answer
Answer
restore
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/etcd-backup.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
# 1) - --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored
# 2) hostPath volume etcd-data → path: /var/lib/etcd-restored
# kubelet auto-restarts etcd; verify:
kubectl get nodes
Explanation

New data-dir, then update BOTH the flag and the hostPath — the most-failed half of this task is forgetting the volume.

Q3
Where do you find the 3 cert paths etcdctl needs?
Show Answer
Answer
find cert paths
grep -E 'cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
# --cert-file → --cert · --key-file → --key · --trusted-ca-file → --cacert
Explanation

They're under /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ by default, but reading them off the manifest is foolproof regardless of the cluster's layout.

Q4
Verify a snapshot file before trusting it.
Show Answer
Answer
verify
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /opt/etcd-backup.db --write-table
# shows HASH · REVISION · TOTAL KEYS · TOTAL SIZE
Explanation

A non-zero key count and sane size confirm the file is a real, complete snapshot — not an empty/aborted one.

Q5
Quorum math: how many failures does a 5-member cluster tolerate?
Show Answer
Answer

2. Quorum = N/2+1 = 5/2+1 = 3, so the cluster keeps working as long as 3 of 5 are up — i.e. it tolerates 2 failures.

Explanation

3 members tolerate 1; 5 tolerate 2; 7 tolerate 3. Even counts add risk without adding tolerance — always odd.

Q6
A restore failed with "data-dir not empty" — why, and the fix?
Show Answer
Answer

You restored into an existing/used directory. Restore into a fresh path (or remove the target first): --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored where that dir doesn't already exist.

Explanation

snapshot restore insists on creating a clean data-dir so it can't silently merge with live data — which is exactly the corruption it's protecting you from.

Q7
Enable encryption at rest for Secrets (outline).
Show Answer
Answer

Write an EncryptionConfiguration (provider aescbc with a 32-byte key, then identity), add --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc/enc.yaml (+ a hostPath volume) to the apiserver manifest, then re-write existing Secrets:

re-encrypt
kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
Explanation

New writes encrypt immediately; the replace forces existing Secrets to be re-written (and thus encrypted). Verify by reading the raw etcd key — it should start k8s:enc:aescbc:.

Q8
External vs stacked etcd — one operational difference.
Show Answer
Answer

Stacked: etcd is a static pod on each control-plane node (kubeadm default) — the kubelet manages it. External: etcd runs on dedicated machines; during a restore you stop the apiservers manually (no kubelet auto-restart of etcd).

Explanation

External isolates etcd failures from the control plane and scales independently, at the cost of more machines to run.

Q9
Check etcd cluster health from the command line.
Show Answer
Answer
health
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=… --cert=… --key=…
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list -w table
Explanation

endpoint health confirms each member responds; member list shows roles and whether the cluster has a leader.

Q10
Automate a nightly etcd backup.
Show Answer
Answer

A root cron entry on the control-plane node is simplest and most reliable (it doesn't depend on the cluster being healthy):

/etc/cron.d/etcd-backup
0 2 * * * root ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/etcd-$(date +\%F).db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
Explanation

Host cron beats a Kubernetes CronJob here: if the cluster is sick, a CronJob may not run — but the backup is exactly what you need then. Ship the files off-node and prune old ones.

⚙️ Chapter 11 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style backup/restore/recovery tasks with the real commands.

Q11
Task: back up etcd to /opt/snapshot.db on the control-plane node.
Show Answer
Answer
backup
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/snapshot.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /opt/snapshot.db --write-table   # verify!
Explanation

Always finish with snapshot status — an unverified backup is worse than none because it gives false confidence.

Q12
Task: restore the cluster from /opt/snapshot.db.
Show Answer
Answer
restore
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/snapshot.db --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored
sudo sed -i 's#/var/lib/etcd#/var/lib/etcd-restored#g' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
# ↑ updates BOTH the --data-dir flag and the hostPath in one shot
kubectl get nodes        # after etcd+apiserver restart
Explanation

The sed trick swaps every /var/lib/etcd reference at once — covering the flag and the hostPath. Confirm there were exactly the two occurrences first.

Q13
snapshot save fails with context deadline exceeded. Cause & fix.
Show Answer
Answer

etcdctl can't authenticate/reach etcd — wrong/missing TLS flags or endpoint. Re-read the exact paths from the manifest and retry:

diagnose
grep -E 'listen-client-urls|cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca-file' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
Explanation

The endpoint must match listen-client-urls (usually https://127.0.0.1:2379) and the three certs must be the etcd ones, not the apiserver's.

Q14
The control plane is down; you have last night's snapshot. Recover the cluster.
Show Answer
Answer

Restore the snapshot to a new data-dir and repoint etcd.yaml (the §11.4 flow). Since kubectl is down, you work entirely on the node; the kubelet brings etcd then the apiserver back from the restored data.

Explanation

The cluster returns to the snapshot's point-in-time — anything created after the snapshot is lost, which is why backup frequency matters.

Q15
etcd raises alarm:NOSPACE and the cluster won't take writes. Fix it.
Show Answer
Answer
NOSPACE recovery
e endpoint status -w table          # note the current revision
e compact <rev>                      # drop old MVCC history
e defrag                            # return freed pages to disk
e alarm disarm                      # clear the alarm → writes resume
Explanation

MVCC history filled the backend quota. Compact removes old revisions, defrag reclaims the disk, and disarm lifts the read-only alarm. Then set --auto-compaction to prevent a repeat.

Q16
Confirm a Secret is actually encrypted in etcd (after enabling encryption at rest).
Show Answer
Answer
read the raw etcd key
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/easypj-dev/easypj-secret \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=… --cert=… --key=… | hexdump -C | head
# encrypted → begins  k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:key1:…   (not readable text)
Explanation

Reading the raw key bypasses the apiserver's decryption, so you see what's truly on disk. k8s:enc:aescbc = encrypted; plaintext keys/values = not.

Q17
Which etcd member is the leader?
Show Answer
Answer
find leader
e endpoint status -w table --cluster
# the IS LEADER column shows true for one member
Explanation

--cluster queries every member; the table's IS LEADER column identifies the current Raft leader (the one handling writes).

Q18
A 3-member etcd loses 2 members. What state is it in, and how do you recover?
Show Answer
Answer

It has lost quorum (only 1 of 3, < the 2 needed) → etcd is read-only/unavailable and the control plane stalls. Recover by restoring a snapshot on the survivor with --force-new-cluster, then re-adding members.

Explanation

Without a majority etcd refuses writes to stay consistent. --force-new-cluster re-bootstraps a single-member cluster from the data so you can rebuild HA.

Q19
Find the etcd data directory currently in use.
Show Answer
Answer
find data-dir
grep data-dir /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
# - --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd
Explanation

The flag in the manifest is authoritative; the matching hostPath volume mounts that same directory into the etcd pod.

Q20
After a restore, nothing changed — the old data is still there. What did you miss?
Show Answer
Answer

You updated the --data-dir flag but not the hostPath volume (or vice-versa), so etcd still mounted the old directory. Fix both in etcd.yaml so they point at the restored dir.

Explanation

The flag tells etcd where to look inside the pod; the hostPath decides what the node actually mounts there. They must agree, or the restore is invisible.

📌 Chapter 11 Visual Summary — the cluster's memory, saved & restorable
   🗄️ etcd = the cluster's memory   (/registry/* — every object; Secrets unencrypted by default)
        │  Raft: leader + followers · quorum N/2+1 · odd members (3→tolerate 1, 5→tolerate 2)
        ▼
   BACKUP   ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /opt/backup.db  --endpoints --cacert --cert --key
        │   verify → snapshot status --write-table
        │
   ─ ─ ─│─ ─ ─ ─ 💥 DISASTER ─ ─ ─ ─
        ▼
   RESTORE  etcdctl snapshot restore … --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-RESTORED   (a NEW dir!)
        │   edit etcd.yaml:  --data-dir  AND  hostPath volume  → BOTH
        ▼
   🤖 kubelet restarts etcd → ✅ cluster back at the snapshot point
   SECURE   TLS in transit (default) · EncryptionConfiguration + --encryption-provider-config (at rest)   ☸️

In words: etcd is the only place cluster state lives, kept consistent by Raft (writes commit on a majority; members are odd so quorum is meaningful). A backup is one snapshot save with the endpoint and three TLS certs — always verified with snapshot status. A restore reads that snapshot into a new data-dir, and you repoint the etcd static pod by editing etcd.yaml in two places.

The takeaway: memorise the four backup inputs and the two restore edits, and disaster recovery is a 2-minute, free-marks task. Then secure what you backed up — TLS protects the wire, and EncryptionConfiguration protects Secrets at rest so a leaked snapshot isn't a breach.

Chapter 12 · Managing the Control Plane

The control plane runs as pods — specifically static pods the kubelet manages from files on disk. That makes managing it a matter of reading logs and editing manifests, often with the apiserver (and kubectl) down. This chapter is where Cluster Architecture meets Troubleshooting: inspect health with and without kubectl, modify components safely, and recover from a bad edit.

  • ✅ Inspect control-plane health — with kubectl, and with crictl + journalctl when it's down
  • ✅ Modify a component safely: back up → edit → wait → verify → recover
  • ✅ Tune the scheduler & controller-manager (profiles, PriorityClass, eviction timing)
  • ✅ The three extension interfaces as a set: CRI · CNI · CSI
🎓 CKA Relevance
Cluster Architecture 25% Troubleshooting 30% control-plane recovery CORE TASK
🎯 Debugging when kubectl itself is dead

The defining skill here is working without kubectl — because a control-plane problem often takes the apiserver offline. The exam loves "the control plane is broken, fix it."

  • kubectl works → kubectl get pods -n kube-system + component logs.
  • kubectl is dead → on the node: sudo crictl ps -a, sudo crictl logs <id>, journalctl -u kubelet.
  • Recovery is always: make the manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ valid — the kubelet does the rest.

12.1 The Control Plane as Static Pods

On a kubeadm cluster, the control plane isn't a set of system services — it's four static pods. The kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and keeps a pod running for each YAML there. No scheduler, no Deployment, no apiserver is involved in their lifecycle — which is exactly why they can bring the cluster up before the apiserver exists, and why you manage them by editing files.

/etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — edit a file, the kubelet restarts the pod
   /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
     ├─ etcd.yaml                     ┐
     ├─ kube-apiserver.yaml           ├─ 🤖 the kubelet WATCHES this directory
     ├─ kube-controller-manager.yaml  │     edit a file   → pod auto-restarts (~30-60s)
     └─ kube-scheduler.yaml           ┘     remove a file → pod is deleted
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   each running static pod is reflected into the API as a read-only "mirror pod"
   (that's why `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` shows kube-apiserver-<node> etc.)
   ⚠️ a YAML typo here = the apiserver won't start = kubectl dies. Fix the file → kubelet recovers it.
📖 Static pod vs mirror pod

The kubelet runs the static pod directly from the file. It also creates a mirror pod in the apiserver so the pod is visible via kubectl — but that mirror is read-only: kubectl delete pod kube-apiserver-<node> just makes the kubelet recreate it. To actually stop one, move its manifest out of the directory (a handy trick to force-restart a component: mv … /tmp; sleep 5; mv … back).

static pod vs regular pod — how each is managed
   REGULAR POD                                  STATIC POD
   ┌───────────────────────────┐               ┌───────────────────────────┐
   │ kubectl apply ─▶ apiserver │               │ YAML placed in            │
   │      ─▶ etcd               │               │ /etc/kubernetes/manifests │
   │           │                │               │        │                  │
   │           ▼                │               │        ▼                  │
   │ scheduler assigns a node   │               │ kubelet detects the file  │
   │           │                │               │ & runs the pod directly    │
   │           ▼                │               │ on THIS node              │
   │ kubelet runs the pod       │               │                           │
   │ ✅ managed by the apiserver │               │ ✅ managed by the kubelet  │
   │ ✅ can run on any node      │               │ ❌ only the local node     │
   │ ✅ kubectl delete works     │               │ ❌ kubectl delete = no-op  │
   │ ✅ can be scaled            │               │ ❌ cannot be scaled        │
   └───────────────────────────┘               └───────────────────────────┘
   the apiserver creates a read-only "mirror pod" for each static pod so it shows in kubectl.
1
File placed

YAML dropped in the manifests dir

2
kubelet detects

inotify + periodic resync

3
Mirror created

read-only copy POSTed to the API

4
Auto-restart

edit the file → pod recreated

5
File removed

delete the file → pod deleted

💥 What breaks when each component fails

Component downWhat still worksWhat breaks
kube-apiserverrunning pods keep runningALL kubectl, all controllers, all scheduling — the cluster is "frozen"
etcdrunning pods keep runningapiserver can't read/write state → effectively a dead control plane
kube-schedulerexisting pods run; kubectl worksNEW pods stay Pending (nothing assigns them a node)
kube-controller-managerexisting pods run; kubectl worksno self-healing — a deleted pod isn't recreated, nodes aren't marked NotReady, etc.
kubelet (a node)other nodes finethat node goes NotReady; its pods aren't managed
💡 This matrix IS the diagnosis

"New pods stuck Pending but kubectl works" → scheduler. "Deleted pods don't come back" → controller-manager. "kubectl itself is dead" → apiserver or etcd. Reading the symptom backwards to the component is half of every control-plane troubleshooting task.

12.2 Inspecting Control-Plane Health

How you inspect the control plane depends on whether the apiserver is up. When it is, kubectl shows everything; when it isn't, you drop to the node and talk to the container runtime and the kubelet directly.

when kubectl WORKS
kubectl get pods -n kube-system            # every control-plane + addon pod
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -E 'apiserver|etcd|scheduler|controller'
kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-scheduler-control-plane   # a component's logs
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'        # apiserver self-check, per gate
kubectl get componentstatuses             # legacy/deprecated, but still appears on the exam
when kubectl is DEAD (on the node)
sudo crictl ps -a | grep -E 'apiserver|etcd|scheduler|controller'   # container states (incl. exited)
sudo crictl logs <container-id>            # WHY a component is crash-looping
sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 50 --no-pager  # the kubelet's view (static-pod errors)
ls -l /etc/kubernetes/manifests/          # are the manifests present & intact?
sudo crictl ps                            # is the apiserver container even running?
ComponentHealth endpoint (on the node)Secure port
kube-apiservercurl -k https://localhost:6443/readyz?verbose6443
kube-schedulercurl -k https://localhost:10259/healthz10259
kube-controller-managercurl -k https://localhost:10257/healthz10257
etcdetcdctl endpoint health (TLS) — or https://localhost:2379/health2379 / 2380
kubeletcurl -k https://localhost:10250/healthz10250
📖 The health endpoints

Each component serves liveness/readiness over HTTP: /healthz (overall), /livez (alive), /readyz (ready to serve) — add ?verbose to see each individual check. The apiserver's readyz is what a load balancer probes before sending traffic to a control-plane node; a single failing gate there explains an "intermittent apiserver."

⚠️ crictl needs its endpoint

If crictl warns about the runtime endpoint, set it: export CONTAINER_RUNTIME_ENDPOINT=unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock (or put it in /etc/crictl.yaml). crictl is your apiserver-independent window into what containers are actually doing on the node.

12.3 Modifying Components Safely

Changing any control-plane component means editing its manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. The kubelet restarts the pod on save — so a good edit is invisible and a bad one takes the component down. The same five-step ritual makes it safe every time.

/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml (excerpt)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: kube-apiserver
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  containers:
  - command:                              # ← ALL the apiserver flags live here
    - kube-apiserver
    - --advertise-address=192.168.56.10
    - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction
    - --etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379
    - --etcd-cafile=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt
    - --service-cluster-ip-range=10.96.0.0/12
    - --tls-cert-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt
    - --tls-private-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.key
    image: registry.k8s.io/kube-apiserver:v1.34.0
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/pki      # ← cert files mounted into the pod
      name: k8s-certs
      readOnly: true
  hostNetwork: true                       # ← uses the node's network directly
  volumes:
  - name: k8s-certs
    hostPath:
      path: /etc/kubernetes/pki           # ← from the node's filesystem
      type: DirectoryOrCreate
📖 Reading this manifest

Two things to internalise: (1) every apiserver setting is just a line in the command: list — adding a flag means adding a list item. (2) the cert files it references are hostPath volumes from the node's /etc/kubernetes/pki — so a flag pointing at a cert that isn't mounted will crash the pod. hostNetwork: true is why the apiserver binds the node's real :6443.

the safe edit ritual — back up → edit → wait → verify → recover
   ① BACK UP    sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml /tmp/
        ▼
   ② EDIT       add/change a --flag under command:  (sudo vim …)
        ▼
   ③ WAIT       ~30-60s — the kubelet kills the old pod & starts a new one
        ▼
   ④ VERIFY     crictl ps | grep <comp>  (new container ID) · get pods -n kube-system
        ▼
   ⑤ RECOVER    broke it? sudo cp /tmp/<file> /etc/kubernetes/manifests/  → kubelet relaunches
control plane · modify a component
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml /tmp/   # ① back up
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml       # ② edit a flag
watch -n2 'sudo crictl ps | grep controller'    # ③/④ wait for a new container ID
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-$(hostname) | tail   # verify it's healthy
sudo cp /tmp/kube-controller-manager.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/  # ⑤ recover if needed
🚨 A typo in kube-apiserver.yaml is special

It takes kubectl down with it, so you can't verify or recover through kubectl — work on the node with crictl logs and restore the backup. This is the same recovery you drilled in Ch 10 §10.3; the apiserver is the one component where the backup isn't optional.

12.4 Scheduler & Controller-Manager Tuning

Two control-plane components have behaviour you'll occasionally tune: the scheduler (how pods are placed) and the controller-manager (how fast the cluster reacts to node failures). Both are configured the same way — flags in their static-pod manifest — and both elect a single active leader.

📋
kube-scheduler

Assigns pods to nodes via filter → score → bind. Tune with scheduler profiles (--config, custom plugin weights) and influence priority with PriorityClass objects (higher priority can preempt lower).

🔄
kube-controller-manager

Runs the reconciliation loops. Key timing flags: --node-monitor-grace-period (how long before a silent node is marked NotReady) and the eviction timing that follows.

Flag (component)DefaultWhat it controls
--node-monitor-grace-period (c-m)~50show long without a kubelet heartbeat before a node → NotReady
--node-monitor-period (c-m)5show often node status is checked
taint-based eviction (tolerationSeconds)300show long a pod tolerates a NotReady/unreachable node before eviction
--leader-elect (sched & c-m)trueonly one replica is active at a time (HA via a Lease)
a PriorityClass (so critical pods win)
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: easypj-critical
value: 1000000             # higher = scheduled first, can preempt lower-priority pods
globalDefault: false
description: "for easypj's must-run web tier"
📖 When you'd touch these

Lowering --node-monitor-grace-period makes the cluster react to dead nodes faster (quicker pod rescheduling) at the cost of being twitchier on flaky networks. PriorityClass + preemption guarantees critical workloads get a node even when the cluster is full. Custom scheduler profiles let one scheduler run multiple policies (Ch 14 covers placement in depth).

12.5 The Extension Interfaces — CRI · CNI · CSI

Kubernetes ships almost no opinion about how to run containers, network pods, or attach storage. Instead it defines three pluggable interfaces and lets you choose the implementation. Knowing the trio as a set explains how the whole system fits together — and why "the runtime/network/storage" is always someone's plugin, not built-in.

three sockets that make Kubernetes pluggable
   🤖 kubelet ───CRI──▶ 🐳 container runtime     "run this container"     (containerd · CRI-O)
   📦 pod     ───CNI──▶ 🌐 network plugin        "give this pod an IP & routes"  (Calico · Cilium · Flannel)
   💽 volume  ───CSI──▶ 🗄️ storage driver        "attach/mount this volume"   (EBS · Ceph · local-path)
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   each is a stable API contract → swap the implementation without changing Kubernetes itself.
InterfaceStands forWho calls itExamples
CRIContainer Runtime Interfacethe kubelet, to run containerscontainerd, CRI-O
CNIContainer Network Interfacethe kubelet, on pod create, to wire networkingCalico, Cilium, Flannel (Ch 9 §9.4)
CSIContainer Storage Interfacekubelet + controllers, to provision/attach/mount volumesAWS EBS, Ceph, local-path (Ch 22)
📖 Why three separate interfaces?

Decoupling lets each layer evolve and compete independently — you can run containerd with Cilium and the EBS CSI driver, or any other mix, and Kubernetes neither knows nor cares. It's the same extensibility philosophy as API groups and CRDs: a stable contract at the boundary, swappable implementations behind it. CRI failures show as pods stuck creating; CNI failures as NotReady/no pod IPs; CSI failures as volumes stuck attaching.

Under the Hood — leader election & how static pods appear in the API

Two mechanics explain how the control plane stays both highly available and visible: the scheduler and controller-manager use leader election so only one is ever active, and the kubelet creates a mirror pod so each static pod shows up in kubectl.

   LEADER ELECTION (scheduler & controller-manager, when you run more than one)
     every replica races to update a Lease object:
       kube-system/kube-scheduler   ·   kube-system/kube-controller-manager
     the one that holds the Lease is ACTIVE; others stand by, watching renewTime
     leader dies → its Lease expires (~15s) → a standby grabs it → becomes active
       (this is why HA control planes run 3 of each, but only ONE does work at a time)

   STATIC POD → MIRROR POD
     kubelet runs /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml directly (no scheduler)
     kubelet also POSTs a read-only "mirror pod" to the apiserver → kubectl can SEE it
     deleting the mirror pod doesn't stop it — the kubelet just recreates it from the file
🔑 Why this matters: on an HA cluster, "the scheduler isn't scheduling" might mean the active leader is wedged while standbys wait — check kubectl -n kube-system get lease to see who holds it and when it last renewed. And knowing static pods are file-driven is the whole recovery model: you never kubectl delete a control-plane pod to fix it — you fix its file.
Beyond the basicsWhat to know
lease timing--leader-elect-lease-duration/-renew-deadline/-retry-period tune failover speed vs stability; defaults give ~15s failover.
secure ports & bind-addresscomponents serve metrics/health on 10257/10259 bound to 127.0.0.1 by default; --bind-address exposes them (rarely wanted).
health gates/livez?verbose and /readyz?verbose list every individual check — invaluable for "apiserver is up but not ready."
profiling/metrics--profiling (off in hardened clusters) and the /metrics endpoint feed Prometheus (Part 13).
kubelet staticPodPaththe watched directory is set by staticPodPath in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml — point it elsewhere and that's where static pods come from.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • The control plane runs AS static pods — 4 manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/; the kubelet owns their lifecycle and auto-restarts on a file change (~30-60s).
  • Diagnose by symptom: Pending pods → scheduler; no self-healing → controller-manager; kubectl dead → apiserver/etcd.
  • When kubectl is down, debug on the node with crictl ps -a + crictl logs + journalctl -u kubelet.
  • Modify safely: back up → edit → wait → verify → recover. A typo in kube-apiserver.yaml takes kubectl with it.
  • CRI · CNI · CSI are the three plug points: runtime · network · storage.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Traps
  • Editing the wrong manifest or forgetting to back up first.
  • Not waiting ~30-60s for the kubelet to restart the pod before declaring it broken.
  • apiserver typo kills kubectl — recover on the node, not through kubectl.
  • Deleting a control-plane pod with kubectl — the kubelet just recreates the mirror; move the file instead.
  • Confusing the symptoms — Pending (scheduler) vs no-recreate (controller-manager).
⚡ Speed Tips
  • apiserver down? sudo crictl ps -a | grep apiserver → crictl logs <id> → fix the file.
  • Force-restart a component: sudo mv <manifest> /tmp; sleep 5; sudo mv /tmp/<manifest> back.
  • kubectl -n kube-system get lease to see which scheduler/c-m is the active leader.
  • Always cp … /tmp before any control-plane manifest edit.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 12)

control-plane management toolkit
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/             # the 4 control-plane static pods
kubectl get pods -n kube-system ; kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$(hostname)
sudo crictl ps -a ; sudo crictl logs <id>     # when kubectl is down
sudo journalctl -u kubelet -f
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/<comp>.yaml /tmp/   # back up before editing
kubectl -n kube-system get lease          # who holds leader election
🧪 Drill — add a flag to the controller-manager, verify, then revert

No peeking — practise the safe-edit ritual on a non-fatal component:

  1. Back up kube-controller-manager.yaml to /tmp.
  2. Add --node-monitor-grace-period=20s and save.
  3. Wait for the pod to restart; verify the flag is live and the component is healthy.
  4. Restore the backup; confirm it's back to normal.
Show solution
terminal (control-plane node)
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml /tmp/
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager.yaml
# add under command:  - --node-monitor-grace-period=20s
watch -n2 'sudo crictl ps | grep controller'        # new container ID appears
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-controller-manager-$(hostname) \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].command}' | tr ',' '\n' | grep node-monitor
# revert
sudo cp /tmp/kube-controller-manager.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/

🧠 Chapter 12 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Control-plane management recall — each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
List the control-plane static pods and the directory they live in.
Show Answer
Answer

etcd.yaml, kube-apiserver.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml — all in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.

Explanation

The kubelet watches that directory and keeps one pod running per file; ls it to confirm what's present.

Q2
The scheduler is down — what's the symptom on new pods, and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

New pods stay Pending with no node assigned (existing pods keep running, kubectl works). Fix: check kube-scheduler.yaml and the pod's logs (crictl logs if needed) — usually a bad flag or a manifest that was moved/corrupted.

Explanation

Only the scheduler assigns spec.nodeName; without it, nothing binds pods to nodes.

Q3
Add a --feature-gates=... flag to a component safely.
Show Answer
Answer
safe edit
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml /tmp/    # back up
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml        # add - --feature-gates=...
sudo crictl ps | grep scheduler                              # wait for new ID
Explanation

Every component is configured the same way: edit its manifest's command: list, save, let the kubelet restart it — always after a backup.

Q4
ALL control-plane components appear down — what's your debugging order?
Show Answer
Answer

Work bottom-up on the node: (1) systemctl status kubelet + journalctl -u kubelet (is the kubelet even running?), (2) ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (are the manifests there?), (3) crictl ps -a + crictl logs per container (why each is failing).

Explanation

If the kubelet is down, nothing static-pod runs — fix that first. Otherwise it's per-manifest errors the kubelet's journal and crictl reveal.

Q5
Change the kubelet's staticPodPath (where it looks for static pods).
Show Answer
Answer
node
sudo vim /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml       # staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests
sudo systemctl restart kubelet
Explanation

staticPodPath is a kubelet config setting; it defines the watched directory. Change it and the kubelet sources static pods from the new path after a restart.

Q6
Scheduler vs controller-manager — one job each.
Show Answer
Answer

Scheduler: assigns unscheduled pods to nodes (filter → score → bind). Controller-manager: runs the reconciliation loops that keep actual state matching desired (recreate pods, mark nodes NotReady, etc.).

Explanation

Scheduler decides where; controller-manager makes desired = actual everywhere else.

Q7
Check a component's health endpoint.
Show Answer
Answer
health
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'         # apiserver, per-gate
curl -k https://127.0.0.1:10259/healthz     # scheduler (on the node)
Explanation

Components serve /healthz, /livez, /readyz; ?verbose lists each check so you see exactly which gate is failing.

Q8
The controller-manager is crash-looping — where do you look?
Show Answer
Answer
diagnose
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-$(hostname)   # if kubectl works
sudo crictl ps -a | grep controller ; sudo crictl logs <id>       # if not
Explanation

Usual causes: a bad flag you added, a missing cert/file the manifest references, or a wrong --kubeconfig path. The logs name it.

Q9
Create a static pod on a worker node, then remove it.
Show Answer
Answer
on the worker
sudo kubectl run dbg --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml \
  | sudo tee /etc/kubernetes/manifests/dbg.yaml    # drop a pod manifest in the dir
# it appears as dbg-<nodename> (a mirror pod). To remove:
sudo rm /etc/kubernetes/manifests/dbg.yaml         # kubelet deletes the pod
Explanation

Any manifest in the kubelet's staticPodPath becomes a static pod — not just control-plane ones. Removing the file is how you delete it (kubectl can't).

Q10
Match CRI / CNI / CSI to runtime / network / storage.
Show Answer
Answer
InterfaceLayer
CRIcontainer runtime (containerd, CRI-O)
CNIpod network (Calico, Cilium, Flannel)
CSIstorage drivers (EBS, Ceph, local-path)
Explanation

Three pluggable contracts: the kubelet uses CRI to run containers and CNI to network pods; CSI handles volume attach/mount.

⚙️ Chapter 12 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style control-plane troubleshooting with the real commands.

Q11
kubectl returns "connection refused." Is it the apiserver or the kubelet? Diagnose.
Show Answer
Answer
on the node
sudo crictl ps -a | grep apiserver        # is the apiserver container up/exited?
sudo crictl logs <apiserver-id>            # why it exited
systemctl status kubelet                   # is the kubelet (which runs it) alive?
Explanation

If the kubelet is down, no static pod (incl. apiserver) runs — fix the kubelet first. If the kubelet is up but the apiserver container crash-loops, it's the manifest.

Q12
New pods are all Pending. Restore scheduling.
Show Answer
Answer
fix the scheduler
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler   # crashloop/absent?
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$(hostname)   # or crictl logs
# fix the flag/manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml (restore /tmp backup)
Explanation

Pending-everywhere is the scheduler signature. Once it's healthy, the backlog of Pending pods schedules automatically.

Q13
Force-restart the apiserver without deleting any objects.
Show Answer
Answer
move-and-return the manifest
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/
sleep 10                                   # kubelet stops the pod
sudo mv /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/   # kubelet starts it fresh
Explanation

Moving the manifest out and back triggers a clean restart — useful after changing a referenced cert/config the apiserver only reads at startup.

Q14
Find which scheduler replica is the active leader.
Show Answer
Answer
leader election
kubectl -n kube-system get lease kube-scheduler -o yaml | grep holderIdentity
Explanation

The holderIdentity on the Lease names the active leader; renewTime shows it's alive. Standbys watch this and take over if it stops renewing.

Q15
Someone deleted kube-scheduler.yaml. Regenerate it.
Show Answer
Answer
regenerate just one component
sudo kubeadm init phase control-plane scheduler
# re-renders /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml; kubelet starts it
Explanation

kubeadm's init phase sub-commands rebuild individual pieces — far safer than a full re-init when only one manifest is lost.

Q16
The apiserver is up but /readyz reports one failing gate. Investigate.
Show Answer
Answer
per-gate health
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'
# [+]ping ok ... [-]etcd failed ... readyz check failed
Explanation

A failing etcd gate points at the etcd connection; a failing poststarthook at a startup task. The verbose output names the exact subsystem to chase.

Q17
Nodes flap NotReady→Ready on a slow network. Make the cluster less twitchy.
Show Answer
Answer

Raise --node-monitor-grace-period on the controller-manager (e.g. to 80s) so brief heartbeat gaps don't flip a node NotReady. Edit kube-controller-manager.yaml (back up first).

Explanation

Trade-off: a longer grace period tolerates flaky networks but reacts slower to genuinely-dead nodes. Tune to the environment.

Q18
Identify the container runtime a node is using.
Show Answer
Answer
runtime
kubectl get nodes -o wide        # CONTAINER-RUNTIME column → containerd://1.7.x
sudo crictl version              # RuntimeName: containerd
Explanation

The node object reports the CRI runtime; crictl version/info confirms it on the node itself.

Q19
A worker's pods are all stuck ContainerCreating. Which interface is likely at fault?
Show Answer
Answer

Usually CNI (the kubelet can't set up the pod sandbox network) or CRI (runtime down). Check: kubectl describe pod events for failed to set up sandbox … cni, the CNI DaemonSet pods, and systemctl status containerd.

Explanation

ContainerCreating = the kubelet is stuck before "running": no network (CNI), no runtime (CRI), or an unmountable volume (CSI). The pod's Events name which.

Q20
You added a bad scheduler flag; kubectl still works but the scheduler crash-loops. Roll it back.
Show Answer
Answer
rollback
sudo cp /tmp/kube-scheduler.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/   # restore backup
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler             # Running again ✅
Explanation

The scheduler being down doesn't kill kubectl (the apiserver is fine), so you can verify the recovery normally — restore the backup and the kubelet relaunches a healthy pod.

📌 Chapter 12 Visual Summary — the control plane as static pods + the 3 plug points
   /etc/kubernetes/manifests/   ── 🤖 kubelet watches ──▶  edit a file → pod auto-restarts (~30-60s)
     etcd.yaml · kube-apiserver.yaml · kube-controller-manager.yaml · kube-scheduler.yaml
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   DIAGNOSE by symptom:   Pending pods → scheduler   ·   no self-healing → controller-manager
                          kubectl dead → apiserver/etcd  ·  node NotReady → kubelet
   WHEN kubectl IS DOWN:  sudo crictl ps -a · crictl logs <id> · journalctl -u kubelet  →  fix the FILE
   PLUG POINTS:   kubelet ─CRI─▶ runtime   ·   pod ─CNI─▶ network   ·   volume ─CSI─▶ storage          ☸️

In words: the kubeadm control plane is four static pods the kubelet runs from files — so you manage it by editing those files, and a good edit just restarts the pod. You diagnose by mapping the symptom to the component (Pending → scheduler, no healing → controller-manager, dead kubectl → apiserver/etcd), and when kubectl is gone you drop to crictl + journalctl on the node. Recovery is always "make the manifest valid."

The takeaway: back up before every control-plane edit, wait for the restart, and read the runtime/kubelet directly when the apiserver is down. And remember the three interfaces — CRI · CNI · CSI — are what make every layer of Kubernetes swappable.

🟡 Part 3 · Recap · Complete

Cluster Installation & Configuration — What You Now Know

You arrived able to drive a cluster; you leave able to build, configure, protect, and repair one. From bare Linux nodes you can stand up a multi-node cluster with kubeadm, tune the control plane by editing static-pod manifests, snapshot & restore etcd, and recover when the apiserver itself is down — the core of the CKA's 25% Cluster Architecture domain.

🔑 Part 3 — Key Takeaways

  • kubeadm (Ch 9): prep every node (swap off · modules · sysctl · containerd SystemdCgroup · toolchain+hold) → kubeadm init the CP → install a CNI (nodes stay NotReady until then) → kubeadm join workers. Save/regenerate the join command.
  • Config (Ch 10): configure the control plane by editing static-pod manifests in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ (kubelet auto-restarts); kubelet via config.yaml + systemd; admission runs mutating → validating; API = core /api/v1 vs named /apis/grp/ver.
  • etcd (Ch 11): it holds ALL state — snapshot save (endpoint + 3 TLS certs) + restore (NEW data-dir, repoint etcd.yaml twice) is the #1 admin skill; quorum = N/2+1, odd members; encrypt Secrets at rest.
  • Control plane (Ch 12): it runs AS static pods — diagnose by symptom, debug with crictl+journalctl when kubectl is down, modify safely (back up→edit→verify→recover).
  • Three plug points: CRI (runtime) · CNI (network) · CSI (storage).
  • 🎯 Exam: 25% lives here; etcd & kubeadm tasks are near-certain free marks once drilled.
  • 🔑 kubeadm init/join/token · etcdctl snapshot save/restore · crictl ps/logs · journalctl -u kubelet
📌 Part 3 Visual Summary — bare nodes → a configured, backed-up, self-managed cluster
   🖥️ bare Linux nodes
        │  Ch 9: prep all → kubeadm init → CNI → kubeadm join
        ▼
   ☸️ multi-node cluster (control plane = static pods in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/)
        │  Ch 10: edit apiserver/kubelet config · admission (mutating▶validating) · API groups
        │  Ch 12: diagnose by symptom · crictl+journalctl when kubectl down · CRI·CNI·CSI
        ▼
   🗄️ Ch 11: etcd snapshot save (+TLS) ──► 💥 disaster ──► snapshot restore (new data-dir) ──► ✅ recovered
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   you now OWN the cluster: build it, bend it to requirements, back it up, and bring it back. ☸️

In words: Part 3 turned you from operator into administrator. You build a cluster from nothing with kubeadm (prep → init → CNI → join), configure its control plane by editing the static-pod manifests the kubelet watches, and protect its memory with etcd snapshot/restore. When things break — even when kubectl itself is gone — you diagnose by symptom and fix the file on the node.

The takeaway: the control plane is files + a watching kubelet + etcd's memory. Master the kubeadm build, the back-up-before-you-edit habit, and the etcd backup/restore dance, and you own the 25% Cluster Architecture domain — the densest scoring ground on the exam.
